Equation (6.1) is the base optimization equation of TinyML since it enrolls the trade‐off between the quality of the predictions and the simplicity of the model design. The equation guides the development of lightweight models with minimum prediction error while controlling complexity. Applying this principle leads to ML functions on resource‐constrained devices for the core goals of this chapter. The term L(f(x;θ),y) is a loss function, which computes the difference between the predicted output (f(x;θ),y) and the actual label y. Minimizing this term increases the accuracy of the model. ∥θ∥2 is a regularization term that penalizes large parameter values to prevent overfitting, where the hyperparameter is responsible for balancing between minimizing the loss function on the training data and keeping the complexity of the model low. It is denoted as minθ for which the objective is to search for the best set of parameters that minimizes the total objective function.

TinyML applications and a few examples, illustrated in Figure 6.2, unveiled such potential in health, agriculture, industrial IoT (IIoT), connected autonomous vehicles, environmental monitoring, and smart home systems. TinyML represents a critical evolution in developing intelligent, resource‐conscious IoT solutions, as marked by the nexus of ML and embedded systems.

TinyML applications span various industries, from predictive maintenance to anomaly detection and asset tracking. For example, [15] presented a TinyML indoor asset‐tracking system based on Bluetooth low energy (BLE) fingerprinting, which reached an accuracy of 88%, increasing to 94% after post‐processing. Similarly, TinyML has been employed for electric vehicle battery health monitoring, providing real‐time predictions of remaining useful life (RUL) and temperature control. Models running on Arduino Nano 33 BLE Sense showed energy efficiency in performing these tasks for battery management [16]. TinyML with online learning (TinyOL) extends traditional TinyML frameworks with the capability for incremental training on streaming data. It empowers the system for continuous learning and adaptation in a dynamic IoT environment by enabling concept drift and device variability challenges [17].

This shift addresses the challenges of traditional ML methods in requiring extensive computational resources and being cloud‐connected, as it will support very low‐power, on‐device inference. TinyML optimizes latency, bandwidth, and data privacy within edge computing environments; hence, its usage is suitable in IoT applications where constant cloud communication is infeasible [18]. A critical enabler of TinyML is the design of specialized workflows and tools targeted for ultra‐low‐power devices. Microcontroller‐class hardware with relatively minimal memory requires lightweight design and deployment processes for ML models. These workflows depend on quantization and pruning to compress ML models with minimal loss of accuracy. The authors propose a closed‐loop workflow for optimizing model deployment, which would iteratively evaluate hardware metrics for model compatibility with microcontroller constraints [19].

The efficiency of ML was further discussed in [20], especially in terms of model size and accuracy with performance latency. The research touches on compression techniques, including quantization and NAS, necessary for deploying ML models in constrained environments. Such innovations form the basis of the work TinyML does to enable devices to have real‐time decision‐making capabilities while reducing energy consumption and prolonging their life [20]. TinyML frameworks, such as TensorFlow Lite for microcontrollers (TFLM) and Edge Impulse, have provided the initial grounds for deploying ML models on resource‐constrained devices. TFLM allows for low‐latency and energy‐efficient operations by optimizing memory allocation for deep neural network (DNN) inference [21]. Further, compiler advancements like TinyTS address the challenges of memory constraints and demonstrate up to 5.92× reductions in peak static random access memory (SRAM) usage [22]. These innovations showcase the critical optimization of intermediate tensor management in resource‐constrained environments.

The importance of embedded intelligence for mobile and wireless networks, such as scalability, energy efficiency, and real‐time decision‐making, was pointed out in [23] with the integration of lightweight ML frameworks into resource‐constrained environments, which is necessary for system adaptability and efficiency. The two main enabling factors of TinyML are lightweight model compression techniques, especially those directed toward embedded hardware. Artificial neural network (ANN)‐based ML is a core enabler of intelligent wireless network operations, citing that an optimized model could work efficiently under the constraints of microcontrollers and IoT devices [24]. The study refers to quantization and pruning that reduce model size and computational requirements, making it possible to deploy such models in real‐time applications on low‐memory, low‐processing devices [24]. Aquila represents a new paradigm in optimization: energy‐aware compression with clustering, in particular. This approach ensures prolonged operation and better routing efficiency in the demanding environments of industrial IoT applications, such as underground coal mines [25].

The author in [23] delves further into how low‐power ML frameworks enhance system reliability and performance in dynamic environments. Later, it was emphasized that TinyML‐enabled systems should balance computational accuracy against resource constraints, especially in autonomous systems and smart agriculture domains. On‐device intelligence greatly benefits these systems by reducing reliance on cloud‐based computation and improving latency and privacy. Similarly, research in [24] demonstrates how TinyML helps in predictive analytics and adaptive resource management, which is key to tackling the heterogeneous demands of modern IoT applications.

Despite its potential, TinyML also faces notable challenges, pointing to the diversity in hardware platforms and the lack of standardized evaluation metrics as major obstacles that complicate deploying universally optimized solutions [23, 24]. In addition to that, it becomes increasingly difficult to reach optimal trade‐offs between accuracy and computational efficiency, most importantly in applications requiring real‐time inference [23–25]. Security and privacy are major concerns, particularly for vertical applications like healthcare and finance. Local processing devices remove risks due to cloud‐based systems; however, secure deployment practices and encryption are active research areas [17, 26].

Energy efficiency is a cornerstone of TinyML research because many devices operate on limited battery power. Quantization and pruning are primary methods to achieve low‐memory and computational requirements without degradation. The continuous learning algorithm balances the model size dynamically for computational load and accuracy, as suggested in [27], enabling negligible accuracy loss while reducing resource usage [5, 7]. Further, tools like Cortex Microcontroller Software Interface Sstandard for Neural Networks (CMSIS‐NN) and STM32Cube.AI optimize DNN inference for ARM Cortex‐M processors, enabling high‐performance ML operations. These tools exemplify the synergy between hardware and software co‐design, where hardware‐aware optimization ensures optimal utilization of microcontroller capabilities [21, 22].

TinyML enables scalable, efficient, and intelligent solutions for IoT and edge applications by leveraging lightweight ML frameworks and advanced compression techniques. Integrating on‐device intelligence reduces dependency on cloud infrastructure while enhancing privacy and energy efficiency. However, overcoming challenges such as hardware heterogeneity and performance benchmarking remains critical to realizing the full potential of TinyML in diverse application domains [5]. These findings highlight the need for ongoing improvements in model optimization and hardware–software co‐design for TinyML to gain further acceptance (Table 6.1).

6.3 TinyML Devices

TinyML devices are an emerging category of microcontroller‐based systems optimized for running ML workloads directly at the edge of the network. These devices normally have very low‐power consumption, compact size, and low cost, making them highly applicable in IoT, healthcare, agriculture, and autonomous systems. Leveraging TinyML capabilities, these devices allow for local data processing, reducing the need for cloud‐based computation and solving issues related to latency, privacy, and energy efficiency.

TinyML devices implement hardware and software optimizations to run ML models within tight resource constraints. On the hardware side, ARM Cortex‐M processors, RISC‐V platforms, and dedicated systems‐on‐chip like the Parallel Ultra‐Low‐Power (PULP)‐based VEGA platform are popular choices [8]. These platforms are power‐optimized for energy efficiency, integrating various techniques such as dynamic voltage scaling, clock gating, and tightly coupled data memory. For instance, the VEGA platform uses a quantization approach to save memory, allowing the system to continuously learn on ultra‐low‐power devices while maintaining accuracy within acceptable limits.

TinyML devices find a wide range of applications in the healthcare sector to develop wearable sensors that continuously monitor health. Devices such as heart rate monitors and pulse oximeters can perform on‐device processing with the help of ML models to identify abnormal events, like irregular heartbeats. These systems reduce dependency on cloud analytics for much faster responses, with the additional benefit of preserving patient privacy. Moreover, Edge Impulse simplifies the complete pipeline from data collection to model deployment and supports efficient health monitoring applications. The TinyML device helps with precision farming to monitor moisture, the temperature of the soil, and the health condition of crops instantaneously. Devices equipped with such models are empowered to analyze all the sensor values and provide actions to be executed to optimize irrigation and decrease water wastage, enhancing yield [7]. The ARM Cortex‐M4 Microcontroller was used for various applications due to its low‐power consumption and robust computational capabilities.

In the case of connected autonomous vehicles (CAV), TinyML devices help process data from sensors like light detection and ranging (LiDAR), radio detection and ranging (RADAR), and cameras directly at the edge. This is very important in lane detection, object recognition, and collision avoidance applications since latency can result in performance degradation. PULP and the STM32 family are platforms optimized for real‐time ML processing on vehicles; these enable quicker decision‐making and reduce dependency on cloud systems. Despite these advantages, TinyML devices have limitations: Memory, computational power, and energy efficiency are the most critical issues. Quantization and pruning techniques and federated learning frameworks are instrumental in overcoming these barriers by minimizing memory usage and enhancing on‐device learning. Besides, microelectronic advancements like the 22‐nm technology used in VEGA illustrate the potential for further improvements in power efficiency and processing capabilities [8].

6.4 TinyML Tools

TinyML tools are instrumental in realizing this vision of ML for resource‐constrained devices to realize real‐time intelligence at the edge [15]. Such tools relate to software frameworks, libraries, and platforms used in the optimization and deployment process of ML models on low‐power devices like microcontrollers and edge sensors [29]. The chapter shall focus on some important TinyML tools and their critical features, roles, and contributions toward the edge AI use case.

6.4.1 TensorFlow Lite for Microcontrollers (TFLM)

TFLM is an extension of the TensorFlow ecosystem. It is explicitly designed to run ML models on microcontrollers with minimal memory and processing power. TFLM reduces the overhead of traditional ML frameworks by focusing on minimal runtime, model quantization, and hardware compatibility [30].

TFLM then utilizes quantization to decrease model weights from 32‐bit floating‐point to 8‐bit integers, which reduces memory and computation. This process could be mathematically expressed by (6.8):

(6.8)

In (6.8), ϖ is the quantized weight, w is the original weight, and s is the scale factor preserving the magnitude of the weights. The key benefit of TFLM is its capability to enable ML on low‐power devices. However, optimizing models to meet microcontrollers' strict memory and latency requirements still presents many challenges [8]. Furthermore, as models become more complex, compatibility with various hardware platforms becomes increasingly difficult to maintain.

6.4.2 Edge Impulse

Edge Impulse is a flexible platform intended to make developing and deploying TinyML models end‐to‐end easier. It allows for data collection, preprocessing, model training, and deployment and is especially fit for applications that require real‐time intelligence at the edge. One of the key features of Edge Impulse is the automation of the preprocessing pipeline that turns raw sensor data into structured input for ML models [31]. This tool generates hardware‐optimized code for various platforms, ensuring low‐latency inference and energy‐efficient operation. Edge Impulse is widely adopted in industrial IoT, where it powers predictive maintenance systems by analyzing vibration data from machinery to detect early signs of wear and tear. It also plays a critical role in agriculture, enabling pest detection and crop health monitoring through real‐time image analysis. Wearable devices in healthcare use Edge Impulse for activity classification and anomaly detection, among other applications, to further enhance the functionality of fitness trackers and health monitors. Although widely praised for its ease of use and automation, Edge Impulse may be limited by its reliance on cloud‐based workflows in environments with restricted connectivity.

6.4.3 PyTorch Mobile

PyTorch Mobile extends the popular PyTorch framework for mobile and embedded systems, bridging the gap from research to deployment. It supports dynamic quantization – a process that incorporates quantization during training that allows models to retain high performance with reduced memory and computational requirements [32]. PyTorch Mobile seamlessly interoperates with models developed in PyTorch; hence, it is the favored choice for researchers going into real‐world deployment. The framework is also particularly good for image recognition tasks, enabling edge devices to classify objects in real time. It is also applied in Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications like chatbots and voice assistants, which enable real‐time speech and text analysis on mobile platforms. PyTorch Mobile empowers augmented reality (AR) applications to detect objects and overlay digital content in real time. While PyTorch Mobile offers flexibility and integration, this comes at the cost of its larger runtime compared to other TinyML tools, such as TFLM, which may limit its usage in ultra‐constrained environments.

6.4.4 TensorFlow Lite (TFL)

TFL is a lightweight version of TensorFlow intended to bring ML capabilities to mobile and embedded platforms. Unlike TFLM, which targets ultra‐low‐power devices, TFL targets devices with moderate computational capabilities, such as smartphones and single‐board computers [8]. It supports a broad set of ML model types, including DNNs, convolutional neural networks (CNNs), and recurrent neural networks (RNNs), and is therefore suitable for many applications. TFL leverages graphics processing units (GPUs), neural processing units (NPUs), and digital signal processors (DSPs) to accelerate inference in terms of speed and energy. The framework finds wide smartphone applications, ranging from on‐device image processing to natural language understanding, enabling photo editing and voice commands without Internet connectivity. In IoT, TFL supports edge sensors for environmental monitoring and predictive maintenance, ensuring timely and efficient decision‐making. However, it has a bigger memory footprint than specialized frameworks like TFLM, which can limit its usage for devices with strict resource constraints.

6.4.5 uTensor

uTensor is a minimalist inference engine built for deploying ML on super‐resource‐constrained microcontrollers. It has very smooth integration with TensorFlow, which means a model trained on TensorFlow can easily be converted into uTensor‐friendly formats for deployment. Due to this fact, it is very lightweight and fits perfectly for battery‐powered IoT devices and distributed sensor networks. For example, environmental monitoring systems use uTensor to process real‐time data from sensor nodes, enabling them to make local decisions independent of cloud resources. It also works effectively in lightweight industrial IoT applications where devices operate on low‐latency decision‐making tasks such as anomaly detection. The customizable nature of uTensor allows developers to optimize the framework for particular hardware requirements. While this minimal runtime comes in handy, the feature set for uTensor is very limited compared to other comprehensive frameworks like TFL or Edge Impulse.

6.4.6 CMSIS‐NN

CMSIS‐NN is a library developed by ARM to optimize neural network (NN) inference on Cortex‐M processors. It aims to enable high‐performance ML operations on microcontrollers by providing highly efficient kernels for various layers, including convolutional, pooling, and fully connected layers. The library is instrumental in reducing computation time and memory footprint, making it ideal for resource‐constrained devices. CMSIS‐NN converts floating‐point neural network models into fixed‐point representations, enabling their efficient execution on Cortex‐M processors. Fixed‐point arithmetic reduces the overhead associated with floating‐point operations, and the convolutional layer's inference time can be expressed in (6.9):

Applications of CMSIS‐NN span across fields like healthcare, including wearable health monitoring systems and industrial IoT, for example, predictive maintenance, and environmental monitoring. At the same time, however, this very advantage of the library limits its adaptability to other platforms due to its reliance on ARM architecture.

6.4.7 STM32Cube.AI and NanoEdge Studio

STM32Cube.AI by STMicroelectronics is a tool designed to let developers run pre‐trained neural networks on STM32 microcontrollers. It supports models generated from TensorFlow, Keras, and Open Neural Network Exchange (ONNX) and allows their conversion into C code compatible with the STM32. STM32Cube.AI offers memory optimizations such as storing weights in external flash and activation buffers in RAM. STMicroelectronics' NanoEdge Studio extends STM32Cube.AI by directly allowing unsupervised learning capabilities on a microcontroller. It provides a virtual environment emulator of the microcontroller, allowing users to test the model before its deployment. In NanoEdge Studio, the runtime update can be easily done with new data and is thus quite effective for real‐world applications such as anomaly detection in predictive maintenance systems.

6.4.8 EmbML

EmbML is a library designed to bring decision trees, neural networks, and support vector machines – supervised learning algorithms – down to the level of low‐cost embedded systems. It allows models created in Scikit‐learn or Weka to be exported into C++ code appropriate for Arduino or Teensy platforms. In applications where low latency is expected in decision‐making, such as smart sensors and environmental monitoring systems, EmbML will be very useful. The main strength of EmbML lies in its flexibility due to the various ML algorithms it supports, but it is relatively less optimized for specific hardware platforms. 6.4.9 FANN on MCU

Fast artificial neural network (FANN) on microcontroller unit (MCU) is an open‐source toolkit for ultra‐low‐power microcontrollers that allows the deployment of neural networks. The focus is to perform neural network execution with a minimum energy consumption while still having high computational efficiency. FANN on MCU relies on the PULP platform, which also supports non‐neural kernels, thus executing with higher performance than traditional neural networks. 6.5 Deployment Procedure of TinyML

The key procedures in deploying TinyML include data collection, preprocessing, feature extraction, model training, deployment, on‐device inference, and continuous improvement. Each of these steps ensures that ML capability is embedded in the edge devices so that real‐time decisions may be made with minimal dependence on cloud computational resources.

Data collection remains a crucial step in creating the base for any application in TinyML. This includes soil moisture, temperature, humidity, and crop health monitoring through agricultural sensors. For example, hyperspectral sensors and thermal cameras can capture precise details about plant stress or nutrient levels, enabling efficient precision farming techniques. In healthcare, wearable devices such as smartwatches, chest straps, and biosensors gather physiological metrics, including heart rate, oxygen saturation (SpO2), and electrocardiogram (ECG) signals. These data streams are crucial for real‐time health monitoring and early diagnosis of chronic conditions. Cameras, LiDAR systems, and ultrasonic sensors in autonomous vehicles collect environmental data such as road conditions and distances of objects, which are crucial for navigation and obstacle detection [33, 34].

Collected data then go through preprocessing to enhance its quality and reliability. Raw data contain a lot of noise and inconsistencies that must be addressed to get an accurate analysis. Filtering, normalization, and data augmentation are some general techniques that could be used in this phase. In agriculture, filtering removes environmental noise from sensor readings, while normalization normalizes the output of various sensors. Wavelet transformation and low‐pass filtering isolate meaningful features such as R–R intervals in ECG signals from healthcare data. Preprocessing in autonomous vehicles requires noise reduction and segmentation of frames for better visibility of objects detected via cameras or LiDAR. TinyML tools such as TFLM and CMSIS‐NN perform these preprocessing steps directly on edge devices, providing an efficient implementation for these processes with minimum power consumption [35, 36].

Feature extraction is the subsequent crucial step, whereby the system identifies the most relevant attributes in the data for further analysis. It simplifies the data by focusing on specific elements crucial for the intended application. Features such as chlorophyll levels, temperature gradients, or pest infestation patterns are extracted in agriculture to monitor crop health and optimize irrigation. Examples of such extracted features in healthcare applications include heart rate variability (HRV), respiration rates, or SpO2 levels used to characterize patients. Object boundaries, lane markers, and road curvature in autonomous vehicles are all feature types that provide the necessary functionality to drive safely. These would be provided as input into various ML models trained on particular tasks [37].

Model training comprises a big portion of the TinyML deployment pipeline. Training usually happens on high‐performance computing systems with software such as TensorFlow, Edge Impulse, or PyTorch [38]. In agriculture, models get trained to classify plant diseases or predict optimal watering times. Healthcare models may involve the identification of irregular heart rhythms or the detection of respiratory anomalies. For autonomous vehicles, training involves object detection models that identify pedestrians, vehicles, and road signs. After training, models are optimized for edge deployment by quantization, which reduces the precision of model weights, and pruning, which removes redundant parameters. These optimizations significantly reduce the model size and computational requirements, making them suitable for deployment on microcontrollers or other resource‐constrained devices [39].

Deployment involves integrating the optimized models into edge devices for real‐time inference. TinyML tools such as TFLM, Edge Impulse, and NanoEdge AI Studio ease this with application programming interfaces (APIs) and frameworks tailored for low‐power hardware. For instance, models deployed on agricultural microcontrollers independently run irrigation systems based on the soil moisture level. Models deployed in healthcare detect anomalies in heart rate or SpO2 and alert caregivers in real time. These models enable real‐time obstacle avoidance and lane navigation for autonomous vehicles, thus providing much safer driving experiences [40, 41].

On‐device inference enables edge devices to independently process incoming data streams with minimum reliance on cloud resources. This is an essential ability for those applications that demand low latency and high reliability. In agriculture, a microcontroller with a deployed TinyML model can immediately adjust the irrigation or fertilization schedule without waiting for instructions from the cloud. Wearables in healthcare can preprocess or analyze data locally, for example, to identify irregular heartbeats, which are especially critical in emergencies. Autonomous vehicles make decisions such as applying brakes upon detection of obstacles with local inference [42].

Continuous monitoring and improvement are crucial to having an effective TinyML system. It involves assessing performance metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score. Any discrepancies or inefficiencies are updated in the models. Techniques like federated learning are employed to update models without compromising data privacy. Federated learning aggregates locally trained models from multiple devices, improving global model accuracy while keeping sensitive data on the device. This approach is of particular value in healthcare, where patient privacy is paramount. In agriculture, models are continuously updated to adapt to the new conditions of the environment, for example, outbreaks of pests or changes in weather conditions. Real‐time updates enable autonomous vehicles to enhance their object detection and navigation in diverse driving environments [43, 44].

In sectors such as agriculture, healthcare, and autonomous vehicles, implementing TinyML will require a structured pipeline from data collection to data preprocessing, feature extraction, model training, deployment, on‐device inference, and continuous improvement. By using tools such as TFL, Edge Impulse, and CMSIS‐NN, the TinyML systems realize real‐time, low‐power intelligence on edge devices. Such a systematic approach reinforces better decision‐making, efficiency in operations, and privacy across multiple domains – a testament to how this little ML can impact reality. Figure 6.4 gives the steps involved in TinyML deployment.

6.5.1 Case Studies of TinyML in the Health Sector Domain

Smart health monitoring systems (SHMSs) revolutionize healthcare by incorporating IoT with TinyML to process data on edge and improve health diagnostics further. Traditional healthcare relied on cloud solutions for data processing, presenting a couple of critical challenges: high latency, reliance on reliable network connections, and privacy exposure in sensitive health data transmission cases. With the advent of TinyML, healthcare applications have transitioned toward decentralized architectures that enable real‐time processing and decision‐making on resource‐constrained devices.

Figure 6.5 illustrates the proposed TinyML approach, which gives an overall view of the SHMS as an application in the health domain, combining local analytics and cloud‐based intelligence. This, therefore, ensures that there is always some form of efficient and timely monitoring of patient health metrics with wearable sensors and TinyML tools and devices to provide an integrated system. TinyML tools such as TFLM, Edge Impulse, and CMSIS‐NN will drive low‐power, edge‐level intelligence, latency minimization, and data privacy. These tools will make it possible to process health data locally while still harnessing the computational power of cloud analytics for advanced insights.

The architecture of the SHMS will be based on two main domains: the local domain, which is responsible for collecting data and preliminary analyses, and the cloud domain, which is responsible for advanced analytics, storage, and application‐level integration. The local domain includes wearable health sensors such as heart rate monitors, pulse oximeters, and ECG devices that constantly collect physiological data. On‐device processing units or microcontrollers become responsible for where the data execute the models of TinyML, taking real‐time analysis. By utilizing ML lightweight models, deploy directly to microcontrollers (TFLM), this can implement real‐time detection of heart‐beating variability anomalies or extreme fluctuations in HRV. Edge Impulse further smooths this process by easing data collection, preprocessing, and model training; hence, it is effective in raw sensor data processing.

In the local domain, resources like microcontrollers or gateways that have TinyML capabilities provide a temporary node for preprocessing and real‐time analysis. Such resources leverage the TinyML models trained with tools such as CMSIS‐NN, an optimized runtime for neural network operations on ARM Cortex‐M processors. For example, the model deployed on the Cortex‐M4 microcontroller can carry out anomaly detection of heart rate and respiration waveforms by using compressed neural network inferences. These local insights are sent to controller services. Controller services handle data flow across the local to cloud domains. Controller services will also take responsibility for coordinating alerts and preliminary health assessments based on local inferences. For instance, if HRV falls below a critical threshold, the system can instantly alert caregivers via mobile notifications.

The cloud domain is important for the SHMS, as it involves complex analysis and long‐term storage. Representational State Transfer (REST) ful APIs are adopted to transmit preprocessed data from the local domain to the cloud. TinyML tools like TFL enable seamless integration with cloud‐based ML models, where advanced analytics algorithms analyze historical and real‐time data to detect patterns indicative of chronic diseases or potential emergencies. For example, analytics in the cloud can identify relationships between HRV trends and stress levels, giving healthcare providers actionable insights. IoT intelligence‐informed analytics unify these models into predictive and prescriptive analytics on patient care. Architecture also contains observer nodes that offer real‐time visualization of the patients' metrics to healthcare providers and caregivers.

Applications powered by Edge Impulse enable these nodes to provide user‐friendly dashboards in which vital health metrics and alerts are presented. Observer nodes can monitor vital signs like heart rate, SpO2, and body temperature. Thus, caregivers will study health trends and quickly act as per alerts. These dashboards ensure healthcare providers have the correct and updated information to make proper decisions. The key differentiating factor of SHMS depends on edge analytics to a greater extent for minimum latency and dependency on cloud services. These TinyML models can be installed on monitoring nodes to make inferences with a local model, reducing continuous data transmission to the cloud. For example, a wearable heart rate monitor can do some preprocessing and directly calculate HRV from the raw data using a model compiled by TFL. For instance, if the computed HRV indicates a probable health issue, the system creates a local alert and enables immediate action. This is especially useful in time‐critical applications, like detecting arrhythmias or sudden drops in oxygen levels.

Edge Impulse and TFL for TinyML enable the SHMS to perform dynamic model updates. In the presence of federated learning, the system aggregates models trained locally from various devices to update the global model with improved accuracy without exposing any raw patient data. This provides a method to enhance the models while keeping private health information confined to the local device.

Apart from accuracy, energy efficiency is another key success factor for SHMS. Given that wearable devices mostly depend on limited battery life, development tools like CMSIS‐NN and TFL have used quantization and pruning methods to attain low computational loads and reduce model size. This will keep the device running for longer periods on a single battery charge without frequent recharges. Quantization, for example, reduces model weights from 32‐bit floating‐point to 8‐bit integers, drastically reducing memory and power consumption. These optimizations are critical to extending the operating life of wearable sensors and microcontrollers in practical healthcare applications. Complementing real‐time monitoring, cloud‐based advanced analytics gives the SHMS retrospective and predictive insights into health data. Deep learning models analyze historical data stored in the cloud for long‐term trends and correlations. For instance, models can be trained to detect arrhythmias or forecast the onset of cardiovascular diseases using a patient's ECG data. TinyML tools seamlessly integrate these cloud‐based models with local devices to enable a cohesive system combining edge and cloud computing strengths.

The SHMS integrates a robust security architecture for sensitive health data protection. RESTful communications from/to the local to/from cloud domains are performed using encryption protocols, like transport layer security (TLS), which guarantees data privacy and is tamper‐proof during transmission. Observer nodes and cloud dashboards use different authentication mechanisms to avoid unauthorized access, adding another layer of protection to sensitive patient information.

The application of TinyML tools in SHMS enhances technical capability and mitigates some of the challenges that most traditional health monitoring systems have been facing. Performing analytics locally minimizes latency and reduces reliance on cloud services, making it more reliable in scenarios with poor network connectivity. The energy‐efficient design of TinyML models ensures that wearable devices can operate continuously without frequent interruptions for recharging. The system will be able to support continuous model improvement through federated learning with no compromise on data privacy.

The integration of tools such as TFL, Edge Impulse, and CMSIS‐NN in the architecture shows the transformational potential of TinyML in smart health applications. The application of these tools within SHMS enables real‐time, scalable, and privacy‐preserving health insights, enabling the healthcare provider to make proactive decisions that improve patient outcomes. The system relies on edge analytics, where critical health issues must be identified and fixed instantaneously, while cloud‐based intelligence provides further detail and long‐term monitoring capability.

Eventually, the system guarantees that healthcare solutions will be delivered with precision, speed, and security to the patient and caregivers via edge‐cloud computing. Further evolution of TinyML technologies will unlock new possibilities in smart health applications and drive innovation in improving the quality of care worldwide.

6.5.2 Case Studies of TinyML in the Agriculture Domain

Smart and precision agriculture has emerged as one of the revolutionary ways to modern farming, adopting advanced technologies like the Internet of Things, ML, and cloud computing to maximize resources, enhance crop yield, and make it more sustainable. The architecture in Figure 6.6 provides an excellent framework for implementing this through the smooth integration of the local and cloud domains to allow for real‐time data collection, analysis, and decision‐making. This case study uses the IoT architecture in a precision agriculture system to demonstrate how sensor nodes, centralized controllers, and cloud‐based analytics can be integrated to present actionable insights for efficient farming. This architecture enhances the efficiency of farming operations. It addresses key challenges such as water conservation, pest management, and predictive decision‐making, making it an invaluable tool in the agricultural domain.

The architecture is tailored for smart and precision agriculture and provides a comprehensive framework for managing data flow, analytics, and decision‐making in modern farming. The diagram represents a well‐structured integration of local and cloud domains, enabling real‐time monitoring and analytics to optimize agricultural practices. This case study explains the components of the architecture, their functions, and their importance in ensuring a scalable and efficient system for precision agriculture.

It originates in the local domain of the system, where data are collected directly from the agricultural environment. At this level, the main data acquisition devices are the sensor nodes, which constantly monitor key parameters regarding soil moisture, temperature, humidity, and light. In general, sensor nodes form an integral part of precision agriculture since they provide, on the one hand, direct knowledge about the soil status in almost real time. For instance, soil moisture sensors placed across a farm in different plots collect granular data about water availability, thus enabling farmers to optimize irrigation schedules. Temperature and humidity sensors likewise provide vital information on threats like frost or heat stress, thus enabling farmers to take timely preventive measures.

The sensor nodes transmit the collected data to field resource nodes acting as local aggregators and preprocessors. These resource nodes act like brokers, combining data from several sensor nodes into something less redundant and more understandable, ready for analysis. For example, readings from moisture sensors spread out over different parts of the field can be combined to describe the overall soil water status. These resource nodes also conduct basic preprocessing tasks, such as filtering noise and normalizing sensor readings to ensure the data are accurate and usable.

6.5.2.1 Irrigation Controller

This module controls real‐time irrigation decisions based on the data gathered and processed in the local domain. Analyzing moisture levels and weather data, the irrigation controller can switch the irrigation systems on or off accordingly. This system also offers more than the above; it ensures that should the soil moisture in any plot fall below a threshold, irrigation is automatically turned on to maintain optimum soil conditions. This reduces water loss and ensures crops have appropriate hydration levels, enhancing yield and sustainability.

The farmer dashboard acts as an interface between the system and the end user. Mobile or web applications allow the monitoring of all field data in real time, receiving alarms, and managing different systems like irrigation. The dashboard visualizes, in a user‐friendly way, critical metrics such as soil moisture, temperature, and crop health to assist farmers in decision‐making. The farmer can look into real‐time data about the dry parts of the field and, from this dashboard, turn on irrigation in that part of the field.

The centralized controller bridges the local and cloud domains, serving as the core node to orchestrate data flow in the system. This layer handles the interaction between the field devices and the cloud infrastructure. For example, it gathers data from all resource nodes, conducts further preprocessing, and ensures that only relevant data are sent to the cloud. By reducing unnecessary data transmission, the centralized controller minimizes bandwidth use and ensures efficiency in the system's operation.

The cloud domain is where advanced analytics and long‐term data storage occur. The cloud gateway facilitates secure communication between the centralized controller and the cloud infrastructure, using REST/WebSocket protocols to ensure reliable data transfer. This gateway is crucial for large‐scale farming operations, where vast amounts of data are collected from multiple fields. For instance, data from various plots can be securely transmitted to the cloud for further analysis.

The database in the architecture represents the farm data cloud, which stores real‐time and historical agricultural data down to the last detail of soil moisture, crop health metrics, and weather patterns. The availability of historical data provides a lot of value in identifying trends and making predictive decisions. For instance, historical weather data can be combined with current soil conditions to forecast irrigation needs for the days ahead. Furthermore, long‐term information on crop health will enable farmers to detect recurring problems, such as pest infestation or nutrient deficiency, and thus take remedial measures in advance.

The crop health analytics component is powered by advanced ML algorithms combined with IoT intelligence. It analyzes data from the farm data cloud to present actionable insights. For example, predictive models analyze soil conditions and weather patterns to recommend optimal planting and harvesting times. Likewise, prescriptive analytics can help with specific recommendations regarding which fertilizers and when to apply them to maximize crop yield. This is critical in precision agriculture, where small changes in farming practices can substantially change productivity and sustainability.

The centralized farm dashboard, extended from the cloud domain, provides real‐time visualization for farmers and agricultural managers based on data and analytics results. It summarizes data from various plots into a digestible form. Farmers, for example, can view line graphs of soil moisture over time, maps with field areas requiring attention, and warnings regarding drought or pests. The dashboard centralizes the information, allowing farmers to make confident decisions based on the data.

The integration of many monitoring nodes ensures the farm's comprehensiveness of the whole area. These nodes will be placed in different sections within the farm to monitor parameters such as soil fertility, water distribution, and pest activities. For instance, a node on one plot can report an outbreak of pests and send an alarm, which the farmer will work to address before the disease spreads to other areas.

The cloud storage and analytics module combines all elements for holistic insights. This module will integrate real‐time sensor data with historical data to create comprehensive reports and forecasts. For example, integrating soil moisture data with weather forecasts allows farmers to plan irrigation events in consideration of forecasted rainfall. In the same way, data on crop health from previous seasons can be used to create better pest management strategies and efficient resource allocation.

6.6 Lesson Learned and Prospects

TinyML has changed how ML is deployed on resource‐constrained devices, enabling a wide range of applications, from agriculture and healthcare to connected autonomous vehicles. The integration of lightweight models optimized for low‐power operation granted TinyML real‐time intelligence on edge devices, minimizing cloud computing while addressing key latency, energy efficiency, and data privacy challenges. This chapter provides insight into the lessons learned from the practical implementation of TinyML and speculates about its future across various domains. As the field matures, there is great potential to scale TinyML applications for global productivity and sustainability, addressing key challenges through emerging innovations.

6.6.1 Lesson Learned

Lessons learned underline the crucial optimization of models for resource‐constrained devices, the viability of edge analytics for real‐time decision‐making, and the importance of energy efficiency toward long‐term operations. Besides, privacy‐preserving methods such as federated learning have been important in sustaining data security and have enabled continuous improvement. These lessons underline the revolutionary potential of TinyML while underlining further areas of innovation that will go a long way in maximizing impact for healthcare, agriculture, and autonomous systems. However, lessons learned from this book chapter are summarized as follows:

  1. Importance of Model Optimization: One of the most important things learned in TinyML is the need for robust optimization techniques. Applications of TinyML operate on devices with stringent memory, computational, and energy constraints. Techniques such as quantization, pruning, and NAS have proven instrumental in reducing model size while maintaining accuracy. For example, quantization reduces model weights from 32‐bit floating‐point to 8‐bit integers at a fraction of the memory and with limited loss in accuracy. The success of tools like TFLM and CMSIS‐NN represents the value of those optimization strategies.
  2. Accuracy‐Efficiency Trade‐offs: A common challenge when working with TinyML is balancing model accuracy and efficiency. Running high‐accuracy models on resource‐constrained hardware has been an inevitable trade‐off during deployments, often impacting real‐world performance. Industrial IoT applications have taught us that over‐optimizing for efficiency can degrade a model's ability to handle edge cases, while prioritizing accuracy may lead to energy and latency issues. The importance of case‐specific adaptive optimization techniques underlines this trade‐off.
  3. Hardware–Software Co‐design: TinyML's success represents tight integration between hardware and software. Tools like STM32Cube.AI and NanoEdge Studio have shown that hardware‐aware model design significantly improves performance. In alignment with the underlying hardware capabilities, software optimizations offer superior energy efficiency and processing speeds.
  4. Scaling Challenges: Scaling TinyML solutions to various applications and environments remains very difficult. Experiences with recent deployments in smart agriculture, healthcare, and industrial IoT make one thing clear: A road to scalability will require adaptive frameworks that can deal with the challenge of diverse data sources and hardware platforms. The lack of common benchmarks further complicates model benchmarking across various domains.
  5. Real‐Time Inference and Latency: TinyML applications usually need real‐time decision‐making, especially in safety‐critical domains such as autonomous vehicles and medical monitoring. Lessons learned from these fields shed light on the necessity of optimizing model size and inference latency. Tools developed for this purpose, such as Edge Impulse, have been effective, but further developments are needed to accommodate ultra‐low‐latency applications.
  6. Data Privacy and Security: TinyML has shown huge potential for enhancing data privacy by having devices process information locally instead of relying on cloud services. However, lessons learned from healthcare and finance reveal vulnerabilities in deploying the models securely. Protecting sensitive data while keeping model integrity intact is crucial and requires improvement on fronts like encryption and secure boot.
  7. Cost and Accessibility: Cost is the main factor in democratizing AI. Tools and devices are becoming very affordable. However, various global deployments have shown that a prohibitively expensive pathway using highly specialized hardware, such as LiDAR or custom accelerators, would inhibit its broad‐scale adoption, especially in developing parts of the world. Affordability and open‐source approaches to TinyML are critical in its universal reach.

6.6.2 Prospects

The future of TinyML is promising, with many possibilities for technological advancement, application diversification, and societal influence. The following are some critical areas where TinyML will evolve in the coming years.

  1. Advanced Model Compression Techniques: While quantization and pruning are some of the existing techniques that have already brought down model sizes by an order of magnitude, future innovations in model compression will be around adaptive and hardware‐specific techniques. Sparsity‐aware training and structured pruning will further improve compatibility with constrained devices. Federated learning combined with TinyML may even allow efficient training on edge devices without compromising privacy.
  2. The integration of TinyML and IoT‐Edge AI will continue to drive a fundamental role in the evolution of edge AI and IoT. Shortly, integrations of TinyML and IoT ecosystems will be faultless, and smart homes, cities, and industries will enable autonomous operations. Such integration could enable advanced sensor fusion that combines the outputs from LiDAR, cameras, and RADAR sensors to create an advanced understanding used by applications like autonomous cars.
  3. Energy Harvesting and Sustainable Systems: Energy efficiency will be the core foundation upon which the development of TinyML will progress. Energy harvesting and integrating TinyML into such technologies as solar panels or piezoelectric sensors will drive research into developing self‐sustaining systems in the future. These advancements will be pivotal in the fields of environmental conservation and disaster management, where remote monitoring is essential.
  4. Improved Security and Privacy: As TinyML applications expand into sensitive domains like healthcare and finance, ensuring data security and privacy will be paramount. Future developments will focus on robust encryption techniques, secure hardware modules, and privacy‐preserving ML methods such as homomorphic encryption and differential privacy.
  5. Standardization and Benchmarks: The absence of standardized benchmarks has been one of the longest‐standing problems when benchmarking TinyML models. The prospects are establishing universal performance benchmarks targeted for edge devices, enabling fair comparisons and fostering innovation. Initiatives like MLPerf Tiny are a step in this direction.
  6. Democratization of TinyML: Future efforts will be oriented toward making TinyML affordable and accessible to people worldwide. Open‐source frameworks such as FANN on MCU and uTensor will play a vital role in enabling developers worldwide to build and deploy TinyML applications. The collaboration of academia, industry, and governments will bridge the gap in the digital divide, especially in underserved regions.
  7. Hybrid Architectures: The future of TinyML will probably be hybrid architectures, where microcontrollers are combined with accelerators or even cloud‐based processing. These architectures enable resource‐intensive tasks to be offloaded in the cloud while retaining the benefits of local processing for critical decision‐making.
  8. Collaboration Across Disciplines: TinyML requires an evolution in ML, embedded systems, hardware design, and cybersecurity through interdisciplinary collaboration; this collaboration between fields brings forward innovative approaches in the use and enlargement of applications by addressing these limitations of TinyML.
  9. TinyML for Climate Action: TinyML will play a major role in climate action by enabling low‐power, distributed systems for environmental monitoring and resource management. Applications ranging from wildland fire detection to air quality and water conservation will be some segments that gain huge scalability and efficiency due to TinyML.

6.7 Conclusion

Advances within TinyML are rapid, illustrating very promising scenarios wherein AI at the edge and in resource‐constrained environments could be game changers. By using optimized frameworks, tools, and techniques, TinyML allows real‐time intelligence at edge microcontrollers and devices. It would address the important challenges for any of those applications' efficiency, latency, and data privacy. Domain integration, including healthcare, agriculture, IIoT, and smart cities, adds varied applicability of TinyML into practical solution spaces.

This paper has reviewed the fundamental tools and hardware that make TinyML possible, their limitations, lessons learned, and future directions. The key takeaways are that model optimization techniques, such as quantization and pruning, are critical to making TinyML possible. Despite the significant progress, challenges remain regarding the standardization, security, and adaptability of TinyML to diverse hardware platforms and various applications. Shortly, TinyML development will likely focus on model compression, energy harvesting, and security. Making the tools more affordable and using open‐source resources are vital in the democratization of TinyML. Interdisciplinary collaboration, including hybrid architectures that merge the edge and cloud, will mark the new frontiers of TinyML. The conclusive development of TinyML presents a very important step toward allowing intelligent systems at the edge with extremely good energy efficiency. Therefore, continuous research and development promise great things for TinyML's prospects in shaping the future of embedded AI – scalable, available, and sustainable to handle most global challenges. It highlights how continued innovation and collaboration can lead to the full utilization of this technology.

Privacy‐Preserving Techniques in TinyML for IoT

7.1 Introduction

The rapid proliferation of Internet of Things (IoT) devices has ushered in a new era of ubiquitous computing, where intelligent decision‐making can occur at the edge of networks [1]. Tiny machine learning (TinyML), the field of deploying machine learning models on resource‐constrained devices, has emerged as a powerful paradigm for enabling such edge intelligence [2, 3]. By bringing computation closer to the data source, TinyML offers benefits such as reduced latency, improved energy efficiency, and enhanced privacy [4]. However, the processing of potentially sensitive data on these devices raises significant privacy concerns that must be addressed to ensure widespread adoption and trust in TinyML systems.

The research landscape in privacy‐preserving TinyML encompasses a wide range of challenges and opportunities. Key areas of investigation [2, 3] include

  1. Adapting privacy‐preserving techniques to resource‐constrained environments
  2. Balancing privacy guarantees with computational efficiency and model accuracy
  3. Developing communication‐efficient protocols for distributed TinyML systems
  4. Integrating privacy‐preserving methods with model compression and quantization techniques
  5. Exploring hardware–software co‐design for privacy‐preserving TinyML operations

This chapter contributes to the field by providing a comprehensive examination of state‐of‐the‐art privacy‐preserving techniques specifically tailored for TinyML environments. Our key contributions include

  1. A systematic analysis of secure multi‐party computation (MPC), homomorphic encryption (HE), and differential privacy (DP) approaches in the context of TinyML
  2. An in‐depth evaluation of recent frameworks such as SecureML, SecureNN, and Falcon, highlighting their advancements in efficient and secure computation for resource‐constrained devices
  3. A critical assessment of the trade‐offs between privacy, performance, and model accuracy in TinyML applications
  4. Identification of key challenges and promising future research directions in privacy‐preserving TinyML

The chapter is structured as follows:

  • Section 7.2 provides an overview of related works in the field of privacy‐preserving machine learning, setting the context for our focused examination of TinyML techniques.
  • Section 7.3 delves into HE in TinyML, covering its fundamentals, various encryption schemes, applications to TinyML tasks, and practical considerations.
  • Section 7.4 explores DP for TinyML, discussing its principles, mechanisms, algorithms, and the challenge of balancing privacy and utility.
  • Section 7.5 examines secure MPC (SMPC) in TinyML, covering its foundations, key techniques like secret sharing and garbled circuits, and efficiency optimizations.
  • Section 7.6 presents case studies and applications of privacy‐preserving TinyML, providing concrete examples of how these techniques are implemented in real‐world scenarios.
  • Section 7.7 offers a discussion of the current state of the field and outlines future research directions, addressing the specific challenges and opportunities in each privacy‐preserving approach.
  • Finally, Section 7.8 concludes the chapter, summarizing the key insights and emphasizing the importance of continued research in privacy‐preserving TinyML.

By providing this comprehensive examination, we aim to equip researchers and practitioners with the knowledge necessary to advance the field and develop secure, efficient machine learning solutions for resource‐constrained devices. As TinyML continues to expand its reach across various domains, from healthcare to industrial IoT, the development of robust privacy‐preserving techniques will be crucial in realizing its full potential while safeguarding user privacy and data security.

7.2 Related Works

Privacy‐preserving techniques for machine learning, particularly in resource‐constrained environments, have garnered significant attention in recent years. This section provides an overview of the key related works that form the foundation for privacy‐preserving TinyML.

HE has emerged as a powerful tool for privacy‐preserving machine learning. Al Badawi et al. [5] made significant strides in this direction with their work on homomorphic convolutional neural networks (HCNNs). They demonstrated the feasibility of running CNNs on encrypted data using graphics processing units (GPUs), achieving classification latencies of 5.16 and 304.43 seconds for MNIST and CIFAR‐10 datasets, respectively. This work represents a crucial step toward practical privacy‐preserving deep learning on encrypted data.

In the realm of federated learning, Bonawitz et al. [6] presented a scalable production system for mobile devices. Their work addressed key challenges in federated learning, including communication efficiency, client availability, and privacy. By demonstrating the practicality of federated learning in large‐scale mobile environments, they paved the way for privacy‐preserving distributed learning in TinyML contexts.

DP has been widely explored as a means to provide strong privacy guarantees in machine learning. Ekenstedt et al. [7] investigated the relationship between DP and syntactic privacy, providing insights into how these models can be interpreted in terms of each other. This work is particularly relevant for TinyML applications, where multiple privacy models may need to be satisfied simultaneously.

The application of DP in social network analysis, as surveyed by Jiang et al. [8], offers valuable insights for TinyML in IoT environments. Their comprehensive review of DP applications in tasks such as degree distribution analysis and subgraph counting provides a foundation for privacy‐preserving analysis of interconnected TinyML devices.

Kus and Levi [9] explored the application of DP in cryptocurrency systems, specifically Bitcoin. Their work on noise addition to transaction amounts and user graph perturbation demonstrates the potential of DP mechanisms in enhancing privacy in distributed, resource‐constrained systems, which is directly applicable to TinyML scenarios.

Mahawaga Arachchige et al. [10] proposed LATENT, a local differentially private algorithm for deep learning in IoT environments. Their approach, which splits the architecture of a CNN into three modules, including a randomization layer, is particularly relevant for TinyML applications where data privacy must be preserved before leaving the device.

Pan et al. [11] provided a comprehensive survey on DP in deep learning, offering taxonomy of privacy attacks and preservation techniques. Their work highlights the importance of integrating DP with deep learning models, a crucial consideration for TinyML applications dealing with sensitive data.

In the context of SMPC, Wagh et al. [12] introduced Falcon, a framework for efficient private training and inference of large machine learning models. Falcon's support for high‐capacity networks and batch normalization, coupled with its malicious security guarantees, makes it particularly relevant for TinyML applications requiring strong security assurances.

Zhao et al. [13] proposed a local DP‐based federated learning approach for IoT, addressing both privacy concerns and communication efficiency. Their work on perturbing gradients and optimizing mechanisms for different privacy budgets offers valuable insights for implementing privacy‐preserving federated learning in TinyML contexts.

Zheng et al. [14] presented Helen, a system for maliciously secure coopetitive learning of linear models. While not specifically designed for TinyML, Helen's approach to SMPC in the presence of malicious adversaries provides important considerations for TinyML systems operating in untrusted environments.

Zhou et al. [15] developed a differentially private federated learning model resistant to poisoning attacks in edge computing. Their weight‐based anomaly detection algorithm and use of DP to protect both data and model privacy are particularly relevant for TinyML deployments in adversarial settings.

These works collectively form a rich foundation for privacy‐preserving techniques in TinyML. They demonstrate the potential of HE, DP, and SMPC in addressing the unique challenges posed by resource‐constrained environments. However, they also highlight the need for further research to adapt these techniques to the specific constraints and requirements of TinyML systems.

7.3 Homomorphic Encryption in TinyML

HE has emerged as a promising technique for enabling privacy‐preserving computation on sensitive data, particularly in resource‐constrained environments such as TinyML [5, 16]. By allowing computations to be performed directly on encrypted data without the need for decryption, HE enables TinyML devices to process and analyze data while maintaining the confidentiality of the underlying information. This section explores the fundamentals of HE, its variants, and its application to TinyML tasks, along with an evaluation of its performance and practical considerations.

7.3.1 Fundamentals of Homomorphic Encryption

HE is a cryptographic technique that enables computations to be performed on encrypted data without revealing the underlying plaintext. The core principle behind HE is the homomorphic property, which allows the encryption function to preserve certain mathematical operations performed on the plaintext. More formally, given an encryption function E(·), a decryption function D(·), and an operation ⊙ on the plaintext space, an encryption scheme is said to be homomorphic with respect to ⊙ if the following holds:

where ⊗ is a corresponding operation in the ciphertext space. This property enables computations to be performed directly on the encrypted data, and the result, when decrypted, matches the result of the same operations performed on the plaintext.

The concept of HE was first introduced by Rivest, Adleman, and Dertouzos in 1978 [17], but it was not until the groundbreaking work of Gentry in 2009 [18] that a fully HE (FHE) scheme was constructed. Gentry's scheme was based on ideal lattices and relied on a technique called bootstrapping to manage the noise growth in the ciphertext. The scheme consists of three main steps:

  • Key Generation: Generate a secret key sk and a public key pk.
  • Encryption: Given a plaintext message m, compute the ciphertext c = Epk(m).
  • Decryption: Given a ciphertext c, compute the plaintext message m = Dsk(c).

The homomorphic property of Gentry's scheme allows for the evaluation of arbitrary circuits on the encrypted data. Given a function f and ciphertexts c1 = Epk(m1) and c2 = Epk(m2), the scheme enables the computation of Epk(f(m1, m2)) without revealing m1 or m2.

Since Gentry's seminal work, significant progress has been made in improving the efficiency and practicality of FHE schemes, making them more suitable for resource‐constrained environments such as TinyML. However, the computational cost and ciphertext expansion associated with FHE remain a challenge for its adoption in TinyML applications.

7.3.2 Partially and Fully Homomorphic Encryption Schemes

HE schemes can be classified into two main categories: partially HE (PHE) and FHE. PHE schemes support a limited set of operations on the encrypted data, typically either addition or multiplication, but not both. Examples of PHE schemes include

  • Paillier Cryptosystem [19]: The Paillier cryptosystem is an additive HE scheme based on the decisional composite residuosity (DCR) assumption. Given two ciphertexts c1 = Epk(m1) and c2 = Epk(m2), the scheme allows for the computation of Epk(m1 + m2) as c1 · c2 mod n2, where n is the public key modulus.
  • ElGamal Cryptosystem [20]: The ElGamal cryptosystem is a multiplicative HE scheme based on the decisional Diffie–Hellman (DDH) assumption. Given two ciphertexts and , where g and h are public key components and r1 and r2 are random values, the scheme allows for the computation of Epk(m1 · m2) as .

On the other hand, FHE schemes support an arbitrary number of both addition and multiplication operations on the encrypted data, enabling the evaluation of any computable function. Some notable FHE schemes include

  • Brakerski–Gentry–Vaikuntanathan (BGV) Scheme [21]: The BGV scheme is an FHE scheme based on the ring learning with error (RLWE) problem. It introduces a technique called modulus switching to manage the noise growth in the ciphertext, allowing for the evaluation of deeper circuits compared to Gentry's original scheme.
  • Brakerski/Fan–Vercauteren (BFV) Scheme [22]: The BFV scheme is another FHE scheme based on the RLWE problem. It employs a technique called scale‐invariant HE, which enables the use of a fixed modulus throughout the evaluation process, leading to improved efficiency compared to the BGV scheme.
  • Cheon–Kim–Kim–Song (CKKS) Scheme [23]: The CKKS scheme is an FHE scheme that supports approximate arithmetic on encrypted real numbers. It is based on the RLWE problem and uses a technique called rescaling to manage the precision loss during homomorphic operations, making it suitable for machine learning applications.

While FHE schemes offer greater flexibility and functionality compared to PHE schemes, they typically incur higher computational costs and ciphertext expansion. Therefore, the choice between PHE and FHE in TinyML applications depends on the specific requirements of the task and the available resources on the device.

Figure 7.1 provides a comprehensive overview of HE schemes, categorizing them into partially HE (PHE) and FHE.

The PHE schemes, including the Paillier and ElGamal cryptosystems, support either additive or multiplicative operations on encrypted data, respectively. In contrast, FHE schemes such as BGV, BFV, and CKKS enable both addition and multiplication, thus allowing the evaluation of any computable function on encrypted data. The diagram also highlights the trade‐offs between these schemes, noting that FHE, despite its greater flexibility, incurs higher computational costs and ciphertext expansion, making the choice between PHE and FHE dependent on specific application requirements and available resources.

7.3.3 Applying Homomorphic Encryption to TinyML Tasks

HE has numerous applications in TinyML, particularly in scenarios where sensitive data need to be processed and analyzed on resource‐constrained devices. Some key areas where HE can be applied in TinyML include

  • Secure Data Aggregation: TinyML devices often need to aggregate data from multiple sources for analysis or decision‐making. HE enables the devices to perform this aggregation on encrypted data, ensuring the privacy of the individual data points. For example, consider a scenario where n TinyML devices each hold a private value xi. The devices can encrypt their values using an additive HE scheme, such as the Paillier cryptosystem, and send the ciphertexts Epk(xi) to a central aggregator. The aggregator can then compute the sum of the encrypted values as , which can be decrypted to obtain the aggregated result without revealing the individual values [24].
  • Privacy‐Preserving Inference: HE can be used to enable privacy‐preserving inference on TinyML devices, where the model parameters and input data are encrypted. This allows the devices to make predictions on sensitive data without revealing the underlying information. For example, consider a TinyML device with an encrypted input Epk(x) and an encrypted model with parameters Epk(wi). The device can compute the encrypted prediction using an FHE scheme that supports both addition and multiplication, such as the BGV or BFV scheme. The encrypted prediction can then be sent to a trusted party for decryption and further analysis [25].
  • Federated Learning: HE can be employed in federated learning scenarios, where multiple TinyML devices collaborate to train a model without sharing their local data. By encrypting the model updates and gradients, HE ensures that the devices can contribute to the learning process while maintaining the confidentiality of their data. For example, consider a federated learning setting with n TinyML devices, each with a local dataset Di. The devices can encrypt their local gradients Epk(∇L(w, Di)) using an FHE scheme and send them to a central server. The server can then compute the encrypted global gradient as , which can be decrypted and used to update the model parameters. This process is repeated iteratively until convergence, allowing the devices to collaboratively learn a model without revealing their local data [6].
  • Secure Multi‐Party Computation: HE is a key enabling technology for SMPC protocols, which allow multiple parties to jointly compute a function on their private inputs without revealing them to each other. In TinyML, HE‐based MPC can be used for tasks such as privacy‐preserving collaborative learning and secure decision‐making. For example, consider a scenario where n TinyML devices, each with a private input xi, want to compute a function f(x1, …, xn) without revealing their inputs to each other. The devices can encrypt their inputs using an FHE scheme and engage in an MPC protocol to compute the encrypted result Epk(f(x1, …, xn)), which can be decrypted by a trusted party. This approach ensures that the devices can collaborate on the computation while preserving the privacy of their individual inputs [26].

When applying HE to TinyML tasks, it is crucial to consider the specific requirements of the application, such as the desired level of security, the computational resources available on the devices, and the performance constraints. The choice of the HE scheme and its parameters should be carefully optimized to strike a balance between security, efficiency, and functionality.

Figure 7.2 illustrates the application of HE to various TinyML tasks, highlighting key areas such as secure data aggregation, privacy‐preserving inference, federated learning, and SMPC.

Each section of the diagram details the specific steps involved in implementing HE for these tasks. For instance, in secure data aggregation, TinyML devices encrypt their data and send it to a central aggregator, which computes and decrypts the aggregated result without revealing individual values. Similarly, in privacy‐preserving inference, model parameters and input data are encrypted to ensure that predictions can be made on sensitive data without exposing it. The diagram also underscores the importance of considering security, resource availability, performance, and optimization when applying HE to TinyML applications.

7.3.4 Performance Evaluation and Practical Considerations

The performance of HE in TinyML applications is a critical factor in determining its practicality and feasibility. The computational cost and ciphertext expansion associated with HE schemes can be significant, especially for resource‐constrained devices. Therefore, it is essential to evaluate the performance of HE in the context of TinyML and to consider various optimization techniques to improve its efficiency.

Several studies have investigated the performance of HE schemes on microcontroller‐based platforms. For example, Carpov et al. [27] implemented and evaluated the BGV scheme on an Arm Cortex‐M4 microcontroller, demonstrating the feasibility of running FHE on resource‐constrained devices. They also proposed optimizations, such as ciphertext packing and parallel processing, to improve the performance of the scheme. Ciphertext packing involves encoding multiple plaintext values into a single ciphertext, enabling batch operations on the encrypted data. This technique can significantly reduce the ciphertext expansion and computational overhead of HE schemes. Parallel processing, on the other hand, leverages the multi‐core architecture of modern microcontrollers to distribute the homomorphic computations across multiple cores, leading to improved performance.

Other works have focused on optimizing HE schemes specifically for TinyML applications. For instance, Bourse et al. [16] proposed a compressed encryption scheme that reduces the ciphertext expansion and computational cost of HE, making it more suitable for resource‐constrained environments. The scheme is based on the CKKS scheme and employs a technique called ciphertext compression, which reduces the size of the ciphertexts by discarding some of the least significant bits. This compression is achieved through a careful analysis of the noise growth during homomorphic operations, ensuring that the discarded bits do not affect the correctness of the computations.

Similarly, Jiang et al. [28] introduced a lightweight HE scheme based on the LWE problem, which achieves better performance compared to traditional HE schemes in terms of both computation time and memory consumption. The scheme employs a technique called dimension reduction, which reduces the size of the LWE problem instances while maintaining the same level of security. This is achieved by carefully selecting the parameters of the LWE problem based on the specific requirements of the TinyML application, such as the desired security level and the available computational resources.

In addition to algorithmic optimizations, the performance of HE in TinyML can be improved through hardware acceleration. Specialized hardware accelerators for HE have been proposed, such as the Homomorphic Encryption Acceleration (HEAX) accelerator [5], which achieves significant speedups compared to software implementations. The HEAX accelerator is designed as a co‐processor for microcontrollers and implements the basic building blocks of HE schemes, such as modular arithmetic and polynomial operations, in hardware. By offloading these computationally intensive operations to the accelerator, the performance of HE in TinyML can be greatly improved, making it more practical for real‐world applications.

When applying HE to TinyML tasks, it is essential to consider the practical aspects of the implementation, such as the memory footprint, power consumption, and latency. The choice of the HE scheme and its parameters should be carefully tuned to meet the specific requirements of the application while ensuring an acceptable level of performance. Furthermore, the integration of HE into existing TinyML frameworks and libraries should be seamless, providing developers with easy‐to‐use tools and interfaces for implementing privacy‐preserving techniques in their applications.

In conclusion, HE is a powerful tool for enabling privacy‐preserving computation in TinyML environments. By allowing computations to be performed directly on encrypted data, HE enables TinyML devices to process and analyze sensitive information while maintaining the confidentiality of the underlying data. The choice between partially and FHE schemes depends on the specific requirements of the application and the available resources on the devices. When applying HE to TinyML tasks, it is crucial to consider the performance implications and to employ various optimization techniques, at both the algorithmic and hardware levels, to ensure the practicality and feasibility of the approach. With ongoing research and advancements in HE schemes and their integration into TinyML frameworks, HE is poised to play a significant role in enabling secure and privacy‐preserving TinyML applications in the future.

7.3.5 Comparison of Homomorphic Encryption Schemes

To determine the most suitable HE scheme for TinyML applications, it is essential to compare the various schemes in terms of their security, efficiency, and functionality. This section provides a comparative analysis of the key HE schemes discussed in this chapter, namely the Paillier, ElGamal, BGV, BFV, and CKKS schemes.

  • Security: All the HE schemes considered in this comparison provide semantic security under appropriate hardness assumptions. The Paillier and ElGamal schemes are based on the DCR and DDH assumptions, respectively, while the BGV, BFV, and CKKS schemes are based on the RLWE assumption. The RLWE assumption is considered to be more secure against quantum attacks compared to the DCR and DDH assumptions, making the BGV, BFV, and CKKS schemes more suitable for long‐term security in post‐quantum scenarios.
  • Homomorphic Operations: The Paillier and ElGamal schemes are partially homomorphic, supporting only additive and multiplicative operations, respectively. On the other hand, the BGV, BFV, and CKKS schemes are fully homomorphic, supporting an arbitrary number of both additive and multiplicative operations. This makes the fully homomorphic schemes more versatile and suitable for a wider range of TinyML applications that require complex computations on encrypted data.
  • Plaintext Space: The Paillier and ElGamal schemes operate on integer plaintexts, while the BGV and BFV schemes support integer or polynomial plaintexts. The CKKS scheme, on the other hand, is designed specifically for real number plaintexts, making it more suitable for TinyML applications that involve floating‐point arithmetic, such as deep learning and signal processing.
  • Ciphertext Size: The ciphertext size of the HE schemes directly impacts the communication overhead and storage requirements in TinyML applications. The Paillier and ElGamal schemes have relatively small ciphertext sizes, typically twice the size of the plaintext.
