13.1 Introduction

The Internet of Things (IoT) [1] has gained significant attention due to its diverse range of smart applications. More recently, advancements in the Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) [2] have enabled sophisticated real‐time processing of vast amounts of data. This development has facilitated progress in areas like anomaly detection, smart manufacturing, and predictive maintenance, demonstrating the transformative potential of IoT technologies across various industries.

Onboard‐embedded technological intelligence refers to learning algorithms that enable devices to make reliable decisions based on collected data. However, implementing machine learning (ML) on small devices is challenging due to significant constraints in architecture, energy, and latency [3]. This is particularly crucial in safety‐critical systems, such as industrial robotics, autonomous vehicles, and medical devices, where delays can have serious consequences [4].

The term tiny machine learning (TinyML), introduced in 2018, represents a paradigm that enables ML on edge devices with minimal processing power and memory requirements. Typically, these systems consume only a few milliwatts of power [5], and their memory footprint ranges between 64 and 256 KB, often not exceeding 1 MB. The computing units in such devices generally operate at frequencies between 40 and 400 MHz. Rapid advancements in TinyML have enabled ML models to operate on low‐power microcontrollers (MCUs) found in IoT devices. The deployment of ML directly on these devices enhances latency and energy efficiency, strengthens data privacy, and reduces reliance on continuous Internet connectivity. With demand continuing to rise, over 25 billion MCUs were shipped in 2019 [6]. By integrating ML into these low‐power embedded devices, the intelligence of IoT applications can be substantially improved. Additionally, significant progress has been made in the development of TinyML algorithms and the optimization of low‐power IoT devices.

The heterogeneity of the TinyML ecosystem poses significant challenges to effective management and large‐scale implementation, particularly in IIoT networks comprising hundreds or thousands of devices. Embedded systems are often customized for specific use cases, resulting in a diverse range of computational and energy efficiency capabilities. These devices incorporate various sensors, processing power, runtimes, and sizes of random access memory (RAM) and flash memory. Developing a TinyML model entails numerous decisions, including selecting the neural network (NN) type, layer combinations, and neuron sizes to optimize performance under different conditions. Furthermore, the preprocessing and postprocessing for each model must be tailored, as meaningful outputs depend on accurately formatted input data. Additionally, the lack of comprehensive documentation accompanying TinyML models contributes to a fragmented ecosystem. TinyML practitioners face numerous challenges, particularly as some of the most advanced technologies, such as contemporary NNs, now require billions of parameters [7].

While larger networks tend to yield better results and broader applicability, their energy consumption increases with size, rendering this trend energetically unsustainable at larger scales [8]. This highlights the importance of pursuing TinyML as a vital area of research. In this context, TinyML empowers developers to implement sophisticated algorithms on constrained devices that are portable, cost‐effective, and energy‐efficient, making them suitable for a variety of applications. Recent market trends further support this approach, emphasizing the demand for less power‐hungry technology; indeed, there is a pressing need for TinyML to become even more compact.

There are two conventional approaches to developing a TinyML solution: the hardware (HW)‐oriented and ML‐oriented approaches, along with a more recent co‐design methodology. In traditional approaches, the development of ML models and HW implementation are treated as separate processes. In the ML‐oriented approach, experts focus on designing, training, and refining the model before deploying it onto suitable HW [9]. The HW‐oriented approach, on the other hand, aims to design optimized HW using simplified models and techniques without prior selection of the HW [10]. The co‐design workflow derives its name from the collaborative efforts of HW engineers and ML specialists, who work together from the outset, actively sharing knowledge throughout the design process [11].

The management of TinyML systems in the industry is significantly complicated by the rapid evolution and diversity of TinyML components, including embedded devices and ML models. A primary challenge is identifying IoT devices in the field that possess the necessary sensors and capabilities for specific ML models without requiring a thorough examination of each device. Additionally, it is essential to locate existing NN models that are compatible with particular embedded devices to avoid unnecessary redundancy when developing new models. Moreover, effective management and repurposing of TinyML components at scale is a critical concern, alongside the need to integrate discovery results into coherent IoT applications.

To address these challenges, a scalable approach is proposed in this chapter for managing TinyML systems utilizing Semantic Web technologies. In this research, semantics encompass HW requirements, information, and NN representations for ML models in TinyML. Additionally, it is recommended to employ the standardized Thing Description (TD) [12] semantics in conjunction with the World Wide Web Consortium's (W3C) Web of Things (WoT) architecture [13] to enhance IoT devices and facilitate the specification of semantic HW. Integrating the proposed TinyML model semantics with the TD semantics enables the alignment of model requirements with IoT device capabilities. This unified knowledge representation, hosted in a central knowledge graph (KG), supports vendor‐agnostic information management and reasoning. Moreover, the use of SPARQL Protocol and RDF Query Language (SPARQL) enhances system administration and interoperability across diverse sectors by enabling the discovery and interaction of TinyML components in various contexts.

This chapter aims to support the community in developing, maintaining, and utilizing KG for TinyML. Examples and code are provided to create semantic representations for NN models in the “.tflite” format, which is compatible with TensorFlow Lite for MCUs. Although the focus of the research has not been on IoT device semantics due to the established TD semantics, the proposed repository includes six semantic descriptions. Moreover, the distribution of models to devices is enabled through knowledge matching, allowing for the orchestration of TinyML components. Additionally, the use of low‐code platforms simplifies TinyML workflows for engineers who lack expertise in SPARQL queries or semantic technologies, facilitating more efficient system management.

13.1.1 Key Contributions of the Chapter

The following are the significant contributions of this chapter:

  1. This chapter comprehensively introduces TinyML, discussing its core principles and the challenges surrounding its broader adoption. It further examines recent advancements in TinyML, including essential workflows, HW, and software for efficient implementation.
  2. A scalable approach is discussed for managing TinyML systems on NNs using Semantic Web technologies. The approach enhances interoperability by integrating model and device requirements into a unified KG, enabling efficient discovery and management of TinyML components across diverse IoT environments.
  3. This chapter showcases a semantic management system using a KG that encompasses six IoT devices and 23 TinyML models. Three case studies illustrate the advantages of this approach, while the performance of TinyEngine is rigorously assessed through comparisons of speed, memory usage, and binary size across frameworks.

13.1.2 Chapter Organization

The remaining part of this chapter is organized as follows. Section 13.2 introduces TinyML, outlining its core concepts and the challenges associated with its widespread adoption. Section 13.3 delves into recent advancements in TinyML, including the required workflow, HW, and software for effective implementation. Section 13.4 provides a detailed methodology on NNs, examining TinyML integration with IoT through three in‐depth case studies. Section 13.5 presents the results and discussion of the TinyEngine, offering a performance comparison based on memory usage and binary size. Finally, Section 13.6 concludes the chapter by exploring future directions and potential advancements in TinyML.

13.2 Introduction to TinyML

The field of TinyML is experiencing rapid growth within both industrial and academic communities. The research [14] outlined the challenges and advancements in the development of embedded ML. Improved algorithms [15] have been designed to optimize deployment in real‐world scenarios, enhance model performance, and increase resource efficiency. Furthermore, the development of ultra‐low‐power artificial intelligence (AI) circuits and accelerators [16] has been proposed to enable continuous, always on ML capabilities, even when operating on battery power for extended periods.

Since TinyML delivers ML solutions to resource‐constrained devices, a holistic approach combining HW and algorithm [17] design is essential to maximize performance. Frameworks for evaluating ML deployment at the edge [18] play a critical role in systematically addressing potential challenges. Several platforms and tools have been developed to accelerate TinyML, such as Google's TensorFlow Lite for MCUs [19], STM's X‐CUBE‐AI, Apache TVM, and various open online courses. Moreover, notable applications of TinyML are emerging across multiple domains [20].

Effective management of the TinyML ecosystem necessitates enhanced transparency and interoperability to address its inherent heterogeneity. TensorFlow Lite metadata provides a structured framework for documenting model characteristics, including input and output data, while the Open Neural Network Exchange (ONNX) serves as an open‐source initiative for sharing ML models across various frameworks. Emphasizing efficiency and limitations, Google's model card [21] establishes a standard for characterizing ML models. However, these systems typically rely on isolated, manually created documentation that lacks interchangeability and interoperability. Within the context of TinyML, the main focus of research is on enhancing the reusability of ML model formats with IoT devices rather than on converting models between different platforms.

The management of ML models has garnered increased attention in recent years. While research [22] introduced a database for tracking ML models, research [23] highlighted the challenges associated with managing models across diverse ML use cases. A KG called FAIRnets aggregates and facilitates the interchange of information regarding publicly available NNs. However, despite their expressiveness, these approaches are insufficient for TinyML, as the growing complexity demands a thorough examination of both HW specifications and ML models.

Semantic Web technologies have been effectively applied within the IoT domain and are particularly adept at representing the diverse knowledge pertaining to TinyML components in a manner comprehensible to both humans and machines [24]. The WoT approach aims to make various IoT devices accessible as web resources. Additionally, the W3C WoT interest group has proposed a formal information schema known as the TD semantic, which semantically characterizes the interfaces and capabilities of these devices.

Despite recent advancements, a disconnect remains between ML models and IoT devices, particularly in the large‐scale management of TinyML components. Key challenges include identifying suitable combinations and initiating extensive deployments. In research [25], a semantics‐based approach for managing on‐device applications across distributed IoT devices was proposed. This approach is adopted by developing an NN semantics tailored for TinyML in conjunction with the TD semantic. To enhance interoperability, research leveraged established semantic vocabularies: the semantic sensor network (SSN) schema, which encompasses sensors and their interactions, incorporates the sensor, observation, sample, and actuator semantics. Additionally, the semantic smart sensor network (S3N) schema extends SSN to provide insights into smart sensors and their characteristics. Another relevant semantic model is iot.schema.org, an extension of schema.org designed to enrich structured data across the Internet.

Finally, TinyML as a service [26] facilitates the deployment of ML models across various embedded devices by creating an abstraction layer over multiple HW compilers and automatically generating compiled ML models for specific HW platforms. This service has the potential to enhance the deployment phase of the presented workflow significantly. Table 13.1 presents a summary of the semantic management of TinyML.

13.3 Recent Advances in TinyML

ML has significantly transformed various domains, such as language, audio processing, and computer vision. Nonetheless, advanced models often require substantial memory and processing resources, which can lead to high deployment costs. To overcome these challenges, researchers are focusing on developing efficient algorithms, methods, and HW tailored to diverse applications. Efficient ML [27] is primarily divided into two categories, as shown in Figure 13.1. CloudML aims to enhance latency and throughput in cloud environments, and EdgeML emphasizes improving energy efficiency, reducing latency, and ensuring privacy on edge devices. These two areas intersect in several ways, including over‐the‐air updates, hybrid inference, and federated learning.

A notable advancement in this field is TinyML, which allows ML on ultra‐low‐power devices that require as little as a few hundred kilobytes of memory. As the number of IoT devices continues to rise, there is an increasing demand for low‐power, on‐device AI that enhances responsiveness and privacy while minimizing the costs associated with wireless communication. This capability is especially critical for real‐time applications, such as autonomous vehicles. Moreover, efforts to develop TinyML enable on‐device training, strengthening privacy by allowing IoT devices to adjust their models locally rather than relying on cloud servers. This approach can enhance various applications, such as email clients that refine their predictive capabilities using personalized language models and home security cameras that recognize unfamiliar faces. Additionally, it facilitates IoT solutions in environments lacking Internet connectivity, including applications in precision agriculture and ocean monitoring.

13.3.1 Latest Hardware Trends Empowering TinyML

TinyML practitioners face significant challenges, primarily due to the high parameter requirements of modern NNs, which can reach billions. While larger networks offer improved performance and versatility, their energy demands make large‐scale deployment unsustainable. Consequently, TinyML emerges as a crucial field that enables developers to implement advanced algorithms on compact, cost‐effective, and energy‐efficient devices suitable for diverse applications. Recent market trends further emphasize the need for low‐power solutions, underscoring the importance of making TinyML even more efficient and compact. One noteworthy trend in the most recent HW design for TinyML is that the emphasis is on reducing power consumption. This suggests that the main focus is on making ML compatible with low‐resource devices, as shown in Figure 13.2. TinyML solutions primarily utilize three HW technologies: application‐specific integrated circuits (ASICs), MCUs, and field‐programmable gate arrays (FPGAs). Notably, FPGAs tend to have significantly higher power consumption than ASICs.

ASICs have gained popularity among researchers and industry practitioners, particularly the RISC‐V architecture. Selecting the most suitable RISC‐V processors, architectures, and ML software frameworks can be challenging. A survey [28] examines various RISC‐V HW implementations and software frameworks for system‐on‐chip development, highlighting newer frameworks that support open HW integration for ML applications. The research [29] focusing on TinyML frameworks for MCUs emphasizes the integration of ML algorithms. It introduces a multi‐radio access network architecture tailored for resource‐constrained networked devices, while another [30] compares seven MCUs for face recognition using convolutional NN (CNNs). This comparison evaluates power efficiency, energy per inference, inference efficiency, and inference time. In FPGAs, the [31] framework utilizes custom function units (CFUs) to streamline the development of ML accelerators for embedded systems. This open‐source toolset enhances central processing unit (CPU) and CFU performance in resource‐limited applications by combining software with FPGA synthesis tools and demonstrating iterative improvements in two TinyML applications: image classification and keyword detection.

13.3.2 TinyML Workflows

The main steps for developing TinyML systems focus on the integration of HW platforms with ML models [32]. While working on both elements simultaneously can yield a more unified and efficient outcome, developers typically start with the area they know best. Industrial limitations give rise to two primary approaches: an ML‐oriented workflow that centers on model design, adaptation, training, and evaluation with predetermined HW and HW‐oriented workflow that starts with HW selection to optimize resource use. Co‐design, a more holistic approach, combines both elements from the outset for improved performance.

13.3.2.1 ML‐Focused Process

The ML‐oriented workflow in Figure 13.3 emphasizes developing, training, and assessing ML models, often with HW platform choices restricted by industry requirements. For example, adapting NN models [33] to embedded devices demands rigorous testing to ensure efficient use of power, latency, and memory. These devices are more limited than in cloud systems. There are five key stages of the workflow. The first stage is the model framework, where models are created and validated with a focus on generalization. The next step is model optimization, balancing efficiency with performance. After this, direct evaluation, assessment, and adjustment of the model will be performed. The next stage is the deployment destination, applying device‐specific optimizations. Finally, the destination evaluation confirms the effectiveness of the model in real‐world use.

13.3.2.2 Hardware (HW)‐Focused Process

In the HW‐oriented approach in Figure 13.4, developers focus on creating advanced HW platforms optimized for embedded applications to support current and future ML algorithms. This process often involves identifying bottlenecks in existing architectures, particularly in ML computations like NNs [34], and designing HW accelerators to boost throughput and reduce energy use, for example, by simplifying convolutional computations or developing efficient, low‐power perceptrons. In some cases, new platforms are built with integrated digital signal processing, requiring optimized computing libraries to enhance performance. The HW‐oriented workflow typically includes three stages. The first stage is HW development, where developers build architectures or accelerator modules to improve performance for specific computational tasks. The next step is designated deployment, which assesses the optimized HW in simulated environments, with a redesign as needed. Finally, performance testing involves the production and testing of the final HW.

13.3.2.3 Co‐design Process

In the integrated design workflow in Figure 13.5, HW design and model optimization are developed together from the start to enhance performance and resource efficiency. Unlike previous workflows that address these as separate stages, this approach focuses on co‐optimization. This may include using HW‐informed training to support NN computations on analog computation‐in‐memory accelerators or creating specialized architectures for certain ML algorithms on FPGAs [35]. The key steps in this workflow are as follows:

  1. a) Requirements Specification: Two teams – one of ML specialists (M1) and the other of HW specialists (H1) – define the device's requirements and capabilities.
  2. b) Problem Evaluation: The teams review various options and select the most suitable architecture.
  3. c) Co‐design: A collaborative design process selects specific HW and software components with an overall system perspective.
  4. d) Final Evaluation: A final assessment ensures that model‐ and device‐specific optimizations are effective for production.

13.3.3 Insights on Learning Through the TinyML Perspective

The taxonomy of learning methodologies within the TinyML framework is divided into three primary categories: model optimization, model architecture, and modeling algorithms, as illustrated in Figure 13.6. This framework provides a comprehensive overview of strategies for creating, optimizing, and implementing modeling algorithms in TinyML. It ensures the development of efficient ML models suitable for resource‐limited embedded systems.

Model optimization [36] focuses on enhancing the efficiency of ML models concerning memory usage, battery life, and computational resource factors that are essential for TinyML applications on resource‐constrained devices. Key techniques include parameter reduction, eliminating unnecessary connections by reducing model parameters. Discretization decreases numerical precision from 32‐bit floating‐point to 8‐bit integer to save memory. Feature distillation transfers knowledge from a larger, more complex model to a more compact one while maintaining performance. Additionally, model parameter optimization seeks to identify the best training parameters to maximize performance and efficiency in embedded systems.

Model design [37] emphasizes the creation of NN architectures tailored to the constraints of TinyML. Two significant elements are neural model optimization and depthwise convolutions. Neural model optimization automates the discovery of optimal structures for specific tasks and the rational function activation, which implements alternative activation functions to enhance efficiency while conserving resources. Moreover, the focus mechanism improves model accuracy by focusing on relevant data features without adding substantial computational overhead. Meanwhile, depthwise convolution boosts efficiency by separating spatial and depthwise convolutions.

Modeling algorithms [38] categorize various ML techniques suitable for TinyML applications. This includes supervised and unsupervised learning, where supervised learning relies on labeled data, while unsupervised learning seeks to identify patterns within unlabeled data. Self‐supervised learning allows models to learn from unlabeled data through proxy tasks, making it ideal for environments with limited labeled samples. Deep reinforcement learning facilitates learning through trial and error. Weakly supervised learning effectively leverages partially labeled data, and meta‐learning enables models to adapt to new tasks quickly. Lastly, continuous learning supports ongoing learning from new data, allowing low‐power devices to adjust without needing complete retraining. Table 13.2 gives an overview of ML algorithms.

13.3.4 Devices and Tools for TinyML

TinyML relies on HW for effective training and inference across various devices. The [29] review examines a range of processors suitable for TinyML applications, from general‐purpose CPUs to specialized architectures like graphics processing units (GPUs), FPGAs [39], and tensor processing units (TPUs). Each type presents flexibility, programmability, and efficiency trade‐offs based on application requirements. While CPUs, particularly the Arm Cortex‐M, are efficient, they may not fully exploit parallelism. In contrast, GPUs excel at parallel processing for ML, and TPUs developed by Google are optimized for tensor operations, offering exceptional performance and scalability for TinyML applications. Table 13.3 shows a comparison of HW options for TinyML.

13.3.5 Software Platforms

The rising demand for HW‐based ML emphasizes the critical role of the software layer in developing TinyML systems. Key frameworks include uTensor, which converts ML models into optimized C++ files for easier integration with arm architectures, and TensorFlow Lite Micro [40], enabling ML model execution on MCUs without an operating system. Edge impulse supports real‐time data processing and cloud‐based training for edge device model development. Additionally, X‐CUBE‐AI automates AI algorithm conversion for STM32 products, while the Embedded Learning Library (ELL) serves as a cross‐compiler for low‐resource platforms. Furthermore, MinUn addresses memory management, bandwidth optimization, and number representation issues in TinyML applications, and uTVM enhances deep learning workloads across various HW. Together, these frameworks significantly advance TinyML research.

13.3.6 TinyML Constraints

Due to the stringent constraints of devices like MCUs, TinyML applications cannot afford the processing resources necessary for the success of deep learning models. Training and implementing AI models on MCUs is challenging because of their significant memory limitations, such as read‐only flash memory (FLASH) and static random‐access memory (SRAM) being less than 256 kB, lack of operating systems, and absence of dynamic random‐access memory (DRAM). Compared to mobile platforms, they have far fewer available resources. Prior studies have either focused on optimizing operator kernels without improving network design or aimed to reduce model parameters without addressing the critical issue of activation bottlenecks. Neither strategy adopts a co‐design perspective, leading to suboptimal solutions for TinyML. Table 13.4 presents a comparative analysis of memory and storage for AI models across mobile platforms.

13.3.6.1 Mobile‐Optimized Models Are Unsuitable for TinyML

Because mobile devices typically have ample memory, optimization efforts for mobile deep learning models are required. MobileNets and ShuffleNet [41] have largely focused on reducing parameters, floating point operations per second (FLOPs), and latency rather than addressing peak memory usage. Although MobileNetV2‐1.4 has a model size that is 4.2× smaller than ResNet‐50, it requires 2.3× more peak memory, further straining the SRAM limitations observed with ResNet, as shown in Figure 13.7. This highlights the need to rethink model design strategies specifically for TinyML applications.

13.3.6.2 Challenges in Adapting Inference Models for Tiny Training

Backpropagation requires storing intermediate activations, making training on resource‐limited systems like MCUs challenging, with memory usage increasing by 6.9 times compared to inference. As shown in Figure 13.7, MobileNet's training memory usage is only 10% lower than ResNet, which remains inadequate for devices with limited SRAM, such as 256 KB. Despite prior efforts to reduce FLOPs or optimize inference memory, even efficient models like MCUNet [42] are not suitable for training on tiny devices. New backpropagation techniques and learning algorithms are needed to reduce activation memory requirements, enabling efficient and accurate training on these platforms.

13.3.7 TinyML Application

The review [43] focuses on the applications of TinyML across various fields, including IoT, environmental challenges, predictive maintenance, anomaly detection, and healthcare. It highlights the benefits of TinyML, such as reduced latency and enhanced data privacy, and examines its integration with low‐power wide‐area network (LPWAN) and 5G technologies. The survey [44] discusses the role of TinyML in healthcare, particularly with wearable devices. It provides insights into optimizing predictive maintenance systems and detecting anomalies, culminating in a taxonomy of existing TinyML techniques across these domains.

13.3.8 TinyML and Large ML Comparison

Building effective models under constraints such as memory, computing, engineering resources, and data is essential for both TinyML [45] and large ML. Although TinyML focuses on optimizing models for small devices, it involves techniques like quantization and sparse learning. It proves valuable for large‐scale applications in cloud environments, making these efficiency methods broadly applicable.

TinyML continues to evolve alongside HW advancements. For example, ResNet‐50 [46], introduced in 2016 with 25 million parameters, was initially considered a large model. Today, it can perform inference under a millisecond on a smartphone digital signal processor (DSP) such as Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Gen1. As HW progresses, models once deemed “large” may become “tiny,” highlighting the need for TinyML to expand and adapt over time. Table 13.5 compares TinyML and large ML features.

13.4 Methodology

The study [47] provides a detailed explanation of the semantic schema along with essential guidelines for establishing the semantics of neural network (NN) models tailored to TinyML. The semantics for TinyML models was designed to integrate with TD, facilitating the expression of IoT device capabilities. To illustrate the semantic management system in action, KG encompassing six IoT devices and 23 publicly accessible TinyML models is presented. Finally, three case studies were included to showcase the benefits of this approach.

13.4.1 Designing a Semantics for TinyML Models

The scope of the TinyML model semantics [48] and the level of detail are defined by establishing five essential requirements. First, it was crucial to develop a method for describing ML models that run on embedded devices, ensuring the semantics could capture the unique attributes of models optimized for embedded applications. Second, the requirement was identifying the necessary metadata for each model, including elements such as the originator, unique identifiers, and references. This metadata provides important context for understanding and effectively managing the models. Third, it was crucial to outline the standard features of embedded ML models, covering aspects like layer configurations, quantization methods, and input/output specifications, which are essential for categorizing and organizing TinyML models in a standardized manner.

The fourth one is information about HW, particularly memory and sensor requirements, which was another essential factor in the design of semantics. Including these specifics allows the semantics to accurately capture the unique demands and limitations of embedded environments. Finally, a developed ontology vocabulary aligned with TD to facilitate seamless integration and compatibility with other frameworks, which is vital for effective data sharing across IoT systems. It emphasized that reusing existing ontologies enhances interoperability and avoids unnecessary redundancy. In line with this approach, the S3N ontology is adopted as the foundational layer, which builds upon the sensor, observation, sample, and actuator ontology (SOSA), semantic sensor network ontology (SSN), and W3C WoT TD ontologies. This choice of S3N enhances compatibility with current web standards and strengthens semantic alignment between ML models and HW, particularly regarding TD and the proposed NN ontology. This decision effectively addresses the requirements for both interoperability and vocabulary alignment. The prefixes and the namespaces of the used semantics are available in [48].

13.4.1.1 Semantic Framework for TinyML Neural Networks

Figure 13.8 presents the semantic schema designed for TinyML models, where an NN is categorized as a subclass of both “s3n” and “schema.” Metadata attributes enrich each ML model, enhancing its functionality and description. For example, a citation attribute allows linkage to a reference uniform resource locator (URL), such as a research article or code repository, while an identifier serves as a unique model identity (ID). Other metadata features include the repository location, details about the training dataset, creation date, author, description, and additional relevant characteristics. These attributes enable effective searching across various criteria for the model's data. A NN consists of three main types of layers: input, output, and hidden or middle layers. Each layer stores specific details such as input and output dimensions as well as quantization details. The type of layer – such as fully connected, quantized, or depthwise Conv2D – defines additional type‐specific properties, allowing for a detailed model representation. Layer indexing further illustrates the structure of the ML model.

The semantics also includes model‐specific information that links it to the HW, providing insights into the characteristics of the model. For instance, accuracy metrics can evaluate model performance on a given training dataset. However, accuracy is only one factor to consider when selecting a TinyML model. Model latency, for example, can be estimated based on the count of multiple MAC operations, as latency scales linearly with the multiply–accumulate operation (MAC) count. To align with TD standards, the RAM and flash memory requirements – critical for evaluating the compatibility of the model with IoT devices – are classified as subclasses of “s3n.” The runtime platform attribute specifies the model format and compatible frameworks. The input source for the model is determined by the types of sensors associated with it, such as a camera, microphone, or accelerometer. Input/output specifications and category attributes provide additional information on the application of the model. Finally, the input and output components of the ML model are represented as subclasses of “ssn.”

13.4.2 Semantic Knowledge Graph (KG) for TinyML Model

The design of the ML model ontology accounted for compatibility with the TD standard, providing a structured approach to describing embedded devices in IoT applications. Leveraging Semantic Web technologies, this semantics enables the representation of ML models and IoT devices within a unified KG by semantically modeling them according to a shared semantic. To evaluate the semantics and demonstrate its potential, a KG is developed for featuring six different IoT boards and 23 publicly available NN models, encompassing a broad range of devices within the TinyML community. These IoT devices typically include various sensors, limited flash memory, and a modest amount of RAM. The provided TinyML models were trained using the TensorFlow Lite Microcontroller library, an open‐source framework that is widely adopted and frequently updated. Each model is under 1 MB, which enhances both the scalability and acceptance of the presented approach within the TinyML community.

The repository also includes scripts and examples for automating the knowledge‐building and information‐extraction process using the semantics. This setup requires minimal manual input for details such as sensor specifications and citation information, streamlining the integration and application of these models in diverse IoT environments. GraphDB and similar tools can be used to visually explore the KG itself, as shown in Figure 13.9. The illustration displays six embedded devices on the right and 23 ML models on the left, with one model (“Model Activity”) highlighted in the center. Due to space constraints, some features and connections are omitted. Graph databases offer valuable flexibility in visualizing relationships within complex TinyML systems, facilitating the efficient maintenance and expansion of the KG as needed. This flexibility ensures that the KG can seamlessly accommodate more complex scenarios and evolving semantic schemas in the future.

13.4.3 Case Study 1

Suppose accelerometer and gyroscope data are used to train a TinyML model for a motion classification task. Based on the parsed results, the model requires a minimum of 128 KB of RAM and 556 KB of flash memory. In the field, there are numerous IoT boards, each with different memory capacities and integrated sensors. Instead of manually reviewing each IoT device, a more efficient way to identify which boards can run the model is through a structured query. As shown below, Algorithm 13.1 produces an organized result that pinpoints compatible boards based on the specified memory and sensor requirements.

Algorithm 13.1 Classification of a motion task for TinyML

SELECT ?Device ?MemoryRAM ?MemoryFlash
WHERE {
?Device a s3n:IoTSensor ;
ssn:hasSubSystem ?subsystem1 ;
ssn:hasSubSystem ?subsystem2 ;
ssn:hasSubSystem ?subsystem3 .
?subsystem1 a sosa_extend:Accelerometer .
?subsystem2 a sosa_extend:Gyroscope .
?subsystem3 a s3n:MicroController ;
s3n:hasSystemCapability ?capability .
?capability ssn‐system:hasSystemProperty ?property1, ?property2 .
?property1 a s3n_extend:RAM ;
schema:value ?MemoryRAM ;
schema:unitCode om:kilobyte .
?property2 a s3n_extend:Flash ;
schema:value ?MemoryFlash ;
schema:unitCode om:kilobyte .
FILTER (?MemoryRAM >= 128)
FILTER (?MemoryFlash >= 556)
}
Result:
Board: 000; RAM: 172 kb; Flash: 628 kb.
Board: 001; RAM: 187 kb; Flash: 785 kb.

13.4.4 Case Study 2

The objective is to enable ML capabilities on a customized IoT board. The board is equipped with a camera sensor and has 164 KB of RAM and 596 KB of flash memory available, based on the report of the operating system. Instead of investing significant effort in developing a new model from scratch, it can explore the model zoo to find suitable pre‐trained ML models that can operate on this board. Algorithm 13.2 can help identify compatible models from the model zoo that meet the board's specifications.

Algorithm 13.2 Empower a specified IoT board with ML functionality.

SELECT ?id ?MACs ?MemoryRAM ?MemoryFlash
WHERE {
?nn a nnet:NeuralNetwork ;
schema:identifier ?id ;
ssn:hasInput ?inputData ;
nnet:hasMultiplyAccumulateOps ?MACs ;
s3n:hasProcedureFeature ?feature1, ?feature2 .
?feature1 ssn‐system:inCondition ?condition1 .
?feature2 ssn‐system:inCondition ?condition2 .
?condition1 a s3n_extend:RAM ;
schema:minValue ?MemoryRAM ;
schema:unitCode om:kilobyte .
?condition2 a s3n_extend:Flash ;
schema:minValue ?MemoryFlash ;
schema:unitCode om:kilobyte .
?sensor ssn_extend:provideInput ?inputData ;
a sosa_extend:Camera .
FILTER (?MemoryRAM <= 164)
FILTER (?MemoryFlash <= 596)
}
Result:
uuid: e3... ; MACs: 7387976; RAM: 126 kb; Flash: 541 kb.
uuid: 10... ; MACs: 7158144; RAM: 84 kb; Flash: 246 kb.

13.4.5 Case Study 3

Suppose you are to explore available ML models for a specific task, such as recognizing “yes/no” commands in speech. At the same time, the aim is to compare the options based on memory requirements, processing delay, and accuracy on a defined dataset. The structure for this scenario is given in Algorithm 13.3 as follows.

Algorithm 13.3 Browser available ML models for a specific task.

SELECT ?id ?Category ?Accuracy ?MACs ?RequiredRAM ?RequiredFlash
WHERE {
?nn a nnet:NeuralNetwork ;
schema:identifier ?id ;
schema:description ?desc ;
ssn:hasInput ?inputSignal ;
nnet:hasCategory ?Category ;
nnet:hasMetric ?metric ;
nnet:hasMultiplyAccumulateOps ?MACs ;
nnet:trainingDataset ?dataset ;
s3n:hasProcedureFeature ?feature1, ?feature2 .
?metric a nnet:Top_1_accuracy ;
nnet:hasMetricValue ?Accuracy .
?feature1 ssn‐system:inCondition ?condition1 .
?feature2 ssn‐system:inCondition ?condition2 .
?condition1 a s3n_extend:RAM ;
schema:minValue ?RequiredRAM ;
schema:unitCode om:kilobyte .
?condition2 a s3n_extend:Flash ;
schema:minValue ?RequiredFlash ;
schema:unitCode om:kilobyte .
?sensor ssn_extend:provideInput ?inputSignal ;
a sosa_extend:Microphone .
FILTER regex(?desc, "yes/no", "i")
FILTER regex(str(?dataset), "speech_commands", "i")
}ORDER BY ?Accuracy
Result:
uuid: 3e...; Category: nnet:Classification; Acc: 0.82;
MACs: 381824; Min_RAM: 9.7 kb; Min_Flash: 9.9 kb.
... (Additional results have been excluded for brevity)

13.5 Results and Discussion

13.5.1 TinyEngine: A Compact and Memory‐Optimized Inference Library

Previously, it was believed that variations in deep learning frameworks only influenced inference speed without affecting accuracy. However, in TinyML, the choice of inference library plays a crucial role in both accuracy and latency. Effective frameworks like TinyEngine [49] maximize the limited resources of MCUs, minimize memory usage, and expand the design search space, enabling the creation of higher‐accuracy models. Unlike interpreter‐based libraries such as TF‐Lite Micro and CMSIS‐NN, which require additional memory for storing meta‐information, TinyEngine adopts a code generation approach. This eliminates the need for runtime interpretation, freeing up memory and enhancing performance. Compared to CMSIS‐NN, TinyEngine boosts inference efficiency by 22% and reduces memory usage by 2.1×, as shown in Figure 13.10.

TinyEngine's compact binary size ensures exceptional memory efficiency for MCUs. Popular deep learning programming languages such as Python and Cython often produce models whose dependencies and package sizes exceed the flash memory capacity of MCUs, making direct execution impractical. In contrast, interpreter‐based frameworks like TF‐Lite Micro introduce significant redundancy by preparing code for every operation, such as convolution and softmax, to enable cross‐model inference, even for unused operations. TinyEngine takes a different approach by compiling only the specific operations a given model utilizes into the binary. This leverages the inherent advantages of compilation over interpretation and introduces model‐specific optimization and specialization. As illustrated in Figure 13.11, this adaptive, model‐focused compilation strategy reduces code size by up to 4.5× compared to TF‐Lite Micro and up to 5.0× compared to CMSIS‐NN.

13.6 Conclusions and Future Scope

TinyML enables private, customized AI applications directly at the data source, bringing deep learning capabilities to resource‐limited devices. Key challenges include redesigning model architectures, adapting learning algorithms for lightweight training, and co‐optimizing models with HW. Recent advancements in TinyML allow AI applications on IoT systems to perform continuous learning and efficient inference. Despite challenges in co‐managing ML models and IoT devices, TinyML brings intelligence to embedded systems. TinyML will require ongoing efforts to enhance energy efficiency and performance as a rapidly evolving field. This chapter introduces a scalable, interpretable, and shareable knowledge framework crucial for advancing the IoT by integrating TinyML with Semantic Web technology. A tailored semantic schema for TinyML NN models, aligned with the W3C WoT TD semantic schema, provides a unified information model for TinyML systems. Tools and techniques for constructing and maintaining a TinyML KG were validated on six devices and 23 ML models and further assessed in three case studies. The framework also supports a low‐code platform for scalable and accessible TinyML management. Future work will focus on incorporating sensor‐specific settings for more precise knowledge management. The framework will be extended to support a broader range of TinyML libraries and enable TinyML as a service for seamless model deployment across platforms. Efforts will also be made to ensure the toolchain and framework are accessible to all users. Additionally, the integration of graph NNs with TinyML will be explored to enhance IoT systems, particularly for large‐scale anomaly detection. Accurately labeling data for on‐device learning presents a significant challenge, particularly for applications where supervision is costly, such as in vision tasks. While techniques like predicting the next input word may be effective in some contexts, they are not suitable for most tasks. A promising solution is the use of self‐supervised learning tasks for on‐device training, which has gained attention as a viable approach.
