14
Fight Poison with Poison: Tiny Machine Learning Resilience Against Poisoning Attacks*

Tomoki Chiba1, Yasuyuki Tahara1, Akihiko Ohsuga1, Agbotiname Lucky Imoize2,3, and Yuichi Sei1

1Graduate School of Informatics and Engineering, The University of Electro‐Communications, Chōfu, Tokyo, Japan

2Department of Electrical and Electronics Engineering, Faculty of Engineering, University of Lagos, Lagos, Nigeria

3Department of Electrical Engineering and Information Technology, Institute of Digital Communication, Ruhr University, Bochum, Germany

14.1 Introduction

Machine learning technology has emerged as an auxiliary tool for human decision‐making processes. Machine learning infers patterns and features from large datasets. Systems that use machine learning have become commonplace and are currently used in many fields, such as autonomous driving and health monitoring [2–4]. Thus, machine learning is increasingly being integrated into many systems, assuming a role akin to social infrastructure. Moreover, the use of machine learning technology to solve cybersecurity problems has been proposed, and such solutions are already in use [5, 6]. Therefore, the safety of the systems and services that use machine learning technology (hereinafter referred to as “machine learning systems”) has become extremely important. If there are vulnerabilities in machine learning systems, other systems that have implemented these machine learning systems could be adversely affected.

Considering these circumstances, as the popularity of machine learning systems grows, the value of attackers who target machine learning systems is increasing. The methods of attack mainly include targeted attacks, which generate mislabeled data and mix it into the training data, and indiscriminate attacks, which cause general misclassification and lead to denial of service, among other things.

The methods of attack on machine learning systems are diverse, and some are difficult to visually detect (Section 14.3.1). Therefore, in the current era of smart cities, if machine learning systems are introduced without countermeasures against such attacks, there is a chance that large‐scale accidents or incidents causing significant financial damage and even loss of life could occur.

Extensive research has focused on attacks on and defenses for machine learning systems and on disseminating knowledge about the vulnerabilities of machine learning systems [7–9]. Various methods of attack on machine learning systems have been reported [10, 11]. The current study focuses on poisoning attacks. A poisoning attack is an attack that degrades the predictive accuracy of a model by injecting harmful data (poisonous data) into the training data [12, 13].

This study aims to mitigate the degradation of the accuracy of machine learning models by poisoning attacks. Specifically, the goals of this study are as follows:

  • To reduce the degradation of model accuracy due to poisoning attacks.
  • To stabilize the accuracy of detecting the harmful data used in poisoning attacks.

In this study, we propose a defense method to achieve these goals, and we verify the effectiveness of the proposed method through evaluation experiments.

The contributions of this study are as follows:

  • We propose a novel approach that reverses the use of poisoning attacks to defend the model.
  • We reduce the false detection of actual data by prioritizing the removal of data.
  • We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method against poisoning attacks through validation experiments in the assumed environment.

The introduction of tiny machine learning (TinyML), which deploys machine learning models on resource‐constrained devices, introduces additional layers of complexity and also potential vulnerabilities to the security landscape. As TinyML systems become integral to various applications, from smart home devices to wearable health monitors, ensuring the security and robustness of these systems is also becoming paramount [14].

TinyML systems operate, by design, under extreme constraints in terms of computational power, memory, and energy consumption [15]. These constraints make necessary the use of highly optimized and often simplified machine learning models, which can inadvertently introduce new attack surfaces. For instance, the low complexity of models in TinyML systems may make them more susceptible to certain types of poisoning attacks that exploit these simplifications.

Furthermore, the deployment environments for TinyML systems are often less controlled than those of traditional machine learning systems, as these devices are common and users interact with them directly. This increases the potential number of attack vectors and the ease with which malicious actors can introduce poisonous data. Therefore, the security strategies employed must be lightweight yet effective and must balance the need for robust defenses with the limited resources available.

In this context, our focus on developing efficient detection and mitigation strategies for poisoning attacks is quite relevant. The proposed defense method, which aims to minimize model degradation and accurately identify harmful data, is particularly suited for the TinyML paradigm. By ensuring that the defensive mechanisms of TinyML systems are computationally efficient and do not overly burden the limited resources of TinyML devices, we can enhance the security of these systems without compromising their performance or functionality.

Additionally, the practical implications of ensuring the security of TinyML systems are significant. As these devices are often connected to critical infrastructure and personal environments, any successful attack could have far‐reaching consequences and impact not just individual users but entire communities. Hence, our efforts to improve the resilience of machine learning systems against poisoning attacks are crucial for the broader adoption of and trust in TinyML technologies.

In conclusion, the integration of robust, lightweight security measures into TinyML systems is essential to safeguarding the next generation of smart devices. Our proposed method contributes to this goal by addressing the unique challenges posed by the resource constraints and deployment scenarios of TinyML and ensures that these innovative systems are powerful and secure.

The structure of this chapter is as follows. In Section 14.2, we present the assumed environment and threat model. Section 14.3 introduces related research and explores the differences between this study and previous studies. The proposed method is described in Section 14.4, and the experimental setup and results are presented in Section 14.5. Section 14.6 discusses the proposed method. Finally, the conclusion to this study is summarized in Section 14.7.

14.2 Problem Definition

In this section, we discuss the assumed environment and the threat model.

14.2.1 Assumed Environment

Machine learning systems are utilized in various scenarios. The use cases are particularly numerous in IoT environments, such as autonomous driving and automated robot control. In these contexts, if a machine learning system is attacked as described in Section 14.1, the damage could be considerable.

In this study, we assume an IoT environment in which the data used for model training is obtained from multiple sources. Our assumed environment is illustrated in Figure 14.1. As an example, we consider data obtained from multiple IoT devices. Here, we envision a context in which a company builds a road sign recognition model for autonomous vehicles. This recognition model is installed in the autonomous vehicle to identify road signs, and the vehicle's speed is adjusted according to the recognition results. In this assumed environment, the attacker executes a poisoning attack by intervening in the data collection process.

Furthermore, this study assumes there exist multiple entities or IoT devices with access to the dataset used for training, and some of them have malicious intent. In other words, some data providers supply harmful data, thereby launching a poisoning attack on the model being constructed by the data collector. Hereinafter, the data providers will be referred to as “devices.”

There are no limitations on the kinds of machine learning systems that we consider to be the target of attacks and defenses. Due to the mechanism of poisoning attacks, the attacker must access the training data before the model is trained and used. Therefore, machine learning systems that learn online easily serve as targets. However, the types of scenarios in which attackers are able to access training data differ. For instance, if the attacker has access to a provider who builds and offers the model as a service, poisoning attacks can occur even if the machine learning system does not learn online.

14.2.2 Threat Model

The attacker assumed in this study intends to perform a poisoning attack, which involves injecting harmful data into the training dataset to undermine the accuracy of the model. The objective of the assumed poisoning attack is not the intentional misclassification of specific data by the attacker but an overall degradation of accuracy. This objective is based on the attacker's intention to cause significant events, such as accidents involving autonomous vehicles, in the assumed environment.

Moreover, the attacker is presumed to have background knowledge about the learning algorithm and to be able to draw or generate data from the distribution of the data used for training. Although this setting may seem unrealistic in general, using proxy training data from the same distribution would be feasible in a real‐world setting [16].

An example of a poisoning attack in a scenario where training data is obtained from multiple devices is illustrated with the case of the Microsoft chatbot “Tay” in Figure 14.2. Tay was a program designed to generate human‐like tweets by learning from conversations with humans. However, some individuals intentionally taught Tay offensive expressions, which led Tay to tweet similarly offensive content. Consequently, Microsoft decided to terminate the service approximately 16 hours after its launch. In our study, we assume data is collected from multiple devices, but the attacker is able to access only a subset of these devices.

14.3 Related Work

We introduce related work in this section.

14.3.1 Poisoning Attacks

As shown in Section 14.1, poisoning attacks involve the insertion of harmful data (poisonous data) into a training dataset to degrade the predictive accuracy of a machine learning model [17]. In this context, harmful data is data whose features have been deliberately modified to cause the model to misclassify normal input data. An example of data that has been intentionally modified is shown in Goodfellow et al. [18]. Here, a slight perturbation is added to an image labeled “panda” that causes a normally functioning model to classify the modified data as “gibbon” with 99.3% confidence. The perturbation is so subtle that it is undetectable to the human eye, which makes annotation‐based detection challenging.

After the model is trained on this data, it misclassifies certain inputs. The targets of poisoning attacks mainly include spam detection and malware detection systems, but online recommendation systems have recently also been identified as targets [19].

For poisoning attacks that occur during model training, the attacker must have access to the training data. For example, online tools for detecting malware in PDFs use feedback from end users to verify the detection results for the provided data [20]. Some systems update classifiers based on these verification results [21]. In this context, end users have access to the training data for the classification system. Another example is web‐based honeypots, which collect malware data for training purposes [17]. Here, too, although it is not possible to obtain different data, arbitrary data can be added to the training dataset. Poisoning attacks have also occurred in scenarios where data is collected via crowdsensing [22], and methods of accessing training data may vary depending on the environment. An example of a poisoning attack is shown in Figure 14.3.

Another variant of the poisoning attack is the backdoor attack. This attack method inserts hidden triggers (backdoor keys) into the model during training, which do not affect the normal behavior of the model. The model is then manipulated so that it performs unexpected actions only when the backdoor key is added to the input data. Unlike regular poisoning attacks, backdoor attacks do not cause the model to misclassify specific backdoor‐keyed data [23]. Therefore, the approaches to defending against poisoning attacks and backdoor attacks generally differ.

As mentioned in Section 14.1, poisoning attacks are classified mainly as two types: targeted attacks and indiscriminate attacks. The objectives of indiscriminate attacks are to undermine the integrity of the target system and to reduce its availability. Targeted attacks seek to maintain normal operation while causing the misclassification of specific samples [24].

Indiscriminate attacks, on the other hand, are intended to reduce the overall predictive accuracy of the model.

The transferability of poisoning attacks has also been studied [25]. Shafahi et al. demonstrated that even if an attacker cannot access the target model, they may still create an attack method in a white‐box environment for use on a self‐generated model that exhibits the same behavior as the target model that would be effective against the target model as well [26].

The expected damage from poisoning attacks depends heavily on the task executed by the target model. There are challenges related to the feasibility of the attacks, such as the right of access to the training data and the difficulty for the model creators and users to verify the training data, which indicates that the definition of feasibility is still unclear.

14.3.2 Defensive Methods Against Poisoning Attacks

Various approaches to defending against poisoning attacks have been studied [27]. The primary objective of existing methods for defense against poisoning attacks is to detect data that negatively impacts the model's accuracy [23]. Other approaches include sanitizing outliers [28], but several problems have been noted [29]. Therefore, the defense method proposed in this paper is intended to mitigate the degradation of model accuracy by detecting data that adversely affects the accuracy and the data sources that provide such data, which is similar to the former approach.

Van et al. proposed a robust training approach that mitigated the effects of data poisoning attacks on machine learning models [30]. They introduced the Healthy Influential Noise‐Based Training (HINT) method, which leverages influence functions to generate “healthy noise” that hardens the model against adversarial data without significantly affecting its generalization ability. They demonstrated the effectiveness of HINT using extensive evaluations on two image datasets, and they showed that the method efficiently protects models from both untargeted and targeted poisoning attacks. Wu et al. investigated the vulnerabilities of reward model learning to malicious preference poisoning attacks [31]. The authors proposed two algorithmic approaches – a gradient‐based framework and a rank‐by‐distance method – and demonstrated their effectiveness in three application domains: autonomous control, recommendation systems, and textual prompt‐response learning. Their findings revealed significant vulnerabilities, where some attacks achieved a success rate of up to 100% with minimal poisoned data.

Although our scenario assumes that training data is collected from multiple devices, defensive methods against poisoning attacks under similar assumptions in IoT environments have been studied [32]. Baracaldo et al. envisioned sensing data from multiple IoT devices aggregated in the cloud for use as training data for models. Among these IoT devices, some carry malicious intent and send these data to the cloud to execute a poisoning attack. Baracaldo et al.'s study demonstrated that the information that links IoT devices to data (provenance data) is robust against tampering [33], and they validated each IoT device by partitioning the training data according to the provenance data. Given the similarity of the assumed environments, Baracaldo et al.'s method is presented as an existing method in this study. As a foundation to Baracaldo et al.'s defensive method, we mention Nelson et al.'s reject on negative impact (RONI) method [16, 34]. Their study proposed an approach that removed from devices data that negatively impacted spam filter defenses. However, Baracaldo et al. compared the defense performance of their method with that of RONI and demonstrated that their method outperformed RONI. Therefore, our study uses only Baracaldo et al.'s method for comparison. There are many studies that address poisoning attacks; however, the capabilities of poisoning attacks are continually improving, which leads to a cat‐and‐mouse game between attacks and defense methods. As a result, existing methods may not always be effective against new poisoning attacks. Our proposed method employs the most recent poisoning attack techniques that are available at the time of use to detect such attacks. This novel approach has the advantage that it is adaptable to new attack methods, provided that the attack algorithms are known.

In TinyML, privacy protection is also essential. When information for machine learning is collected from individuals, differential privacy techniques are sometimes used to protect privacy [35]. Differential privacy is a crucial technology that has recently been used by companies such as Google and Apple [36]. However, it has the drawback of being vulnerable to poisoning attacks. Cao et al. introduced the first comprehensive study of poisoning attacks against key‐value data with local differential privacy (LDP) protocols [37]. They formulated the attacks as two‐objective optimization problems to maximize both the estimated frequency and mean values of the target keys. Their approach, which was called maximal gain attack (MGA), demonstrated good effectiveness in compromising the privacy and integrity of the key‐value data. They also proposed and evaluated defenses against these attacks and found them to be somewhat effective, thereby highlighting the need for protective measures that are more robust in LDP protocols. Wu et al. explored the susceptibility of LDP protocols for key‐value data to poisoning attacks [38]. They developed new poisoning strategies that targeted the frequency and mean estimation of keys, which proved the efficiency of their attacks through both theoretical and empirical analyses. Their findings suggest that although some defenses can mitigate the impact of these attacks under certain conditions, there remains a significant need to develop stronger and more adaptive defenses to protect the integrity of LDP‐based systems. Sun et al. investigated the vulnerability of LDP protocols to poisoning attacks, and they focused specifically on recovery mechanisms and their robustness [39]. The authors proposed various attack strategies for manipulating the data aggregated by LDP protocols, and they showcased how adversaries could inject fake users to significantly alter the analytic outcomes of the data. They highlighted the challenges and limitations of existing defenses and called for improved methods to detect and mitigate poisoning attempts by fake users.

Table 14.1 shows a comparison of our work with existing methods.

14.3.3 Other Attacks on TinyML

Traditional machine learning algorithms do not consider attacks of an adversarial nature, and their performance degrades significantly when they are used in adversarial settings [20, 40].

In addition to the poisoning attacks mentioned in Section 14.3.1, attacks on machine learning models include evasion attacks [41] and examples of adversarial attacks [42]. These attacks target machine learning systems in a way similar to poisoning attacks. Evasion attacks manipulate the machine learning model so that it fails to detect events that should be detected, particularly in applications like anomaly detection.

Attacks that infer model parameters after training have also been studied [43]. By inferring the parameters of models used in existing services, attackers are able to generate models that respond to inputs similarly to the target model. This technique can be used to generate adversarial examples that cause the target model to reject large amounts of input. Another attack on machine learning systems that is related to privacy invasion is the membership inference attack [44].

Some attacks in TinyML environments generate a large burst of data to overwhelm the system. In IoT environments in particular, where individual device performance is often insufficient, it is critical to identify such data sources quickly and efficiently [45]. As there are a variety of attacks on TinyML, this chapter focuses on attacks that degrade the accuracy of machine learning models through poisoning.

14.4 Proposed Method

We propose our new method in this section.

14.4.1 Overview

As described in Section 14.1, our proposed method aims to mitigate the degradation of model accuracy, caused by poisoning attacks, in a multi‐device scenario. To achieve this objective, we partition the data according to device, and we compare the accuracies of the model before and after the data of each device is filtered to define the impact of each device on the model's accuracy. In this context, filtering is defined as the process of excluding from the training data the data obtained from a specific device. Subsequently, a method is proposed for removing data from devices deemed harmful by comparing the defined metrics for each device with their impact on the model. The flowchart for the proposed method is shown in Figure 14.4.

A schematic diagram of the proposed method is shown in Figure 14.5. As described in Section 14.2.1, this study assumes a model built in an environment where data is obtained from multiple IoT devices, and some of these devices launch poisoning attacks by providing harmful data. In other words, the training data that is used to build the model includes harmful data (the dataset includes poisonous data). The defense system of the proposed method removes the harmful data from the training data. The data that is obtained through this process is referred to as “the dataset” after the defense method, and the model trained on these data is referred to as the “defense model.”

The proposed method can be broadly divided into the following three steps:

  1. Filter the data from the target device to create filtered training and validation datasets (hereinafter referred to as “filtered train set” and “filtered validation set”). Train a model on the filtered train set to create a filtered model (Figure 14.6). Compare, on the filtered validation set, the accuracies of the filtered model and the unfiltered model to evaluate the impact of the device on the model's accuracy.
  2. Create datasets where each device's data is replaced with harmful data; generate adversarial models that are trained on these datasets. Replace the unfiltered model used in step (1) with the adversarial model and calculate the “adversarial impact” by comparing the accuracy of the filtered model.
  3. Based on the values defined in steps (1) and (2), derive the confidence level for use in judging the target device as harmful and determine the proportion of data to be removed. If this proportion is neither 0% nor 100%, use a data removal priority algorithm to decide which data to remove considering the priority and the amount of data to be removed (Figure 14.7).

The above steps are repeated for each device. The data that remains after removal is considered to be the data after defense, and the model that is trained on these data is the defense model proposed in this method.

The algorithm of the proposed method is presented as Algorithm 14.1. The definitions for the symbols used in this algorithm are shown in Table 14.2. The proposed method receives , , and as inputs. is a list of device identifiers that represent the source for each data sample. The original dataset is first divided into training and validation data ( and ). The validation data generated here is used as test data to verify the accuracy of the model within the method. and are lists of indices that represent the correspondence between and within , respectively. Next, and are divided into data for each device using along with and . As the proposed method evaluates the validity of data based on device rather than the data itself, processing the data by device is necessary. The processing for each device then begins. and refer to the training and validation data, respectively, that are provided by device . First, the filtering process defines . The filtering process removes from and the data belonging to device . This processing corresponds to the steps shown in Figure 14.6.

In the for loop, the introduced in Section 14.4.2 and the described in Section 14.4.3 are calculated. Using these impact values, the data that is selected to be removed is removed using the function . The function is described in Section 14.4.4. During this process, the aim is to improve detection accuracy by defining the priority for removing data from among the data deemed to be harmful. By removing data that is deemed to be harmful from the and for each device, and ultimately become the datasets after defense by the proposed method. Finally, the two datasets are concatenated and is output. These processing steps are shown in Figure 14.7.

14.4.2 Negative Impact

As indicated in Section 14.3.1, poisoning attacks degrade the model accuracy by injecting harmful data into the training dataset. Therefore, when we search for and remove harmful data from a dataset, one of the criteria to consider is the “impact on the original model's accuracy.”

This method uses the RONI [16] concept to evaluate the effect of each device's training data on the accuracy of a model. The effect on model accuracy is defined as the difference between the accuracy of the unfiltered model on the filtered validation set () and the accuracy of the filtered model on the filtered validation set ( ).

(14.1)

The higher the value of , the more negatively it affects the model accuracy. Thus, with the proposed method, the higher the value of , the greater the likelihood that the data is harmful. To prevent the harmful data from having an effect on the validation, the filtered validation set is used to confirm and .

If the value of equation 14.1 is less than or equal to 0, the impact on the model accuracy is considered, at the least, not to be negative. In such cases, the device is judged to be normal by the proposed method regardless of the in Section 14.4.3. The data obtained from devices that are judged not to be normal is not subject to removal; thus, no further steps are taken. Conversely, if is greater than 0, then the data is considered to negatively affect the model accuracy, and the data becomes candidates for removal. The formula for the number of data points to be removed is described in Section 14.4.4.

The function for calculating is shown in Algorithm 14.2. This function requires the validation data that is used to calculate model accuracy and the models and . The algorithm simply calculates the accuracy of the two input models on the input validation data, and it stores the accuracy data in and , respectively. The process for calculating accuracy corresponds to the function in the algorithm. The result of Equation 14.1 is then stored in and returned as the output of the function .

14.4.3 Adversarial Impact

Unlike existing methods, the proposed method defines an adversarial impact for each device. By executing a poisoning attack on the defense side and injecting harmful data into the filtered dataset, the method is able to virtually output the model accuracy if the data being validated is harmful data (referred to as ). The difference between and is defined as the threshold, as shown in equation 14.2:

(14.2)

Here, it is assumed that even if an attack is executed by the use of harmful data, the harm caused to the model remains. This assumption is based on our preliminary experimental results. When a normal device is inspected, an executed attack on that device's data renders the data harmful data, which increases the proportion of total data that is harmful data. Conversely, when a harmful device is inspected, an attack on its data does not increase the total amount of harmful data according to the aforementioned assumption. Consequently, the value of is expected to be low for normal devices and high for harmful devices. Similarly, is expected to be higher for harmful devices than for normal devices. Therefore, the value of itself does not vary significantly between normal and harmful devices. However, compared with , which is a factor in normal/harmful judgments, the for normal devices is expected to be lower than the . As a result, for normal devices does not fall below the value of , thereby preventing the false detection of normal devices. For harmful devices, the values of and are expected to be similar, which makes harmful devices easier to detect than normal devices.

The function for calculating is shown in Algorithm 14.3. The inputs required by the function are the data for the target device , the filtered training and validation data and , the model trained on , and the model before training . Unlike the algorithm for calculating , the function first needs to generate harmful data. Therefore, harmful data is generated using the function based on . The algorithm specifically for depends on the attack method used, which is determined by the user of the defense system (the proposed method). In the experiments run for this study, the attack method proposed by Biggio et al. [17] was used. The generated harmful data is stored in , and then is concatenated with and stored in . This way, virtually recreates the unfiltered data while assuming device is a harmful device. Subsequently, the accuracy values and are calculated using the function . The calculated accuracies are then used to compute the value of according to equation 14.2, and the result is stored in , which is returned as the output of function .

14.4.4 Data Removal

Finally, the proportion of data to be removed is calculated by using the relationship between the impact on model accuracy defined in Section 14.4.2 and defined in Section 14.4.3. The equation for the data removal rate is shown as equation 14.3:

(14.3)

In the proposed method, if the value of the negative impact is less than or equal to 0, the device is judged to be normal, and the corresponding data is not removed. This policy is based on the definition of negative impact, where data from a device with a value less than or equal to 0 does not adversely affect (degrade) the accuracy of the other data. When is greater than 0 but less than , the removal rate is defined as the ratio of to . If exceeds 0, it adversely affects the model accuracy and thus becomes a candidate for data removal. However, in this study, we calculate an independent removal rate and apply it to each device instead of removing all the data from a device marked for removal. The value of represents the value that assumes that all data from the target device is harmful. The closer is to , the higher the likelihood that the data from the device is harmful. Therefore, the removal rate is determined from the proximity of to . If exceeds , it is considered to be worse than the value that would be assumed if all the data were harmful, and the removal rate is set to 1.0, which indicates that all the data from the target device will be removed.

After the data removal process, the removed data is excluded from all subsequent data that is used for validating the next device. That is, no data that is deemed harmful exists in the data used after the judgment. Therefore, the data judged as harmful does not affect the judgment of subsequent devices.

The algorithm that is used to calculate the data removal rate is presented as Algorithm 14.4. The function takes the training and validation data and , the filtered data and , and the negative impact and adversarial impact used for calculating the removal rate, as well as the number of data points from the target device as inputs.

This function processes the conditions according to Equation 14.3 to determine the removal rate within those conditions. The first conditional branch of the algorithm checks whether exceeds the value of , which corresponds to the last case in equation 14.3. If this condition is met, the data removal rate is 100%, and the training and validation data is set to the filtered data, which effectively removes the data from the target device. The second conditional branch checks whether is greater than 0 but does not exceed , which corresponds to the middle case in equation 14.3. If this condition is met, the removal rate is calculated by dividing by . After the removal rate is calculated, the number of data points to be removed is determined using on both training and validation data. Then, the function for determining the removal priority is called to store the priority lists in and . Finally, the function is called with the original data to be removed, the number of data points to be removed, and the priority lists to perform data removal according to the priority. After data removal is carried out, the training and validation data and are returned. If neither condition is met, then is less than or equal to 0, and no data is removed as the device is judged to be normal.

14.4.5 Removal Priority

Harmful devices can be classified into two types: those that provide only harmful data (all data is harmful) and those that provide both harmful and non‐harmful data (some data is harmful). This section describes the scenario where only some of the provided data is harmful.

This functionality is called only when the algorithm in Section 14.4.4 determines that part of the data should be removed. The priority for removing data is set highest for data whose features are furthest away from the opposite side of the Support Vector Machine (SVM) decision boundary. In other words, data that deviates significantly from the SVM prediction is preferentially removed. First, the data from the target device is compressed into two dimensions using principal component analysis (PCA). Then, the distance between the SVM and the mapped data is calculated in the two‐dimensional space. The data whose SVM prediction is incorrect is prioritized for removal according to the calculated distance, starting from the largest. If the number of data points that are removed by this method is less than the number of data points to be removed as determined by the removal rate, the data points whose SVM prediction is correct but that are close to the SVM boundary are prioritized for removal.

The algorithm for this functionality is shown in Algorithm 14.5. The function takes as inputs the training and validation data and , the device identifier , the data from the target device and , and the filtered data and . Because the removal priority is determined within a two‐dimensional plane, dimensionality reduction is needed for data whose dimensionality exceeds two. In this study, PCA is used to reduce the dimensionality of , , and . Next, to determine whether the data is on the opposite side of the SVM decision boundary, an array mesh grid is generated to represent the two‐dimensional plane. The model boundary can be understood by predicting the components of this mesh grid. The prediction results are stored in . Then, for each data point, the following are calculated:

  1. Distance from the decision boundary.
  2. Whether it is located on the opposite side of the boundary.

These values are stored in and , respectively. After all data points are processed, is split into training and validation and stored in and , respectively. These two lists are returned as the output of the function .

Although this algorithm assumes a binary classification, in the case of multi‐class classification, a single data label value can be assumed to be binary against other labels. By generating a linear SVM as in Algorithm 14.5 and calculating the distance to the target data, the priority can be determined in the same manner as in binary classification.

14.5 Evaluation Experiment

This section presents the evaluation results.

14.5.1 Overview

We conducted experiments to verify the effectiveness of the proposed defense method against the poisoning attacks presented in this paper. The accuracies of the following four models were compared in the experiments:

  • Model trained with data containing no harmful data (Perfect defense)
  • Model trained with data containing harmful data (No defense)
  • Model defended by the proposed method (Proposal)
  • Model defended by the existing method (Existing)

The accuracies of these models were evaluated using test data independent of the experimental environment.

Furthermore, the attack method and existing method used in this study were implemented according to the open‐source code provided in Nicolae et al. [46]. To shorten the duration of the experiment, the harmful data generated by the attack method was prepared and used in advance. We varied the number of malicious devices and compared the accuracy of each defended model against the proportion of harmful data. Additionally, the threshold for determining harmful devices in the existing method was set to values of 0.0 and 0.2 (the default value set in the open‐source code by Nicolae et al. [46]) for comparison. The experimental results reported in the present study are the values averaged over 10 runs.

The following datasets were used for experiments:

  • Modified National Institute of Standards and Technology (MNIST)
  • Synthetic data
  • Environmental sensor telemetry data

The experimental settings and the results obtained on each dataset are described in Sections 14.5.2–14.5.4.

14.5.2 MNIST

14.5.2.1 Experimental Setting

In this experiment, the MNIST dataset of handwritten digits was used. Although the original dataset has 10 classes labeled from 0 to 9, we set up a binary classification task for digits 0 and 4, similar to the experiment settings by Biggio et al. Harmful data was generated using the attack method proposed by Biggio et al. [17]. Their attack method is an algorithm that generates harmful data in a poisoning attack that targets SVM. The experiment was conducted in two ways: with and without determining the removal priority. For the case with the removal priority determination, the proportion of harmful data in malicious devices was also used as a parameter to verify the effectiveness of the removal priority described in Section 14.4.5. For the case without the removal priority determination, the proportion of harmful data in each malicious device was set to 100%, and the experiment was conducted in an environment in which all the data provided by the malicious devices was harmful.

14.5.2.2 Results

The graph depicting the accuracy of the defended models is shown in Figure 14.8a. The results in this figure do not represent the case that used the removal priority described in Section 14.4.5. As shown in Figure 14.8a, both the existing method and the proposed method significantly outperform the model with no defense up to a proportion of harmful data of 40%. However, when the proportion of harmful data exceeds this level, the accuracy deteriorates even compared with the model without defense. This is likely because an increase in the proportion of harmful data in the training data causes the values for both the existing method and the proposed method to be high for normal data, which indicates that normal data is judged to have a negative impact on model accuracy.

Furthermore, the F1 score and accuracy for the harmful data detection rate of the existing method and the proposed method are shown in Figures 14.8b and c, respectively. The proposed method with a threshold of 0.2 significantly outperforms the existing method on the F1 score. However, the existing method, with a threshold of 0.0, has nearly the same values as the proposed method. These results suggest that the definition of the removal rate in the proposed method (equation 14.3) causes it to produce results similar to the existing method with a threshold of 0.0.

Figures 14.9a and b show the precision and recall results for harmful data detection in the above experiment. From the results in (a), it is evident that the proposed method outperforms the existing methods on both threshold values of 0.0 and 0.2 up to a proportion of harmful data of 40%. In (b), however, at a threshold of 0.0, the results for the existing method generally surpass those of the proposed method. These results indicate that the proposed method suppresses false positives with its removal rate formula, but that it also has difficulty detecting a large amount of harmful data.

Figure 14.10 shows, using a box plot, the distribution of F1 score values from the detection accuracy of the experiment in Figure 14.8. As can be seen, both the existing and proposed methods exhibit similar shapes, which indicates that neither has superiority in detection stability.

Figures 14.11 and 14.12 show the experimental results for the case when removal priority is determined. As mentioned in the previous section, the proportion of harmful data in each malicious device was set to 50%. Therefore, even if all of the 10 devices were malicious, the proportion of harmful data in the entire dataset would be only 50%.

Because the MNIST data is used for a binary classification task in this experiment, the task is relatively simple. Therefore, as shown in Figure 14.11a, the accuracies of the models are generally high after each of the defense methods is used. However, it can be observed that the accuracies of “Existing_0.0” and the proposed method are higher than that of “No defense” up to a proportion of harmful data of 25%. This indicates that the proposed method's defense effectively reduces the degradation in the model's accuracy for a proportion of harmful data of up to 25%. Figures 14.11b and c show the detection accuracy of harmful data in terms of F1 score and accuracy, respectively. These results show that the proposed method generally shows higher detection accuracy than the existing method.

Figures 14.12a and b show the precision and recall results for the detection of harmful data in the above experiment. For precision, the proposed method generally shows higher accuracy. Particularly, the difference is dramatic when the proportion of harmful data is in the range from 5% to 35%. In contrast, the results for recall show that, at a threshold of 0.0, the existing method generally outperforms the proposed method. These results suggest that although the proposed method suppresses false positives, it has greater difficulty detecting harmful data than the existing method.

To summarize these results, there is no significant difference in model accuracy between the proposed method and the existing method; however, the proposed method demonstrates a much higher detection accuracy for harmful data. This indicates that the proposed method's model accuracy would improve in complex tasks in which the detection and removal of harmful data have a significant impact on model performance (Figure 14.13).

14.5.3 Synthetic Data

14.5.3.1 Experimental Setting

The dataset and harmful data generation method that are used for the poisoning attack in this experiment are based on the method used in Zhou et al. [47]. Figure 14.14 shows a sample of the synthetic data. This attack algorithm specifies a parameter () that represents the strength of the attack, with values ranging from 0 to 1. The strength of the attack indicates how much the generated harmful data deviates from the original distribution, where data that is farther from the original distribution shows greater deviation. As can be seen from Figure 14.14, the light gray and dark gray plots represent normal data, whereas the medium gray represents harmful data. With the attack parameter set to 0.5, the harmful data is distributed around the midpoint between the ight gray and dark gray normal data. An attack parameter value set close to 0 represents a weaker setting, whereas a value close to 1 represents more harmful data.

We conducted experiments with three different values for the attack parameter (0.3, 0.5, 0.7). As was done in the experiments in Section 14.5.2, the total number of devices was set to 10, where each device provided 100 data points. The thresholds for the existing method were set the same values as in Section 14.5.2.

14.5.3.2 Results

The results for the accuracy of each model after the defense methods were implemented are shown in Figures 14.15a, 14.16a, and 14.17a. The accuracy of the models that were trained without any defense decreases as the proportion of harmful data increases, whereas the existing and proposed methods maintain their accuracy relatively well. Additionally, with higher values of the attack parameter, the accuracy of the models for each defense method decreases.

The rate of detection of harmful data when the attack parameter value is set to 0.5 is shown in Figures 14.16b and c. These results indicate that the proposed method is slightly better at detecting harmful data than the existing method. Regarding the F1 score, it can be seen that the detection rate increases as the proportion of harmful data increases up to a proportion of 60%. This may be because the degree of influence of false positives decreases with an increase in the number of harmful data. However, the detection rate drops sharply when the proportion of harmful data reaches 70%. When the proportion of harmful data is 70%, the ratio of harmful data to the total data exceeds 50% for both the existing and proposed methods. Therefore, it is thought that the reason for this is the difficulty in judging whether harmful data has an adverse effect on the model. Figure 14.18 shows the negative impact values for a given ratio of harmful data to total data. As can be seen from this figure, the difference in negative impact between normal and harmful devices is small, which indicates that the lower detection rate may be due to the above reason.

Similar to the accuracy results for each model, the rate of detecting harmful data decreases for higher values of the attack parameter. This result is likely due to the following two factors:

  • The stronger effect of harmful data makes it easier to detect the proportion of harmful data up to a certain value.
  • The stronger effect of harmful data makes it more difficult to detect a smaller amount of harmful data compared with weaker parameters.

Figure 14.19 shows, using box plots, the distribution of F1 scores for the detection accuracy from the experiment with . Although there is no significant difference between these box plots and the box plots in Figure 14.10 for the MNIST experiment, a closer look reveals that except when the proportion of harmful data is 40% and 60%, the proposed method's box plots are generally higher and smaller.

14.5.4 Environmental Sensor Telemetry Data

14.5.4.1 Experimental Setting

The dataset used in this experiment was obtained from the data analysis platform Kaggle [48]. This sensing data was generated by an environmental sensor array [49]. The breadboard‐based sensor array is connected to a Raspberry Pi single‐board computer. These IoT devices are intentionally placed in physical locations under various environmental conditions, such as temperature and humidity conditions, to collect data. The attributes of these data are shown in Table 14.3.

In this experiment, we aim to predict the “light” attribute value using other sensed data except for “motion.” The reason for excluding “motion” from the explanatory variables is to avoid making the task overly simple, as “motion” is a Boolean value.

The experimental settings are similar to those of the experiments in Sections 14.5.2 and 14.5.3, with the total number of devices set to 10. The number of data points for each device is set to 20 and 100, and we conduct experiments for both settings. The proportion of harmful data in the malicious devices is set to 50% and 100%, as was done in Section 14.5.2. When the proportion is set to 50%, the algorithm for determining the removal priority is used, and it is not used when the proportion is set to 100%.

14.5.4.2 Results

The results obtained when the number of data points per device is 20 and the proportion of harmful data in the malicious devices is 100% are shown in Figures 14.20 and 14.21. Both the existing method and the proposed method can detect harmful data up to a proportion of harmful data of 40%. However, when the proportion exceeds 40%, neither method detects harmful data effectively. Correspondingly, the model accuracy shown in Figure 14.20a is almost the same as that for the no defense for this proportion (Figure 14.22).

Table 14.4 shows the values for each device in the experiment with three to five malicious devices. The results, which are averaged over 10 runs, show that as soon as the number of malicious devices reaches four (i.e., 40% harmful data), the values for all malicious devices become 0. As was defined in equation 14.1 of Section 14.4.2, is the difference between the accuracy of the filtered model and that of the unfiltered model. A value of 0 indicates that both models have either endpoint accuracy values (0 or 1) or the same accuracy value. Because the accuracy values are not extreme, as is shown in Figure 14.20a, the accuracy of the filtered and unfiltered models is taken to be the same. This means that including or excluding the data from a single malicious device does not affect the model accuracy.

Figures 14.23 and 14.24 show the experimental results for the number of data points per device set to 100 and the proportion of harmful data in malicious devices set to 50%. In this experimental setting, the removal priority is defined, and the data is removed accordingly. Figure 14.23a shows the results for the prediction accuracy of the model, and the accuracy did not differ significantly from the results for the previous experimental setting (Figure 14.20). The No defense model reaches its lower accuracy limit when the proportion of harmful data is 10%. In Figure 14.20a, the lower limit is reached at a proportion of harmful data of approximately 30%, but in this setting, it is 10%, which indicates that the proportion of harmful devices to the total number of devices has a more significant impact on model accuracy than does the proportion of harmful data alone. This means that the increase in the number of harmful devices has a greater negative impact on the accuracy of the model than does the proportion of harmful data within those devices.

Furthermore, Figure 14.25 shows the box plot of the F1 score values for the detection accuracy in the experimental setting shown in Figure 14.23. The results in Figure 14.24 indicate that in a setting where the proportion of harmful data is set to 5%, the existing method consistently detects the harmful data with high accuracy. However, the proposed method sometimes achieves higher detection rates than the existing method, but it generally has lower average detection rates. When the proportion of harmful data is set to 10% and 15%, the median values indicate that the proposed method obtains higher detection rates than the existing method. When the proportion of harmful data is set to 20% or higher, there is no significant difference in detection stability between the existing method and the proposed method. These results suggest that in the experimental settings for this section, when the proportion of harmful data in malicious devices is 50%, there is little difference in detection stability between the existing and proposed methods.

Figures 14.26 and 14.27 show the results of experiments conducted with the number of data points per device set to 20, the proportion of harmful data in malicious devices set to 100%, and the attack method changed to “label flip.” “Label flip” is an attack in which the labels of the attack data are simply flipped in the binary data.

As shown in Figure 14.26a, the accuracy of the models after each defense method is applied drops to almost zero, except for the “perfect defense” model. Additionally, the accuracy of the models tends to rapidly decrease when the proportion of harmful data reaches 50%, and the accuracy takes values that are opposite to those for the settings where the proportion of harmful data is 0% to 40%. These results suggest that the increase in reversed data due to the label flip caused significant learning interference in the training data, which resulted in reversed prediction outcomes. This means that for the settings where the proportion of harmful data was 60% or higher, the normal data became a minority and was treated as harmful data.

The results for the accuracy in detecting harmful data are shown in Figures 14.26b and c and 14.27. These results show there is almost no difference in detection accuracy between the existing and proposed methods.

Figure 14.28 shows the distribution of F1 score values from the detection accuracy of the experimental setting described above using a box plot. In the results for proportions of harmful data of 70% or higher, both the existing and proposed methods detected almost no harmful data, and this is consistent with the results for model accuracy. For the settings where the proportion of harmful data is set to 10%–60%, both methods detect some harmful data, but the box plots cover a wide vertical margin, which indicates instability in detection.

14.6 Discussion

We discuss several issues related to our proposed method in this section.

14.6.1 Attack Methods Utilized

The method proposed in this study is a defense mechanism against poisoning attacks that leverages the harmful data generated by the attack algorithms. In the evaluation experiments presented in Section 14.5, both the attack and defense sides use the same poisoning attack method as in the setting. However, in real‐world scenarios, it is unlikely that the defense would be able to use the same methods as the attackers. The proposed method takes advantage of the characteristic that harmful data does not revert to normal data, even when the attack algorithm is rerun. Therefore, it is necessary to verify in the future whether this premise holds when different attack algorithms are combined.

14.6.2 Adversarial Impact of Each Device

Baracaldo et al. [32] used a fixed threshold to determine the harmful or benign status of each device. In contrast, the method proposed in this study defines a unique threshold, , for each device. Table 14.5 shows the values of for the normal and harmful devices according to the proposed method. From these results, it can be seen that normal devices have values of that are relatively more likely to be judged as harmful. Intuitively, smaller values of for the harmful devices would be expected to improve detection accuracy. The results presented in Section 14.5 suggest that the accuracy of the proposed method is not inferior to that of the existing method for two reasons: Normal devices with an less than or equal to zero are judged as benign, regardless of , and harmful devices having values close to undergo higher data removal rates (Table 14.6).

14.6.3 When Harmful Data Constitutes the Majority

As described in Section 14.4.2, the proposed method adopts the strategy of judging all devices with a value of less than or equal to zero as normal and not removing the corresponding data. However, when more than half of the dataset under protection consists of harmful data, it is conceivable that “normal data have an adverse effect on harmful data.” In other words, the roles of normal and harmful data are essentially reversed. In such a case, the defense algorithm proposed in this paper may detect a greater number of normal devices than harmful devices because the of normal data would have a relatively high value.

14.6.4 Against Attackers Aware of the Defense Method's Internal Structure

As described in Section 14.2.1, this study assumes an environment in which data is collected from multiple devices in an IoT setting. However, the proposed method could be applied to many sources of data outside such environments. For instance, consider the scenario in which the annotation of training data is outsourced. In this case, data providers may be divided by company or employee. If an attacker is among these providers, the attacker can execute a poisoning attack. This scenario assumes that modifications to the data before and after the annotation are not detected by comparing hash values.

Additionally, it is conceivable that attackers could possess partial or complete knowledge about the algorithms of proposed method. In such cases, attackers may attempt to minimize to evade detection. Because the proposed method uses the impact on the accuracy of the model as a criterion for identifying harmful data, reducing would make detecting harmful data more challenging. However, reducing also reduces the effectiveness of an attack. Therefore, this method could potentially serve as a deterrent to attacks.

14.6.5 Limitations

Our proposed method determines whether the received data has been subject to a poisoning attack by applying known poisoning attacks to the data and then checking if the accuracy of the machine learning model subsequently decreases. If the server receives data that has been subject to an unknown poisoning attack, our proposed method may not correctly detect the attack. Existing defense methods for detecting poisoning attacks, other than our proposed method, may also be vulnerable to unknown attacks. Therefore, this drawback is not unique to our method. However, it is necessary to further evaluate how robust our method is against unknown attacks.

Additionally, the proposed method requires that the machine learning model be repeatedly trained, which results in significant computational cost. It will become necessary to explore ways to reduce this computational burden in the future.

14.7 Conclusion

The advent of TinyML, which focuses on deploying machine learning models on resource‐constrained devices, introduces additional layers of complexity and potential vulnerabilities to the security landscape. As TinyML systems become integral to various applications, from smart home devices to wearable health monitors, ensuring the security and robustness of these systems becomes paramount. TinyML systems, by design, operate under extreme constraints in terms of computational power, memory, and energy consumption. These constraints necessitate highly optimized and often simplified machine learning models, which may inadvertently introduce new attack surfaces. For example, the reduced complexity of models in TinyML systems could make them more susceptible to certain types of poisoning attacks that exploit these simplifications.

Furthermore, the environments in which TinyML systems are deployed are often less controlled than those of traditional machine learning systems, as these devices are widely distributed and interact directly with the physical world. This increases the number of potential attack vectors and the ease with which malicious actors can introduce poisonous data. Therefore, the security strategies employed must be lightweight yet effective to balance the need for robust defenses with the limited resources available.

In this context, our study focuses on developing efficient detection and mitigation strategies for poisoning attacks. The proposed defense method, which is intended to minimize model degradation and accurately identify harmful data, is particularly suited to the TinyML paradigm. By ensuring that the defensive mechanisms are computationally efficient and do not overburden the limited resources of TinyML devices, we can enhance the security of these systems without compromising their performance or functionality.

Additionally, the practical implications of securing TinyML systems are considerable. As TinyML devices are often embedded in critical infrastructure and personal environments, any successful attack may have far‐reaching consequences and impact not only individual users but also entire communities. Hence, our efforts to improve the resilience of machine learning systems against poisoning attacks are crucial for the broader adoption of and trust in TinyML technologies.

In conclusion, the integration of robust, lightweight security measures into TinyML systems is essential to safeguarding the next generation of smart devices. Our proposed method contributes to this goal by addressing the unique challenges posed by the resource constraints and deployment scenarios of TinyML, and it ensures that these innovative systems are both powerful and secure.
