15
TinyML for Real‐Time Medical Image Classification and Diagnosis

Jelil O. Agbo‐Ajala1, Lateef A. Akinyemi1,2, Olufisayo S. Ekundayo1, and Ernest Mnkandla1

1Centre for Augmented Intelligence and Data Science, School of Computing, University of South Africa, Johannesburg, South Africa

2Department of Electrical and Smart Systems Engineering, School of Computing, University of South Africa, Johannesburg, South Africa

15.1 Introduction

Medical image classification and diagnosis involve the analysis and interpretation of medical images, such as X‐ray, computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and ultrasound images, to detect and classify various diseases, medical conditions, and abnormalities [1, 2]. This process classifies medical images into different conditions using their visual features and patterns. The diagnosis of medical images goes a step further by using classified images to make a diagnosis, identify the type and stage of the conditions, and detect the location and severity of injuries [3, 4].

Real‐time medical image classification and diagnosis are critical in health care, with accurate and timely information to make reliable decisions and appropriate patient care [5]. Conventional methods like machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) have limitations, including requiring large amounts of training images, being computationally expensive and resource‐intensive, and susceptibility to overfitting, especially with small data. However, these limitations led to delayed diagnoses and encouraged ongoing research in deep learning and real‐time medical image classification and diagnosis, as well as alternative techniques to address these limitations [6, 7].

Recently, TinyML (Tiny Machine Learning) has proven to be a promising technology in medical image analysis, supporting real‐time classification and diagnosis in resource‐constrained devices. TinyML focuses on developing tiny and lightweight models that can run efficiently and effectively on devices with limited computational resources, such as edge devices, smartphones, and embedded systems. These benefits make TinyML suitable for real‐time analysis and interpretation of medical images. TinyML empowers healthcare professionals to make more accurate and timely diagnoses that reduce healthcare costs, improve patient outcomes, and increase accessibility in remote and resource‐constrained areas [8, 9]. This research aims to explore TinyML models for real‐time medical image classification and diagnosis (Figure 15.1), achieving the following objectives:

  1. We present a comprehensive review and detailed analysis of various methods used in medical image classification and diagnosis.
  2. We conducted a comparative study between TinyML models and other machine learning methods, including traditional machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL).
  3. We also explore the advantages and benefits of TinyML models over other approaches, particularly in real‐time classification and diagnosis performance across different datasets, and their potential to improve the field.
  4. We also present a description of popular datasets and evaluation metrics used in medical image classification, especially breast cancer, brain tumor, and COVID‐19.
  5. We then examine future research and development directions for TinyML, in medical image classification and diagnosis.

This work serves as a comprehensive guide for researchers interested in employing TinyML for medical image classification and presents new and advanced methods utilized in this area that provide important insight into the current and existing works.

The rest of this work is arranged as follows: Section 15.2 presents a comprehensive review and analysis of medical image classification and diagnosis methods, with a thorough examination of various methods/models used for medical image classification and diagnosis. Section 15.3 presents the performance of conventional methods, including Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL), as well as novel TinyML models. In Section 15.4, we present the results of our findings, highlighting the benefits of TinyML models while stating the limitations of other mechanisms. Finally, we summarize our contributions and highlight future research directions, which provide a conclusion to our work in Section 15.5.

15.2 Literature Review

This section presents a comprehensive review of existing work, including research focusing on machine learning and deep learning techniques for medical image analysis. Despite varying degrees of success, these studies have collectively advanced the field, highlighting key methodologies, achievements, and challenges.

15.2.1 Methods Employed in Medical Image Classification and Diagnosis

Medical imaging is a significant area of computer vision research, with many publications published over the last few decades [10]. Machine learning algorithms, particularly deep neural networks, have become popular in this field of image analysis. Therefore, this section presents a comprehensive and detailed analysis of the most recent and relevant work (see Tables 15.1 and 15.2), including TinyML, on the classification and diagnosis of three popular diseases: breast cancer, brain tumor, and COVID‐19. We aim to present an overview of the current and recent methods, understand the complexities of the field, identify application areas for novel TinyML, and highlight areas that require further exploration.

  • Breast Cancer: In [11], the authors presented a novel channel attention model that employed “multiscale grid average pooling,” for the segmentation of breast cancer on ultrasound images. This module incorporated both local and global spatial information, to enhance the segmentation task. The proposed network was trained and validated on popular dataset of breast cancer ultrasound images. The experimental results demonstrated the ability of the proposed model to perform the segmentation task. In [12], the authors introduced a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture for automatic breast cancer segmentation. The model was trained on a diverse, large, and evenly distributed dataset and evaluated on popular benchmark datasets. Robust training on these datasets enabled the model to achieve excellent generalization that demonstrated its capacity to accurately segment breast cancer. In [10], the authors presented a novel method for breast cancer segmentation in ultrasonography images that addressed the challenges posed by complex noise and artifacts. They introduced an integrated architecture that combined ultrasonography image pre‐processing, “linear iterative clustering,” and a U‐Net model. This approach enhanced the accuracy of breast cancer diagnosis and provided medical professionals with a valuable tool for improved patient outcomes. Also, the authors in [13] developed an effective and intelligent method for breast cancer diagnosis and segmentation of breast cancer images. They proposed a novel pre‐processing technique for pathological images and an image recognition technology for breast cancer. This intelligent architecture for breast cancer employed digital image processing technology and filtering techniques to improve the clarity of the image data. Moreau et al. [14] proposed a model that automated the segmentation of metastatic breast cancer lesions on positron emission tomography (PET) and CT images. The novel model was evaluated on benchmark datasets. The results showed that the proposed model can accurately segment lesions in images with metastatic breast cancer. Similarly, in [15], the authors developed an automatic method for evaluating histopathological cancer sections. Using the whole images of breast cancer collected from Norway, they proposed a convolutional but cascaded neural network model, H2G‐Net, to segment the regions with breast cancer from histopathological images. The design also employed a patch‐wise technique and a convolution autoencoder. To validate the proposed model, they investigated ablation study to analyze the importance of the chosen regions on cancer segmentation. In [16], the authors investigated a novel model that combined a multiscale CNN with a joint transformer, for segmenting breast cancer in “Dynamic Contrast‐Enhanced MRI (DCE‐MRI).” This two‐stage segmentation method first employed a U‐Net network model to delineate the breast area in MRI images. The model was then evaluated using standard evaluation metrics, where it achieved excellent results in the segmenting and classifying of breast cancer lesions. In [17], the authors proposed a breast cancer model that detected and classified cancer at its early stage. They developed a diagnosis and segmentation method for breast cancer using both deep neural networks and transfer learning that is validated on a publicly available dataset. The results showed that the proposed method achieved a high accuracy for both binary and multi‐class classification of cancer cases. In [18], the authors presented a model for automatic diagnosis of high‐resolution breast cancer of pathological images. The proposed model is based on a “dual‐path feature extraction network” for breast pathology, which utilized dilated convolution networks to encode rich contextual information. Additionally, they introduced a “channel attention mechanism” and a feature attention and fusion module to selectively filter and combine features. This fused approach achieved excellent performance on the image data while reducing the computational complexity associated with existing models. Patra et al. [19] presented a novel approach for automatic breast cancer segmentation using “DCE‐MRI.” Their framework employed a multiple‐level thresholding technique, with an optimization algorithm, to segment breast lesions in the DCE‐MRI images. Additionally, they utilized an enhanced “simple metaheuristic algorithm (SMA)” with a “quasi‐opposition‐based learning mechanism,” to determine the optimal threshold values. This approach showed superior performance compared to existing methods. In [20], Xianjun et al. employed an attention‐learning approach for breast cancer segmentation of mammography images. The proposed model comprised a novel architecture, an attention‐based scheme, and a method for learning image labels. This multi‐task approach integrated multiscale feature fusion and an enhanced U‐Net architecture that improves the segmentation capability. The model achieved significant success when evaluated on benchmark datasets. In [21], Liping et al. presented a novel breast cancer segmentation method that comprises a hybrid “AttendSeg architecture” and “gravitational clustering optimization” method. The proposed hybrid method was employed to segment breast cancer images into various regions such as normal, malignant, and benign. The model demonstrated great performance when evaluated using some evaluating metrics, such as recall, precision, Dice coefficient, and Jaccard index. Ahmed et al. [22] introduced a deep learning‐based model for classifying, detecting, and segmenting cancerous regions in mammogram images. They introduced a pre‐processing mechanism to remove noise, artifacts, and muscle regions, followed by converting the pre‐processed image into 512 512 patches. The model was trained on two benchmark breast cancer datasets and evaluated on popular metrics where it achieved excellent performance in terms of area under the receiver operating curve (AUC‐ROC), average precision, and accuracy. These results demonstrated the proposed model's potential to assist medical practitioners in breast cancer classification and segmentation. Balaha et al. [23] proposed a novel approach for diagnosing breast cancer at its early stage. They suggested a hybrid framework for breast cancer classification and segmentation, consisting of two phases: classification and segmentation. The classification phase employed five different CNN models, with the Aquila optimizer used to calculate the optimal hyperparameters for the transfer learning architectures. The framework was trained on common datasets, and the results demonstrated good performance in binary and multiclass classification, as well as in the segmentation task. Also, Raza et al. [24] proposed an efficient and robust deep‐learning model, “DeepBreastCancerNet,” for breast cancer detection and classification. The novel architecture employed “clipped rectified linear unit (ReLU) and leaky ReLU activation functions,” cross‐channel normalization, and batch normalization. Experimental results showed that the proposed model achieved comparable performance with other state‐of‐the‐art models on classification accuracy.
  • Brain Tumor: In [25], Bag et al. proposed an advanced CNN technique for detecting abnormalities in MRI scans, aimed at supporting prompt decision‐making by radiologists. The technique comprises three stages including pre‐processing of brain MRI images, application of machine learning feature extraction methods to identify significant features from these images, and utilization of CNN models to classify the detected regions in the MRI images. The results showed the effectiveness of the automated abnormal brain growth detection model in real‐world scenarios, showcasing its potential to save medical practitioners time and facilitate early diagnosis. In [26], Vaiyapuri et al. introduced an ensemble learning‐driven diagnosis model that employed deep learning techniques and CNNs on MRI scans. The model featured a Gabor filter to enhance image quality and utilized popular CNNs like EfficientNet, MobileNet, and DenseNet for feature extraction. Hyperparameter tuning was performed using the “social spider optimization algorithm.” The proposed model achieved significant success compared to other methods. Similarly, Dhakshnamurthy et al. [27] explored a algorithms for detecting and classifying brain tumors using transfer learning models, for medical imaging. They employed three CNN‐based models: VGG16, AlexNet, and ResNet‐50. The ensemble of VGG16 and ResNet‐50 models showed exceptional performance on benchmark datasets, with remarkable results in specificity, sensitivity, accuracy, and F1 score. Also in [28], the authors proposed a deep transfer learning architecture for brain tumor diagnosis. They applied four different transfer learning architectures of DenseNet121, VGG19, InceptionV3, and MobileNet. They also employed images from three benchmark datasets of Br35H, Figshare, and SARTAJ, to validate the models. The experimental results showed that the MobileNet outperformed other existing models achieving great accuracy. Similarly, in [29], Noreen et al. proposed a method utilizing pre‐trained models, where features are extracted from down layers. They employed a multilevel feature extraction and concatenation technique for early detection and diagnosis of brain tumors. They specifically used the pre‐trained DenseNet201 to extract features from different DenseNet layers, which were then concatenated and transferred to a softmax classifier. The two models achieved excellent performance in detecting brain tumors when evaluated on a three‐class brain tumor dataset. Güler and Namlı [30] presented a novel deep‐learning model for detecting brain tumors on MRI images. Their automatic brain tumor diagnosis and classification system aim to assist radiologists by eliminating the need for manual diagnosis. The authors trained and evaluated their proposed model on a large dataset of 7022 brain MR images. Initially, they employed machine learning methods to classify the extracted features, followed by an ensemble learning approach. The model demonstrated outstanding results, confirming the effectiveness of the employed techniques and methods. In [31], Mohammed and Hilai developed a hybrid model that integrated CNN and support vector machine (SVM) kernels for brain tumor classification. They utilized a CNN‐based model to identify regional variations and classify brain tumors, using already pre‐trained CNN models, including VGG19, EfficientNetB0, and NASNetLarge. The extracted features were then classified using an SVM classifier, which demonstrated comparable performance to existing models. Rasool et al. [32] proposed a novel approach that combined SqueezeNet with SVM for brain tumor classification. The hybrid deep learning method utilized a pre‐trained CNN for feature extraction phase and an SVM for pattern classification, where it achieved high accuracy on MRI scans. Parveen et al. [33] developed an automated brain tumor diagnosis and classification model using an equilibrium optimization method and deep learning. Their model employed a Wiener filtering technique to remove noise from images and a ShuffleNet model for feature extraction. The model was validated on the benchmark Br35H dataset, comprising 1500 tumor and 1500 non‐tumor images, and demonstrated significant success over existing techniques.
  • COVID‐19: In [34], Jin et al. proposed a hybrid model that included a feature extractor, feature selector, and classifier. They primarily pre‐trained AlexNet CNN for the feature extraction phase before employing ReliefF algorithm for feature sorting and selected important features using a trial‐and‐error technique. The proposed model showed great performance compared to other state‐of‐the‐art models. Sufian et al. [35] introduced a novel image processing technique for grayscale medical images where it employed “histogram equalization and contrast‐limited adaptive histogram equalization,” to produce a “three‐channel image representation.” The proposed representation technique improved the classification performance when evaluated on six popular pre‐trained models. Al et al. [36] developed a deep transfer learning (VGG16) model for the diagnosis of COVID‐19 infection in chest X‐ray images. They developed six different classifiers for different chest X‐ray image data before combining them into a final classifier, and this demonstrated an encouraging capability of the model in COVID‐19 detection. Zazzaro et al. [37] proposed a deep learning and ensemble technique for automated COVID‐19 detection on chest CT images. They employed transfer learning techniques of a CNN originally pre‐trained on popular ImageNet dataset, to allow for feature extraction from CT images. Babukarthik et al. [38] also proposed a genetic deep learning and CNN model, for COVID‐19 prediction. The model was trained from scratch, to extract features needed for the classification task. The model achieved a good performance on precision, accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity, in COVID‐19 diagnosis. Ozyurt et al. [39] proposed an automatic COVID‐19 detection method using transfer learning of a lightweight deep learning approach. They used a lightweight (ShuffleNet) architecture and a multilevel activation visualization layer, to detect COVID‐19 pneumonia from large‐scale chest radiographic images. Owais et al. [40] proposed a method for analyzing and diagnosing COVID‐19 infection from large‐scale radiographic image datasets. They used a lightweight network with an ensemble design of ShuffleNet, MobileNet, and FCNet, for the diagnosis of COVID‐19, and it achieved good performance when compared to existing and conventional procedures. In [41], Polsinelli et al. developed a lightweight CNN‐based model that used SqueezeNet architecture for the diagnosis of COVID‐19 in CT images. The model achieved good accuracy and competitive results. Ullah et al. [42] employed a holistic approach using ShuffleNet CNN architecture, to detect and classify COVID‐19 from CT scans, chest radiographs, and electrocardiogram (ECG) images. The extensive classification experiments demonstrated the ability of the proposed method on the classification task. Alghamdi et al. [43] introduced an enhanced deep learning approach for the multiclass classification of COVID‐19 infection of chest X‐rays. They utilized various deep CNN models, data normalization and augmentation, and approaches, to improve performance. The model successfully classified the images into five different cases, including normal, COVID‐19, and other lung infections. Akpinar et al. [44] developed a CNN‐based model using SqueezeNet for detecting abnormalities in chest X‐ray images, and this achieved great success after experimental evaluations. Mehmood et al. [45] proposed an automated system (CP_DeepNet) for detecting COVID‐19 infections in lung X‐ray images. They utilized a pre‐trained SqueezeNet model and convolution layers and employed data augmentation, to avoid overfitting.

In general, despite the significant advances in medical image classification and diagnosis presented in the literature, TinyML still outperforms state‐of‐the‐art methods in classification and diagnosis of medical images, particularly in real‐time applications.

15.2.2 TinyML Models and Architecture Used in Real‐Time Medical Image Classification and Diagnosis

Medical image classification and diagnosis involve developing models and architectures to analyze and process medical images, such as computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), X‐rays, and ultrasound images, to support disease classification and diagnosis. These models and architectures are typically optimized for accuracy, memory constraints, and computational efficiency, making them suitable for deployment on resource‐constrained devices, including smartphones, tablets, and embedded systems. In this section, we therefore present some popular TinyML models and architectures used in real‐time medical image classification and diagnosis.

  • MobileNet: MobileNet is a renowned lightweight neural network model developed by Google researchers, specifically designed for embedded devices and devices that are memory‐constrained. Its efficient design has made it a popular choice among computer vision researchers, who adapt it for various applications, including medical image classification, detection, and segmentation. MobileNet excels in managing computational resources and memory usage, making it an ideal choice for mobile devices, smartphones, and other resource‐constrained devices. The architecture employs “depthwise separable convolutions” that significantly reduce the number of parameters and computational requirements. The MobileNet family includes several variants, such as MobileNet‐v1, MobileNet‐v2, MobileNet‐v3, and MobileNet‐v3‐Small, which are commonly used to classify medical images, classify magnetic resonance scans, and detect breast cancer. These variants offer developers a variety of options to choose from, depending on their specific requirements and constraints [46].
  • ShuffleNet: ShuffleNet is a lightweight CNN architecture that has demonstrated exceptional performance in various medical image classification tasks, including breast cancer and lung nodule. The model was designed for mobile devices with limited computing power, and ShuffleNet was introduced in 2018 by researchers at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, China. Its architecture combines “depthwise separable convolutions,” pointwise convolutions, and channel shuffle operations, to achieve efficient computation and memory usage. The network has several variants: ShuffleNet‐v1, ShuffleNet‐v2, and ShuffleNet‐v3, which hold great promise for various real‐world computer vision applications, such as detecting brain tumors, classifying MRI scans, diagnosing Alzheimer's diseases. ShuffleNet's efficiency and accuracy make it an attractive solution for resource‐constrained devices and real‐time applications [47].
  • SqueezeNet: SqueezeNet is a compact and lightweight neural network architecture widely used in medical image classification tasks, including cardiovascular disease detection, diabetic retinopathy detection, chest radiograph classification, and skin lesions. SqueezeNet was developed by DeepScale, specifically for deployment on resource‐constrained mobile and embedded devices. Its unique architecture enables reduced parameters and computations while still maintaining accuracy. This is achieved through a combination of techniques, including fire modules, depthwise separable convolution, squeeze layers, and expand layers [48].
  • Tiny CNN: Tiny CNN is one of the common lightweight CNN architectures that have been used in medical image classification and the diagnosis of breast cancer and prostate cancer. The CNN architecture was specifically designed to be used on resource‐constrained devices (smartphones, embedded systems, and other mobile devices). It is commonly used for detecting cardiovascular diseases, classifying ultrasound images, and classifying mammography images. Tiny CNN has several key benefits including low memory usage, fast inference times, power efficiency, and its ability to work on resource‐constrained devices including mobile and embedded systems. It also has its usability in medical devices, Internet of Things (IoT) devices, and autonomous vehicles [49].
  • NASNet: NASNet (neural architecture search network) is a search‐based CNN architecture that has shown promising applications in medical image classification, diagnosis, and segmentation. NASNet was designed to be highly efficient and has achieved state‐of‐the‐art accuracy on the popular ImageNet dataset, with exceptional performance. With neural architecture search techniques, NASNet can automatically learn optimal network architectures, making it a powerful tool for various computer vision tasks, including medical image analysis [50].
  • ESPNet: ESPNet is another lightweight CNN architecture, designed for medical image classification and segmentation. It is particularly useful in classifying MRI, classifying CT imaging, and detecting prostate cancer. The model employed spatial pyramid architecture, channel shuffle operations, “depthwise separable convolutions,” hierarchical feature fusion, and spatial attention techniques to reduce memory usage and computational complexity and achieve high accuracy and fast inference for efficient feature extraction [51].
  • EfficientNet: EfficientNet is a family of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) proposed by Mingxing Tan and Quoc VL. The model is renowned for achieving state‐of‐the‐art accuracy in medical image classification with reduced computations and parameters when compared to other models. The EfficientNet model is specifically designed for classifying medical images, including CT scans, and detecting diabetic retinopathy. The EfficientNet family comprises various variants, such as EfficientNet‐B0 and EfficientNet‐B1, each offering a unique trade‐off between model size and accuracy for deployment in different applications [52].
  • PeleeNet: PeleeNet is also a lightweight neural network architecture optimized for the efficient classification of medical images. The model was introduced by Robert Cheng et al. in their paper “Pelee: A Real‐Time Object Detection System on Mobile Devices,” and PeleeNet is a streamlined variant of the singleshot detector (SSD) network, specifically designed for mobile and embedded devices. It uses a simple architecture with reduced computation requirements and parameters that enable real‐time medical image detection on resource‐constrained devices, making it an ideal solution for applications where computational resources are limited [53].

In summary, TinyML models and architectures, such as MobileNet, ShuffleNet, SqueezeNet, and Tiny CNN, have demonstrated exceptional promise in medical image classification and diagnosis, achieving outstanding accuracy and efficiency. These models are particularly valuable in resource‐constrained devices, including mobile devices and embedded systems, where computational resources and memory are limited. With techniques like model compression, quantization, and pruning, TinyML models can attain high accuracy with significantly reduced computational requirements, making them ideal for real‐time classification and diagnosis of medical images. As medical imaging continues to advance, TinyML models and architectures are poised to play a vital role in enabling accurate and efficient image classification, ultimately improving patient care and outcomes.

15.2.3 Application Areas of TinyML in Medical Image Classification and Diagnosis

The rapid advancement of medical imaging technologies has led to an increase in the number of medical images generated daily [54]. However, a timely and accurate interpretation of these images was a challenge, particularly in real‐time scenarios [55]. Recently, with the advent of TinyML, a solution has been provided for classification and diagnosis tasks. TinyML can run on resource‐constrained devices while still maintaining its high accuracy and real‐time processing abilities, making it a promising solution for timely diagnostics and remote healthcare services [6, 8, 56]. In this section, we therefore study a comprehensive overview of TinyML applications in medical image classification and diagnosis, exploring their applicability in various medical imaging modalities, including CT, MRI, X‐rays, and ultrasound images. Some of those application areas include the following.

  • Detection of Diseases: TinyML can be used to detect several diseases, including cancer, Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, brain tumor, cardiovascular disease, diabetic retinopathy, pneumonia, skin, and lung, among others types. The model is utilized to analyze images to detect signs of infections in MRI, CT, X‐rays, and ultrasound images [57, 58].
  • Classification of Medical Images: TinyML can also be used to classify medical images into different categories, such as normal or abnormal, tumor or non‐tumor, and benign or malignant. TinyML has numerous applications in medical image classification, including skin disease classification, tumor disease classification, orthopedic disorder classification, and lung disease classification [57, 59].
  • Segmentation of Medical Images: TinyML is also used in segmenting medical images to identify specific structures or features such as organs, tumors, or tissues. The model has its applications in lesion segmentation, tissue segmentation, organ segmentation, and tumor segmentation. It can also segment different tissues such as muscle, bone, and fat [60, 61].
  • Denoising of Medical Images: TinyML can also be employed to remove noise from medical images, to improve their quality and diagnostic ability. It can be used to reduce noise in medical images, including CT, MRI, X‐ray, ultrasound, mammography, and fluoroscopy [62].

TinyML therefore has varying and vast applications in medical imaging including medical image classification, segmentation, disease detection, diagnosis, and image denoising, and it therefore has the potential to improve medical imaging by enabling efficient, accurate, and personalized diagnosis and treatment. It helps to improve accuracy and efficiency that enhances patient care and outcomes, reducing computational resources and energy consumption, among others.

15.3 Methodology

In this section, we present a description of three state‐of‐the‐art approaches in medical image classification and diagnosis. These methods include the following.

15.3.1 Machine Learning (ML)

Machine learning (ML) is an aspect of artificial intelligence (AI) technology that allows machines to learn from data, identify the patterns, and automatically make decisions without human intervention [76]. In medical image classification and diagnosis, ML models play a vital role because they can learn from medical images and adapt to them, identify the patterns in those images, and produce reliable results on new image data, among other key characteristics. ML is also useful in medical imaging to interpret medical images employing computer‐aided design (CAD) and algorithms where it applies ML techniques, to CT scans, X‐ray scans, MRI scans, etc. The conventional ML models rely on structured datasets with predefined techniques for each step. However, new algorithms can adapt to missing data, ensuring robustness in disease classification and diagnosis [77].

15.3.2 Deep Learning (DL)

Deep learning (DL) is also a branch of machine learning that has been widely applied in computer vision and image processing. It utilizes multiple processing layers or multiple layers of complex structures that included multiple nonlinear transformations. Recently, various medical image processing and image recognition tasks have adopted deep learning methods on CT images, MRI images, ultrasound images, X‐ray images, pathological images, etc. Deep learning technology has applications in medical imaging to detect, classify, and segment infections. The key benefits of deep learning techniques lie in their ability to replace manual feature learning with unsupervised or semi‐supervised feature learning and hierarchical feature extraction efficiency. Some of the popular deep learning models used in classification tasks include GoogLeNet, VGGNet, and ResNet. In medical imaging, deep learning has demonstrated exceptional capabilities in segmenting diseases, discriminating between diseases, and classifying diseases [64].

15.3.3 TinyML

TinyML utilizes intelligence on edge layers and mobile devices, such as smartphones and tablets. TinyML techniques are designed to perform effectively on mobile devices with limited computational resources and battery restrictions. This technique focuses on deploying compressed and optimized machine learning models on low‐powered, tiny devices like micro‐controllers and embedded systems. TinyML was inspired by mobile machine learning features, including resource constraints, low latency, and moderate cost. The model emerged from technical breakthroughs in the IoT field and can be applied in various areas, particularly in medical image classification. TinyML technology addresses the need to apply intelligence in a wide range of applications previously hindered by the high power and computing requirements of standard machine learning models [78].

15.4 Results and Discussion

This section contains information on the medical imaging data used for this study, the popular evaluation metrics used to evaluate TinyML models, comparative analysis, and presentation of the results of our findings.

15.4.1 Description of Datasets Employed in this Work

Medical image classification and diagnosis play an important role in the healthcare industry. To develop and evaluate accurate classification models, researchers rely on various datasets. These datasets consist of labeled medical images, annotated with essential information such as the presence of severity and other relevant features of the disease. This section reviews popular datasets used in medical image classification research, focusing on three popular applications: breast cancer, brain tumor, and COVID‐19 diagnosis.

  • BreakHis (Breast Cancer on Histopathology Images): BreakHis dataset was collected to be used in medical image classification, for binary and multiclass problems. The dataset consists of 7,909 microscopic images of breast tumor samples collected from 82 patients with different magnification factors, including 10, 100, 200, and 400 of histopathological images of BC. The dataset is divided into 5,429 malignant image samples and 2,480 benign image samples. Those image samples were pre‐processed and resized to 224 224 pixels [79].
  • Brain Tumor MRI: Brain tumor MRI dataset consists of medical images of human brain MRI scans, consisting of information about the location, presence, and characteristics of the brain tumor. Those MRI images are classified into 4 classes, namely, pituitary, glioma, meningioma, and no tumor. This dataset is essential for training computer vision algorithms to automate brain tumor detection, to help with early diagnosis and treatment planning [80].
  • COVID‐19 CXR Dataset: This dataset comprises COVID‐19 positive and negative chest X‐ray (CXR) images obtained from various sources, including the BIMCV‐COVID19+ database, a German medical school, Eurorad, SIRM, Kaggle, GitHub, and other COVID‐19 repositories. The images, representing both male and female subjects, were curated to facilitate detection of lung damage caused by COVID‐19 pneumonia. Specifically, subjects with confirmed cases and clinical symptoms are likely to exhibit abnormal lung X‐ray patterns, allowing researchers to develop accurate diagnostic models for early detection and treatment planning [81]. Some of the sample images are presented in Figures 15.2–15.4[[dot]].

15.4.2 Model Evaluation Metrics

Evaluation metrics are essential in medical image classification where they help to evaluate the performance of machine learning models. In this work, we focus on common and benchmark evaluation metrics comprising true positive (TP), false positive (FP), false negative (FN), and true negative (TN). TP refers to correctly classified positive images, FP refers to incorrectly classified positive images, FN represents incorrectly classified negative images, and TN refers to correctly predicted negative images. We analyze our findings using five performance evaluation metrics: accuracy, precision, sensitivity (recall), specificity, and F1 score. This can be defined and calculated as follows.

  • Accuracy: Accuracy is a fundamental evaluation metric in medical imaging tasks, where it measures the percentage of correctly classified images by the proposed model. The metric provides an overall assessment of the model performance. However, accuracy can be influenced by class imbalance in the datasets, potentially masking underlying issues. However, the higher the accuracy, the better the performance of the model [82]. Accuracy is therefore calculated as in equation (15.1):

  • Precision: Precision is a vital evaluation metric in medical imaging, calculating the proportion of true positives among all possible positive classifications made by the model. This metric is particularly sensitive to false positives, making it invaluable in applications where incorrect detections have significant consequences, such as cancer diagnosis or disease monitoring. A higher precision value indicates fewer false positives, ensuring that positive predictions are reliable [83]. Precision is calculated as in equation (15.2):

  • Sensitivity (Recall): Sensitivity, also known as recall, measures the proportion of actual positive possibilities that are correctly evaluated by the developed model. This metric is particularly useful in applications where missing true positives has significant effects, like in medical diagnosis or disease detection [84].   • Specificity: Specificity measures the value of actual negative occurrences that are correctly classified by the model, which provided insight into its ability to avoid false positives. This metric is crucial in situations where false positives can lead to unnecessary treatment, costly interventions, or adverse consequences. High specificity indicates that more actual negative instances are accurately identified, reducing the risk of unnecessary actions [85]. Specificity is calculated as in equation (15.4):

  • F1 Score: F1 score metric is a widely used measure of performance in computer vision, providing a balanced evaluation of recall and precision through its harmonic mean. A higher F1 score indicates a better balance between recall and precision that makes it a valuable metric in applications where both false positives and false negatives are important. Specifically, the F1 score is extensively utilized in medical image classification, detection, and segmentation [86]. 15.4.3 Results of Key Findings

In this section, we present the performance evaluation results (Figures 15.5–15.7) of existing and recent state‐of‐the‐art methods used in the classification and diagnosis tasks for breast cancer, brain tumors, and COVID‐19 diseases.

  • Results of Breast Cancer Models: From Table 15.3, the accuracy results of the latest models are as follows: 99.87% on ResNet50, 99.86% on lightweight CNN, 99.28% on DenseNet, 99.15% on SVM and 98.95% on VGG19. The ResNet50 model was observed to achieve the best result; however, the lightweight and TinyML models achieved comparable results despite having lighter models with lower resources. Regarding precision metrics, custom and lightweight CNN achieved a perfect score of 100%, outperforming machine learning models like SVM (99%) and deep learning models like VGG19 (98.95%), ResNet50 (98.77%), and DenseNet (97%). For sensitivity, the SVM machine learning model achieved the best result (99.0%), while the DenseNet, VGG19, and ResNet50 deep learning models achieved comparable results but used more resources and were not suitable on devices limited in resources. The specificity results were 98.95% for VGG19, 89.69% for VGG, and 84% for deep belief networks. Furthermore, DenseNet achieved the best F1 score result (99.48%). In particular, TinyML achieved comparable results with significantly lower memory usage, making it suitable for real‐time applications.

  • Results of Brain Tumor Models: Table 15.4 shows the results of brain tumor classification. The models achieved the accuracy scores of VGG16‐ResNet50 (99.98%), EfficientNetb0 (99.78%), Lightweight CNN (99.74%), MobileNet (99.60%), and DenseNet201 (99.51%). Deep learning models demonstrated the best results, while TinyML of EfficientNetb0, lightweight CNN, and MobileNet achieved comparable results with enhanced resource efficiency. On precision metric, EfficientNetb0(TinyML) achieved 99.78% (best result), fusion of EfficientNet, DenseNet, and MobileNet achieved 99.26%, DenseNet201 achieved 99.0%, SqueezeNet achieved 98.30%, and ShuffleNet achieved 97.30%. The result on sensitivity metric, DenseNet201, achieved 100% but EfficientNetb0 (TinyML) achieved a comparable result of 99.78%. Also, on the specificity metric, VGG16‐ResNet50 achieved the best result (99.98%), and EfficientNetb0 (TinyML) achieved comparable result of 99.78%. On F1 score, DenseNet201 achieved 100%, while TinyML models such as EfficientNetb0 and SqueezeNet achieved comparable result of 99.78% and 98.50%, respectively.

  • Results of COVID‐19 Models: As summarized in Table 15.5, TinyML‐based models for COVID‐19 detection achieved outstanding accuracy results, with ShuffleNet achieving 99.98% and SqueezeNet achieving 99.62%. Other models' results are also recorded in the table. In terms of precision, ShuffleNet (TinyML) excelled with a perfect score of 100.0%. Another ShuffleNet model achieved 99.98%, followed by SqueezeNet (99.78%) and DenseNet121, MobileNet, and InceptionV3 (99%). Regarding sensitivity, ShuffleNet also achieved a perfect score of 100%, with another ShuffleNet model achieving 99.98%. SqueezeNet attained 99.52%, while DenseNet121, MobileNet, and InceptionV3 produced 99%. AlexNet achieved 98.64%. For specificity, the results were 99.97% (ShuffleNet), 99.69% (SqueezeNet), 98.64% (AlexNet), 97.70% (NASNetMobile), and 97.00% (Generic CNN). Lastly, the F1 score results were 100% (ShuffleNet), 99.98% (ShuffleNet1), 99% (DenseNet121), 98.64% (AlexNet), and 95.94% (Ensemble‐Net).

15.4.4 Discussion

This section presents a discussion of the significance and interpretation of key findings within the context of classification of medical imaging in real‐time scenarios. Furthermore, we evaluate the results of the study highlighting areas for improvement by exploring the advantages and disadvantages of TinyML models compared to other approaches including the following:

Traditional Machine Learning (ML) Approaches: From our findings, we observed the following key differences between TinyML and traditional ML:

  • TinyML is designed for resource‐constrained devices, while traditional ML was designed for powerful hardware.
  • TinyML models are compact, efficient, and optimized for inference, while traditional ML models are complex, large, and optimized for training.
  • TinyML typically uses pre‐processing techniques like pruning, while traditional ML typically uses techniques like deep learning and ensemble methods.
  • TinyML focuses on real‐time inference and low latency, while traditional ML focuses on high accuracy and large datasets.
  • TinyML is used for edge AI applications, while traditional ML is often used for cloud‐based applications.

Deep Learning (DL) Approaches: The following are some of the comparisons and key differences between TinyML and other deep learning approaches:

  • TinyML employs lightweight models such as MobileNet, SqueezeNet, etc., while DL uses large, complex models like CNNs, recurrent neural networks (RNNs), etc.
  • TinyML uses shallow model architectures, while DL uses deep model architectures with many layers.
  • TinyML focuses on efficiency, interpretability, and generalization, while DL focuses on high accuracy, often at the cost of interpretability.
  • TinyML requires a small amount of training data, while DL requires a large amount of training data.
  • TinyML typically uses techniques like feature engineering, regularization, and early stopping, while DL typically uses techniques like batch normalization, dropout, and transfer learning.
  • TinyML is designed for resource‐constrained devices, while DL requires powerful hardware and large datasets.

We can therefore deduce that in medical image classification, TinyML offers several advantages over other approaches, including

  • TinyML approach enables real‐time medical image diagnosis, which allows for timely and accurate diagnoses, improved patient outcomes, and enhanced healthcare delivery.
  • TinyML is also suitable for battery‐powered devices and remote applications, which has led to significant reductions in power consumption and enables the development of efficient, portable, and wearable medical devices that can perform image classification tasks in real time.
  • TinyML allows for efficient storage and transmission. The models are designed to be compact and efficient, with small model sizes that offer several advantages in reduced memory usage, and faster inference.
  • TinyML models can achieve comparable accuracy when compared with larger models. They are designed to achieve comparable accuracy to larger models despite their smaller size and computational requirements.
  • TinyML enables analysis on edge devices, which offers several benefits including reducing latency and dependence on cloud systems.
  • TinyML enables medical image analysis in resource‐constrained areas, achieving faster diagnosis and treatment, a cost‐effective solution, that offers scalable and sustainable medical image analysis benefits.
  • TinyML can update and refine models with new data, and this ensures the medical image analysis remains accurate and effective.
  • TinyML enables autonomous medical devices, such as robots and drones, to perform remote healthcare tasks that expand access to medical care.

Limitations of the Study: Although the study on TinyML for real‐time medical image classification and diagnosis showed significant potential, it also has several limitations, including the following:

  • The compact nature and limited model size of typical TinyML models may compromise their ability to capture complex patterns in medical images.
  • The limitation in terms of dataset size may not provide a comprehensive representation of all medical image diagnosis scenarios and may affect model training and performance.
  • The memory and computational limitations of most mobile and edge devices reduce the processing power, which may affect the model's performance.
  • Issues with a class imbalance in most medical imaging datasets result in the under‐representation of certain diseases, which impacts the model's performance.

Future research in developing TinyML models should provide solutions to these challenges in order to further improve their accuracy and suitability of the model in medical image analysis.

Future research in developing TinyML models should focus on addressing these challenges to further enhance their accuracy, robustness, and suitability for medical image analysis applications.

15.4.5 Lessons Learned and Future Research Direction

Some of the key lessons learned from the study on TinyML for real‐time medical image classification and diagnosis include the following:

  • The novel TinyML models can achieve high accuracy in medical image classification and diagnosis despite computational resource constraints.
  • Class imbalance issues must be considered when preparing and pre‐processing datasets.
  • The size and diversity of the dataset can affect the generalization of TinyML model.
  • Using appropriate model optimization techniques can enhance model performance.
  • Real‐time medical image classification and diagnosis improve speed and diagnostic accuracy.
  • TinyML‐based models enable point‐of‐care and real‐time diagnostics.
  • Transfer learning techniques applied to pre‐trained models can improve performance.
  • Hyperparameter tuning is very important for optimal model performance.
  • Combining models through ensemble methods improves model robustness.

Despite the existing challenges, the future research directions of TinyML in medical image classification and diagnosis are promising. More research in areas such as transfer learning, distributed learning, and the collection of larger and diverse datasets will continue to advance the field to achieve robust, faster, more accurate, and accessible diagnosis and treatment of various medical conditions.

15.5 Conclusion

In conclusion, TinyML has the potential to improve the diagnosis and classification of medical images in real‐time scenarios, particularly on devices limited by resources, while maintaining an accurate and accessible diagnosis and treatment of various medical conditions. The model has various applications in the diagnosis of medical images, including tumor detection and classification, disease diagnosis, image segmentation, and denoising. Among these numerous benefits, its efficiency and effectiveness make it an invaluable tool in medical imaging.

16
Biometric Authentication in TinyML: Opportunities and Challenges

Oleksandr Kuznetsov1,2, Emanuele Frontoni3, Marco Arnesano1, Oleksii Smirnov4, and Boris Khruskov5

1Department of Theoretical and Applied Sciences, eCampus University, Novedrate, Italy

2Department of Information and Communication Systems Security, V. N. Karazin Kharkiv National University, Kharkiv, Ukraine

3Department of Political Sciences, Communication and International Relations, University of Macerata, Macerata, Italy

4Department of Cyber Security and Software, Central Ukrainian National Technical University, Kropyvnytskyi, Ukraine

5Department of Cyber Security and Information Technology, University of Customs and Finance, Dnipro, Ukraine

16.1 Introduction

In the era of ubiquitous computing and the Internet of Things (IoT), securing access to devices and protecting sensitive information has become a paramount concern [1, 2]. Traditional authentication methods, such as passwords and personal identification numbers (PINs), often fall short in providing the necessary level of security and user convenience required by the diverse range of IoT applications. Biometric authentication, which relies on the unique physiological or behavioral characteristics of individuals, has emerged as a promising solution to address these challenges [3].

The integration of biometric authentication techniques into tiny machine learning (TinyML) systems has gained significant attention in recent years [4]. TinyML refers to the deployment of machine learning algorithms on resource‐constrained devices, such as microcontrollers and low‐power IoT nodes [5, 6]. By combining the power of biometric authentication with the efficiency and scalability of TinyML, it becomes possible to develop secure and user‐friendly authentication mechanisms for a wide range of IoT applications.

This chapter explores the opportunities and challenges associated with the integration of biometric authentication techniques into TinyML systems. It provides a comprehensive overview of various biometric modalities, including fingerprint recognition, facial recognition, iris scanning, voice recognition, gait recognition, and ear recognition [7]. The chapter delves into the fundamental concepts, algorithms, and performance metrics associated with each modality, highlighting their strengths and limitations in the context of resource‐constrained environments.

One of the key challenges addressed in this chapter is the adaptation of biometric techniques for TinyML systems. The limited computational power, memory capacity, and energy budget of microcontrollers pose significant constraints on the implementation of biometric algorithms. The chapter discusses various strategies for developing resource‐efficient biometric algorithms, such as lightweight feature extraction, template compression, efficient matching, and hardware acceleration. It also explores the hardware considerations for integrating biometric sensors into IoT devices, focusing on factors such as sensor selection, form factor, power consumption, and interface requirements.

The chapter presents a comparative analysis of different biometric authentication methods, evaluating their performance based on metrics such as accuracy, efficiency, and user acceptance. The analysis provides valuable insights into the trade‐offs and suitability of each modality for specific TinyML applications. It also highlights the potential of multimodal biometric authentication, where multiple biometric traits are combined to enhance the overall security and reliability of the system.

Furthermore, the chapter discusses the privacy and ethical considerations associated with the deployment of biometric authentication in IoT devices. It emphasizes the importance of establishing clear privacy policies, implementing robust data protection measures, and adhering to relevant regulations and standards. The chapter also explores future research directions in the field of biometric authentication for TinyML systems, including the development of novel biometric modalities, optimization techniques for energy efficiency and real‐time performance, and the integration of biometric authentication with other security mechanisms.

The key points covered in this chapter are

  • Overview of biometric authentication techniques and their relevance to TinyML systems
  • Comparative analysis of different biometric modalities, including fingerprint, facial, iris, voice, gait, and ear recognition
  • Adaptation of biometric techniques for resource‐constrained environments, focusing on resource‐efficient algorithms and hardware considerations
  • Future research directions and opportunities in the field of biometric authentication for TinyML systems

The chapter is organized as follows: Section 16.2 presents the related work. Section 16.3 provides an overview of various biometric authentication techniques, discussing their fundamental concepts, algorithms, and performance metrics. Section 16.4 presents a comparative analysis of these techniques, evaluating their strengths and limitations in the context of TinyML systems. Section 16.5 focuses on the adaptation of biometric techniques for resource‐constrained environments, exploring resource‐efficient algorithms and hardware considerations. Finally, Sections 16.6 and 16.7 conclude the chapter by summarizing the key insights and emphasizing the potential of biometric authentication in enhancing the security and user experience of TinyML systems.

16.2 Related Work

The integration of biometric authentication techniques into TinyML systems has garnered significant attention from the research community in recent years. This section provides an overview of the relevant literature, highlighting the key contributions and advancements in this field.

Agarwal and Joshi [8] proposed a secure and effective self‐error‐correctable physical unclonable function (PUF) for tiny IoT nodes. They employed systematic Golay code and decoding algorithms to improve the reliability of PUF‐based authentication in IoT applications. Using an efficient error correction mechanism, their hardware implementation on an field‐programmable gate array (FPGA) board demonstrated good performance with 45% uniqueness and 97% reliability.

Awad et al. [9] conducted a comprehensive review of artificial intelligence (AI)‐powered biometrics for IoT security. They analyzed the interdependencies between AI, biometrics, and IoT domains, covering the applications of AI and biometrics in the context of IoT. The authors highlighted the current challenges and future research directions for the deployment of intelligent biometrics in various IoT application domains.

Coelho et al. [10] presented a security management approach for authentication that combines two convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for the biometric identification of users. Their approach relies on federated learning (FL) to support data management and privacy by training decentralized models collaboratively without effective data exchange. The authors combined photoplethysmography (PPG) and electrocardiogram signals to improve identification accuracy and establish multimodal authentication.

Cremonezi et al. [11] provided a comprehensive state‐of‐the‐art review of identity management (IdM) systems, presenting the fundamental concepts and challenges when developing an IdM for IoT applications. They explored existing works that propose solutions to address at least one component of IdMs in response to the current challenges, including the scalability of identity provisioning, authentication for IoT devices, and concerns regarding the performance and management of the authorization processes.

Ding et al. [12] introduced a fuzzy‐based temporal convolutional autoencoder (FTCAE) framework for gait recognition from inertial gait time series. They incorporated an interval type‐2 fuzzy set (IT2FS) dense layer to handle uncertainties, imprecision, and noise of feature maps, enabling the learning of curious representations in fuzzy latent space. Their experimentation on public gait sensory datasets validated the efficiency of the proposed FTCAE with accuracies of 98.48% and 95.11% for authentication and identification, respectively.

Galasso et al. [13] focused on classifying subjects' physical activity levels using kinematic features provided by wearable wireless inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensors. They employed the neighborhood component analysis (NCA) algorithm to process the statistical feature space and select the most significant ones. Their approach resulted in a significant increase in accuracy for various classifiers, with an improvement of approximately 20%.

Kamruzzaman and Alruwaili [14] proposed a new methodology named optimizing computer vision with AI‐enabled technology (OCV‐AI) for solving image classification, object classification, and facial recognition problems in 6G wireless networks. They introduced deep learning 6G proposed frameworks (Dl‐6G) to recognize pattern recognition and intelligent management systems and provide a driven methodology planned to be provisioned automatically.

Khalid et al. [15] summarized the state‐of‐the‐art approaches for preserving privacy in AI‐based healthcare applications. They elaborated on prominent privacy‐preserving techniques such as FL and hybrid techniques, along with potential privacy attacks, security challenges, and future directions.

Oliveira et al. [4] comprehensively reviewed the emerging concept of the Internet of Intelligent Things (IoIT), adopting an integrated perspective centered on the areas of embedded systems, edge computing, and machine learning. They performed an extensive state‐of‐the‐art survey to identify recent works that have implemented TinyML models on different off‐the‐shelf embedded devices, analyzing the development of practical solutions and discussing recent research trends and future perspectives.

Praveen Kumar and Priyanka [16] provided a comprehensive overview of the security issues related to various hardware‐level attacks, memory attacks, hardware Trojans, and their countermeasures in different domains. They investigated the use of primitive hardware techniques, such as physically unclonable functions (PUFs), to generate unique keys for devices by preventing unauthorized access to the hardware during authentication for different domains.

Sodhro et al. [17] conducted a survey on intelligent authentication for securing IoT‐5G devices deployed in the healthcare domain. They reviewed IoT‐5G device authentication, radio‐frequency fingerprinting, and mutual authentication and envisioned the use of AI to integrate the attributes of the physical layer and 5G networks to empower intelligent healthcare devices.

Wan et al. [18] proposed a novel approach for biometric authentication using PPG signals and deep learning techniques. They designed and trained a multiscale feature fusion deep learning (MFFD) model that takes the relevant features extracted from PPG signals as input and learns to differentiate between individuals based on their unique PPG patterns. Their evaluation demonstrated the effectiveness of the PPG‐based biometric authentication system, achieving high accuracy while addressing key security concerns.

These studies collectively contribute to the growing body of knowledge on biometric authentication techniques for TinyML systems. They encompass various aspects, including the development of resource‐efficient algorithms, the integration of AI and deep learning techniques, the exploration of novel biometric modalities, and the consideration of privacy and security challenges. The insights gained from these works provide a solid foundation for further research and development in this field, paving the way for the widespread adoption of biometric authentication in IoT and TinyML applications.

Despite the significant advancements in biometric authentication techniques for TinyML systems, there is still a need for a comprehensive and systematic approach that addresses the unique challenges posed by resource‐constrained environments. Our work aims to fill this gap by providing a holistic framework that encompasses the adaptation of biometric techniques, the development of resource‐efficient algorithms, and the consideration of privacy and security aspects, enabling the effective deployment of biometric authentication in a wide range of TinyML applications.

16.3 Overview of Biometric Authentication Techniques

Biometric authentication has emerged as a robust and reliable means of verifying user identity in various domains, including access control, financial transactions, and personal device security [19, 20]. This chapter provides a comprehensive overview of the most prevalent biometric modalities, focusing on their fundamental principles, algorithmic foundations, and suitability for integration into TinyML systems. By examining the strengths and limitations of each technique, we aim to guide researchers and practitioners in selecting the most appropriate biometric solution for their specific TinyML application.

16.3.1 Fingerprint Recognition

Fingerprint recognition stands as one of the most widely adopted biometric authentication techniques, owing to its long‐standing use in forensic investigations and its high accuracy in identifying individuals [3, 21]. The unique patterns of ridges and valleys on the surface of a finger, formed during embryonic development, provide a distinctive and permanent signature that can be captured and analyzed for authentication purposes [21].

The flowchart in Figure 16.1 delineates the comprehensive process of fingerprint recognition, highlighting each critical stage from acquisition to matching. Initially, a high‐resolution fingerprint image is obtained through dedicated sensors, followed by preprocessing techniques to enhance image quality. Subsequently, feature extraction algorithms identify unique characteristics such as minutiae points and additional features like ridge orientation and texture descriptors. The matching phase involves comparing the query template with stored database templates using sophisticated algorithms. This process is underscored by the inherent properties of fingerprints, including their unique patterns, permanence, and high reliability in identification.

At the core of fingerprint recognition lie two fundamental concepts: feature extraction and matching [22]. The first step involves acquiring a high‐resolution image of the fingerprint using a dedicated sensor, such as an optical, capacitive, or ultrasonic scanner [9, 17]. Preprocessing techniques, including image enhancement, segmentation, and normalization, are then applied to improve the quality and consistency of the captured image.

Feature extraction algorithms subsequently analyze the preprocessed image to identify and encode the discriminative characteristics of the fingerprint. The most common features employed in fingerprint recognition are minutiae points, which represent the local discontinuities in the ridge patterns, such as ridge endings and bifurcations [22]. Minutiae‐based methods, such as the widely used crossing number (CN) algorithm, detect and map these points, recording their spatial coordinates and orientation [9, 21].

In addition to minutiae, other feature sets, such as ridge orientation maps, frequency maps, and texture descriptors, can be extracted to complement the minutiae‐based representation [3, 17]. These additional features capture the global and local structural properties of the fingerprint, enhancing the discriminative power of the biometric template.

Once the features are extracted, the matching process compares the query fingerprint template with the enrolled templates stored in a database. Matching algorithms, such as the minutia cylinder code (MCC) and the iterative closest point (ICP) algorithm, assess the similarity between two templates by aligning their feature sets and computing a matching score. The comparison can be performed in a one‐to‐one (verification) or one‐to‐many (identification) manner, depending on the application requirements.

Despite its widespread adoption and proven accuracy, fingerprint recognition faces challenges when applied to TinyML systems. The limited computational resources and memory constraints of microcontrollers necessitate the development of lightweight and efficient algorithms for feature extraction and matching. Furthermore, the form factor and power consumption of fingerprint sensors must be optimized to ensure seamless integration into IoT devices.

Ongoing research efforts in fingerprint recognition for TinyML focus on developing compact and energy‐efficient sensing technologies, such as thin‐film transistor (TFT) and microelectromechanical system (MEMS) sensors [3, 21]. Additionally, researchers are exploring the use of deep learning techniques, such as CNNs, to enhance the robustness and accuracy of fingerprint recognition algorithms in resource‐constrained environments.

The flowchart in Figure 16.2 illustrates the challenges and research directions in fingerprint recognition for TinyML systems. It identifies the primary challenges, such as limited computational resources, the need for lightweight algorithms, and sensor optimization. Research directions focus on developing compact sensors, optimizing algorithms, applying deep learning techniques, and ensuring integration with IoT devices. These efforts aim to overcome TinyML system limitations and enhance performance in resource‐constrained applications.

As the demand for secure and convenient authentication in IoT devices continues to grow, fingerprint recognition remains a promising biometric modality for TinyML systems. By addressing the challenges of resource efficiency and sensor miniaturization, researchers can unlock the full potential of fingerprint‐based authentication in a wide range of TinyML applications, from smart homes and wearables to industrial IoT and beyond.

16.3.2 Facial Recognition

Facial recognition has gained significant attention as a biometric authentication technique due to its non‐intrusive nature and the ubiquity of cameras in modern devices [9, 14]. Leveraging the unique features and geometry of an individual's face, this modality offers a natural and intuitive means of verifying identity in various applications, including access control, surveillance, and user authentication on mobile devices [23, 24].

The process of facial recognition involves several key stages: face detection, preprocessing, feature extraction, and matching [3, 25]. Face detection algorithms, such as the Viola–Jones framework, and deep learning‐based methods, like Single Shot MultiBox Detector (SSD) and You Only Look Once (YOLO), localize and isolate the facial region from the input image or video frame. These algorithms exploit the distinctive characteristics of facial features, such as eyes, nose, and mouth, to rapidly identify faces in real time [3, 25].

Once the facial region is detected, preprocessing techniques are applied to normalize the image and mitigate the impact of variations in illumination, pose, and expression. Common preprocessing steps include face alignment, which involves rotating and scaling the face to a canonical pose, and illumination normalization, which compensates for uneven lighting conditions using techniques like histogram equalization and homomorphic filtering.

Feature extraction is a critical step in facial recognition, as it aims to capture the discriminative information that distinguishes one individual from another. Traditional approaches, such as principal component analysis (PCA) and linear discriminant analysis (LDA), project the high‐dimensional facial data onto a lower‐dimensional subspace, retaining the most salient features. These methods, often referred to as holistic or appearance‐based techniques, treat the entire face as a single entity and learn a compact representation of facial variations [3, 25].

In recent years, deep learning techniques have revolutionized facial recognition by enabling the learning of hierarchical and abstract features directly from raw pixel data. CNNs, such as DeepFace, FaceNet, and ArcFace, have achieved remarkable performance in face verification and identification tasks [26–28]. These networks employ a series of convolutional and pooling layers to extract local and global facial features, followed by fully connected layers that learn a compact face embedding [3, 25].

The derived facial features, whether obtained through traditional methods or deep learning, are then compared during the matching stage to determine the identity of an individual [29, 30]. Matching algorithms compute the similarity between the query face and the enrolled face templates stored in a database. Common similarity measures include Euclidean distance, cosine similarity, and learned similarity metrics optimized by the deep learning models.

The flowchart in Figure 16.3 illustrates the key stages and methodologies in the facial recognition process. It begins with face detection using algorithms like Viola–Jones, SSD, and YOLO, followed by preprocessing to normalize the image and adjust for illumination and pose variations. Feature extraction employs both traditional methods like PCA and LDA and modern CNN‐based approaches, including DeepFace, FaceNet, and ArcFace. The final stage, matching, compares the extracted features with database templates using similarity measures such as Euclidean distance and cosine similarity. This structured approach highlights the integration of advanced techniques to enhance the accuracy and reliability of facial recognition systems.

Facial recognition systems face several challenges, particularly when deployed on resource‐constrained TinyML platforms. The high dimensionality of facial data and the complexity of deep learning models pose significant computational and memory requirements. To address these challenges, researchers have explored techniques such as model compression, quantization, and pruning to reduce the size and computational cost of facial recognition models without compromising accuracy.

Another critical aspect of facial recognition in TinyML is the acquisition of high‐quality face images under varying environmental conditions. Low‐resolution cameras, limited processing power, and constrained energy budgets of IoT devices necessitate the development of efficient face detection and preprocessing algorithms that can operate in real time with minimal overhead.

Privacy concerns surrounding the collection and use of facial data have also spurred research into privacy‐preserving facial recognition techniques. Approaches such as FL, homomorphic encryption, and differential privacy enable the training and deployment of facial recognition models without the need for centralized storage of sensitive biometric data.

16.3.3 Iris Scanning

Iris scanning has emerged as a highly accurate and reliable biometric authentication technique, leveraging the intricate patterns of the human iris for identity verification [3]. The iris, the colorful ring surrounding the pupil, contains a complex arrangement of features, including furrows, ridges, and crypts, which remain stable throughout an individual's lifetime [7, 31]. These unique characteristics, along with the iris's protected location behind the cornea, make it an ideal candidate for biometric authentication in various domains, including high‐security access control and border control systems.

The process of iris recognition begins with image acquisition, where a specialized camera captures a high‐resolution image of the eye under near‐infrared (NIR) illumination. NIR light is preferred due to its ability to penetrate the surface of the iris and reveal the underlying texture details, while minimizing reflections and artifacts caused by ambient light [32, 33].

Preprocessing techniques are then applied to the captured image to isolate the iris region from surrounding structures, such as the pupil, sclera, and eyelids [32, 34]. This segmentation step typically involves a combination of edge detection, Hough transform, and active contour models to precisely localize the iris boundaries. Once segmented, the iris region undergoes normalization, which unwraps the circular iris into a rectangular block of fixed dimensions, accounting for variations in pupil size and image orientation.

Feature extraction is a crucial step in iris recognition, aiming to capture the discriminative information within the normalized iris texture. The most widely adopted approach is Daugman's algorithm, which applies 2D Gabor wavelets to the iris image to extract a binary feature vector known as the IrisCode. The Gabor wavelets, with their ability to capture both spatial and frequency information, effectively encode the local and global iris patterns into a compact representation [29, 35].

Other feature extraction techniques have also been explored, including the use of discrete cosine transform (DCT), wavelet packets, and deep learning‐based methods. These approaches aim to capture complementary iris features and enhance the discriminative power of the extracted representation.

During the matching stage, the extracted iris features are compared against a database of enrolled iris templates to determine the identity of an individual. The comparison is typically performed using the Hamming distance, which measures the dissimilarity between two binary IrisCodes. A decision threshold is applied to the Hamming distance to classify the comparison as a match or a non‐match.

Figure 16.4 illustrates the process of iris recognition, highlighting the sequential stages from image acquisition to matching. The process begins with capturing a high‐resolution image of the eye under NIR illumination. Preprocessing techniques then isolate the iris, segment the image, and normalize it. Feature extraction is performed using methods such as Daugman's algorithm and other techniques, followed by the matching stage, which compares the extracted features with database templates using similarity measures like the Hamming distance.

Deploying iris recognition on TinyML platforms presents several challenges due to the resource constraints of microcontrollers. The high‐resolution imaging requirements and the computational complexity of iris segmentation and feature extraction algorithms demand efficient implementations that can operate within the limited memory and processing power of TinyML devices.

Researchers have explored various techniques to optimize iris recognition for resource‐constrained environments. These include the use of lightweight segmentation algorithms, such as the integro‐differential operator and the Hough transform, which reduce the computational burden while maintaining accurate iris localization. Feature extraction methods based on compressed sensing and sparse representations have also been investigated to minimize the storage and processing requirements of iris templates.

Figure 16.5 outlines the properties, challenges, and research directions for iris recognition, particularly in the context of TinyML platforms. It underscores the high accuracy and reliability of iris patterns, their security advantages, and key applications. The challenges include limited resources and computational complexity, while research directions focus on algorithm optimization, compact sensors, and robust preprocessing techniques to handle varying conditions.

In addition to computational efficiency, the integration of iris scanning into TinyML systems must address the challenges of image acquisition in uncontrolled environments. The development of compact and low‐power NIR cameras, along with robust preprocessing algorithms that can handle variations in lighting, distance, and user cooperation, is crucial for the practical deployment of iris recognition in IoT devices.

16.3.4 Other Emerging Biometric Modalities

While fingerprint recognition, facial recognition, and iris scanning have established themselves as the most widely adopted biometric authentication techniques, researchers continue to explore novel and emerging modalities to address the limitations of traditional approaches and cater to the diverse requirements of TinyML applications. This subsection delves into three promising biometric modalities: voice recognition, gait recognition, and ear recognition, discussing their principles, advantages, and challenges in the context of TinyML systems.

16.3.4.1 Voice Recognition

Voice recognition, also known as speaker recognition, leverages the unique acoustic characteristics of an individual's voice for biometric authentication [36]. The human voice contains a wealth of information, including the fundamental frequency, pitch, and timbre, which are determined by the physical structure of the vocal tract and learned speaking habits. Voice recognition systems aim to capture and analyze these distinctive features to verify or identify speakers.

The process of voice recognition typically involves two main stages: feature extraction and matching [3, 37]. During feature extraction, the speech signal is segmented into short frames, and various acoustic features are computed from each frame. Common feature extraction techniques include Mel‐frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs), linear predictive coding (LPC), and perceptual linear prediction (PLP). These features capture the spectral and temporal characteristics of the speech signal, providing a compact representation of the speaker's voice.
