19
Benchmarking TinyML Encrypted Federated Learning with Secret Sharing in Medical Computer Vision

Ruduan B. F. Plug1, Putu H. P. Jati1, Samson Y. Amare1, and Mirjam van Reisen1,2

1Leiden University Medical Center, Leiden University, Leiden, Netherlands

2Tilburg School of Humanities and Digital Sciences, Tilburg University, Tilburg, Netherlands

19.1 Introduction

Federated learning (FL) allows us to train models over distributed data in an efficient and privacy‐preserving manner [1]. This is done by iterative optimization at the data source and sharing the gradients from each optimization step to collaboratively build a global model. This provides privacy by design, which is important in fields such as health care [2] where this is a basic requisite to perform analytics. However, the federated learning process requires a high degree of trust between participating parties, as a malicious participant may be able to reconstruct data from other parties by collecting gradients, the difference between their own model weights and the newly broadcast global model weights, which is also known as the gradient reconstruction attack vector [3, 4].

Recent studies have demonstrated this vulnerability and have shown that sensitive patient information can be leaked from gradients [5, 6], allowing complete reconstruction of original data in some cases. To prevent this from happening, we can incorporate security mechanisms within the federated learning process, such as encrypted federated averaging and splitting gradients in secret shares to prevent information leakage toward a single malicious party [7].

These measures are, however, not without drawbacks, as both encryption and secret sharing incur additional computational overhead on both clients and the aggregator. In this chapter, we investigate the exact impact of these measures on the performance on the federated learning process using medical computer vision (CV) as the use case. We conduct an ablation study using the ResNet18 model pretrained on ImageNet‐1K [8], which we fine‐tune for binary classification of chest X‐ray images from the ChestMNIST dataset [9]. Our approach uses homomorphic encryption on gradients at the client level and decrypts only after aggregation has completed [7]. Secret sharing distributes partial decryption keys from each client to the aggregator, so that only with all participants, consent the total gradient can be decrypted. The ablation is performed by measuring model performance and computational time with these security measures enabled or disabled, while both versions use the exact same federated learning setup otherwise.

In our study, we measure the difference in model performance by evaluating precision, recal, and score directly between the models. For computational performance, we measure the total training time, time spent on gradient descent (graphics processing unit [GPU]‐bound), time spent on encryption overhead (central processing unit [CPU]‐bound, secure only), and the distribution of these timings across all training runs for each benchmark. These benchmarks are run for clients to additionally measure the model performance and overhead for federated learning setups of varying sizes.

19.2 Related Work

The federated learning method introduced by McMahan et al. [1] is one of the most important privacy‐preserving machine learning methods. Federated learning has been well‐researched with articles covering the main challenges and opportunities [10, 11]. The main principle of federated learning is to maintain data locality; however, this does not guarantee privacy and security. Hitaj et al. demonstrated an attack where an adversarial client could train a generative model to infer other clients' data in a collaborative learning setting [3]. Similarly, Zhu et al. have shown that gradients shared during federated learning can be inversely used to reconstruct training images, also known as the deep leakage from gradients attack vector [4].

Bonawitz et al. proposed secure aggregation, where client updates are encrypted using homomorphic encryption such that the server only recovers the aggregated sum of updates, but not any individual update [12]. This paper is highly influential for this chapter. It ensures that individual gradients remain confidential as long as a threshold amount of clients do not collude. Extensions and improvements of secure aggregation continue to be explored, including methods to handle user drop‐outs and verifiability [6, 13, 14] (i.e., using group signatures or verifiable secret sharing). Phong et al. explored additive homomorphic encryption in federated averaging [15]. However, applying homomorphic encryption directly on ciphertexts proved to be orders of magnitude slower and produce much larger message sizes than standard federated averaging. Recent works like BatchCrypt aim to reduce this overhead by quantizing and batching gradients before encryption, achieving more efficient homomorphic operations [16]. The addition of key‐based secret sharing in secure distributed machine learning as proposed by Plug. et al. may reduce computational overhead when compared to using full ciphertext to provide security during federated averaging [7].

Implementations of secure multi‐party computation such as SecureML [17] and SecureNN [18] allow a small number of parties to jointly compute an arbitrary algorithm without revealing their inputs. This provides stronger security guarantees than federated learning but has significant overhead. Hybrid approaches with less overhead have been proposed [19], for instance, using threshold secret sharing so that only an aggregate result is reconstructed [13]. These approaches can achieve privacy similar to secure aggregation.

There is extensive literature analyzing the tradeoff between privacy guarantees and model performance or system efficiency in FL [11, 20]. Adding differential privacy noise to gradients can protect against inference attacks at the cost of reduced accuracy [21]. Cryptography‐based methods do not cause reductions in accuracy but can dramatically slow down training and may not scale to large models or many clients without specific optimizations [15, 16]. Our work contributes to this area by quantitatively benchmarking these overheads in a realistic medical imaging scenario. Examples of prior performance evaluations are studies such as Wagh et al. [18] on the much similar multi‐party computation, as well as others for federated learning [15, 22]) have identified security and performance challenges.

19.3 Methodology

The machine learning architecture that we have implemented for this experiment uses a standard client–server federated learning setup [1]. We have modified the federated learning loop by adding gradient encryption and secret sharing in the process, which can be turned on or off during initialization of the benchmark. We will evaluate these additions with ablation. In this section, we describe in detail each of the components of our architecture.

19.3.1 MedMNIST Dataset

For our benchmark, we use the standardized version of the ChestX‐ray8 dataset [9] from the MedMNIST benchmark repository [23]. The dataset consists of 112,120 chest X‐ray images downsampled to a resolution of 28  28 pixels and labeled for 14 common thoracic symptoms and conditions from infectious and chronic conditions. The dataset consists of 60,412 healthy samples and 51,708 samples with one of the included pathologies. Refer to Table 19.1 for the full overview of the data.

Note that the pathologies have a very skewed distribution, and the most common label comprises 12.6% of the data, while the least common one accounts for only 0.2% of the total data set. For our benchmark, we converted the dataset from a multi‐label disease classification problem into a binary disease detection task by converting one‐hot encoding with a row‐wise OR operation. Even when only considering binary classification, we still need to account for the uneven nature of the underlying distribution, as this will have a significant effect on our final performance if we do not take measures to prevent over‐ and underfitting.

For our benchmark, we focus our classification task on distinguishing X‐ray images that show no pathology compared to those that show at least one pathology present. This simplified task mirrors typical clinical workflows, where initial screenings prioritize identifying abnormal cases for further diagnosis or use of more specialized models [24, 25].

To increase generalization and reduce the effect of skewed label distribution, we apply data augmentation techniques to improve generalization. For augmentation, we use random rotations, horizontal mirroring, affine transformations, and label smoothing (smoothing ground truth labels with a factor to prevent overconfidence [22]). Another technique we use is mixup augmentation [26], in which we mix pairs of training images and labels at set ratios to boost generalization capability of small CV models.

19.3.2 ResNet18 Model Architecture

To perform image classification on ChestX‐ray8, we use a ResNet18 convolutional neural network [8]. ResNet18 is a lightweight version of a deep residual network with 18 layers, which can be fine‐tuned after pretraining. We initialize ResNet18 with pretrained weights from ImageNet [27], leveraging transfer learning to improve convergence on the medical imaging data with minimal training. The final fully connected layer of the ResNet18 model is replaced and fine‐tuned during training to produce a single output for binary classification. The original article has used ResNet50 to perform multi‐label classification [9]; however, as we are only interested in performing binary classification on downsampled images, we opted for the smaller and more memory‐efficient ResNet18 model.

To address the inherent class label imbalance in the ChestMNIST dataset, which will affect our binary classification task, we use a modified loss function to fine‐tune the ResNet18 model. We train with the focal loss function [28] instead of a standard binary cross‐entropy. Focal loss is defined as

(19.1)

where is the predicted probability for the true class. We set focusing parameter (starting with ) so that the loss down‐weights well‐classified examples and puts more emphasis on hard, misclassified examples [28]. We also use a balancing factor (hyper‐parameter optimized on validation data) to reduce the effect of upstream class imbalance due to us combining labels. This will reward hard‐to‐classify examples while making easy classifications less rewarding. Focal loss helps the model learn from the few difficult positive instances that resulted from rare source labels. The model is optimized using the Adam optimizer [29] with a fixed learning rate, which we selected through preliminary experiments.

To further speed up training, we implemented automatic mixed precision (AMP) for the training loop [30] to accelerate training and reduce memory usage by using floating point precision of 16 bits (rather than 32‐bit precision) on convolutions. This has no significant effect on accuracy down the line when applied on deep learning tasks [30] such as the CV classification task we are training our model on.

19.3.3 Federated Learning Architecture

To train our global and client‐side ResNet18 models, we follow a synchronous client–server process with iterative rounds of training and aggregation [1] as described by McMahan et al. In our setup, there is one aggregator and client nodes. From a high‐level perspective, each training round consists of the following steps:

  1. Weight Distribution: The global ResNet18 model with weights is first initialized at by the aggregator. Hyperparameters such as are globally shared. The initialization state is shared to initialize all local federated models with an identical state. If , then for each new round , the aggregator shares the current model weights .
  2. Local Training: Each local model receives and trains on its local dataset for one iteration. Local models can be trained with varying batch sizes according to their memory and performance profile. Each client computes the gradient of the loss with respect to global weights on its local data to get . Let denote the gradient computed by client during round such that .

  3. Gradient Sharing: This step differs from whether we apply encryption and secret sharing or not.

    In the non‐secure version, each local model client serializes and directly transmits the gradient to the aggregation server, which then performs federated averaging on these gradients to update the global model. This process is described in more detail in the next step.

    In the secure version, each gradient is encrypted using additive homomorphic encryption. Through the property of homomorphic encryption, the encrypted gradients from different client models can be added together directly in their encrypted form. To allow the aggregator to decrypt the final gradient, each client also uses Shamir's secret sharing to distribute partial shares of the private encryption key to the aggregation server. After the server aggregates all encrypted gradients, it reconstructs the private encryption key from the collected secret shares and can decrypt the final gradient. As a result, the server learns only the aggregated gradient, while individual gradients remain confidential throughout transmission and aggregation.

  4. Weight Aggregation: The aggregator consumes gradients that are shared by clients . Upon receiving all of them, the aggregator computes the (weighted) average gradient as follows:
    (19.2)
    where is the weight given to . Typically, this weight is set as a fraction of the total data size or support compared to the support among all clients. In our case, we use support since we deal with skewed data and are interested in data containing pathologies within our set, such that . This weighted averaging corresponds to federated averaging (FedAvg) with one local epoch [1]. The weighted average gradient is then used to update the global model at the aggregator:
    (19.3)
    where is the learning rate. In our implementation, local model training applies the stochastic Adam optimizer. Consequentially, once we aggregate the optimization iterations that result from this, we do not have to apply this again at the global level and we can suffice with a relatively simple learning rate multiplier.
  5. Model Evaluation: The aggregator evaluates the new global model with weights on a labeled holdout test set. In our case, we measure accuracy, precision, recall, score, and support. If max iterations or any stopping condition has not been met, another training loop begins (Figure 19.1).

After rounds, the aggregator obtains the final model . This model is not necessarily the last obtained model. Each global model during the training loop is evaluated on a held‐out test set to compute performance metrics, and we keep track of the best global model weights, which are saved. The final model is equivalent to these weights.

The above process is identical for the secure and non‐secure settings except for step 3: gradient transmission. The gradient averaging and model updating are mathematically the same in both cases, which means that any differences in the final model performance will be a result from the stochastic properties of training the models, rather than the addition of encryption and secret sharing. Therefore, we expect the secure and non‐secure runs to reach very similar model accuracy, precision, recall, and scores.

19.3.4 Encryption and Secret Sharing

We implement two security measures to secure gradients during transmission and aggregation: encryption and secret sharing. The goal is to ensure that malicious parties cannot read individual gradient updates, while still allowing the aggregation server to obtain the gradients needed to update the model from remote model clients.

Each client encrypts its computed gradient using additive homomorphic encryption. In our case, we use ConcreteML [32], which implements a fast version of fully homomorphic encryption (FHE). We use a relatively simple operation (add) to compile the circuit required for homomorphic encryption (HE)‐based encryption and decryption. Each client first quantizes their gradient vector into integer representations compatible with ConcreteML's encryption scheme. The quantized gradients are then individually encrypted on a compiled add circuit using a generated public key, producing ciphertexts . Since ConcreteML provides FHE, these ciphertexts can be aggregated directly without decrypting them.

The aggregated ciphertext is subsequently decrypted by reconstructing the corresponding private key, distributed among the participants via Shamir's secret sharing. This ensures that the server obtains only the aggregate gradient and cannot recover or infer individual gradients from the ciphertexts. We use the additive HE property that , where is the decryption function, which means we get the combined gradient to update the global model. The overhead introduced by torus‐based fully homomorphic encryption (TFHE)‐based homomorphic encryption primarily depends on the quantization precision and ciphertext size. Since we already use mixed precision to train the ResNet18 model, we only need 16 bits of precision without losing model information.

To enable the server to ultimately decrypt and aggregate the gradients without any single party having full knowledge of the encryption keys, we use a secret sharing scheme for the keys. We adapt Shamir's threshold secret sharing [33] to our encryption key shares. In our implementation, each client splits its symmetric key into shares and distributes their share back to the aggregator. We configured a secret threshold such that the aggregator can not reconstruct the key from fewer than shares.

In our setup, for simplicity, clients provide shares of their key to the aggregator directly. For a full secure multi‐party computation (SMPC) setup of key sharing, this could be done by having each client share its key among a few other clients such that at least out of of them collaborate to reconstruct it. This is conceptually similar to the secure aggregation approach in which each pair of clients shares random data masks (here, the mask is effectively the encryption key) [12]. We chose in our experiments, meaning that all shares are needed to reconstruct the original key. This is intentional because in our situation we require consent from all parties. This is, however, a worst case for computational overhead but maximizes confidentiality since no single share is useful alone. The secret sharing and distribution are done at the beginning of each federated learning iteration.

Both security measures introduce additional computational overhead. First of all, using ConcreteML to encrypt the gradient with FHE at the client side increases the computational time of each training round. Additionally, sharing keys to other parties further increases communication overhead. The communication overhead for key shares is expected to be relatively small, but it is an operation that has to be performed frequently across every client. Finally, the aggregation server has to perform addition over encrypted data and then decrypt it. This also increases the overhead on calculating the next step in the global model, which requires client models to wait before they can continue.

19.3.5 Experimental Setup

In our ablation experiments, we isolate the model performance and runtime impact of the security measures we described in the previous section. In this section, we describe the data partitioning strategy, training setup and parameters, and the metrics we have chosen for the evaluation of our experiment.

To simulate data localization, we partition the training dataset into equal subsets, where is the number of clients for a given federated benchmark. Each subset serves as the local data for one federated model client. We use an independent and identically distributed (IID) partitioning strategy such that the data is shuffled randomly and split evenly into parts. Each client gets approximately images, with class labels following a uniform distribution among the clients due to the simple random sampling used. This makes it such that each client has a similar class distribution approximating the overall dataset.

We use IID partitioning because we want to ensure equal training behavior for a set given both secure and unsecure setups, avoiding bias due to data heterogeneity. In a non‐IID scenario, model performance might be randomly lower than expected due to data heterogeneity [11], which is outside the scope of our ablation study focusing on security. Each client in our experiments is expected to have an equal distribution of normal and abnormal X‐rays. For example, with clients, each client gets approximately 15.7 thousand training images with an expected amount of 8.15 thousand images without pathology and 7.55 thousand images with any pathology. All clients participate in every round (synchronous FL as described), so all available training data will be seen every round during training.

For our experiment, we fix the number of federated learning rounds to 200 with 1 epoch per client per round for all configurations. This was determined to be sufficient for the model to reach a plateau in validation performance in preliminary runs, since we only aim to fine‐tune the ResNet 18 model. During each round, each client runs 1 epoch, meaning one full pass through its local data. To speed up training and make the effect of overhead consistent, we use a fixed batch size of 4096. This results in batches in every epoch for every local model. As the number of clients increases, the amount of batches in every epoch decreases since each local model sees less of the total data individually. We run each benchmark loop on client configurations, with one full benchmark loop on the secure version and one on the non‐secure version, resulting in 20 full federated learning training sessions.

For the Adam optimizer for local model training, we use the default initial learning rate of . For focal loss, we use and as suggested by the original paper [28]. Label smoothing with a factor of 0.1 was applied to soften the target distribution and reduce overfitting. Instead of assigning a probability of 1.0 to the correct class, the smoothed label is set to 0.9 for the true class and the remaining 0.1 is uniformly distributed across the other classes; i.e., for classes, each incorrect class receives a target probability of .

Finally, MixUp was applied with a probability of 0.5 during training, meaning each input had a 50% chance of being augmented. When applied, two random samples and were linearly combined as and , where with . This encourages the model to generalize better by smoothing decision boundaries.

All experiments were run on a dedicated desktop with an Intel 13900K CPU, 64GB 5600MHz CL40 DDR5 RAM, and a NVIDIA RTX4090 GPU on Windows 11 running Python 3.12, CUDA 12.6, and PyTorch 2.6.0. The clients and their dataloaders were simulated as separate processes on this machine to measure per‐client computational time. This also means that there is no networking or communication overhead, as we are not interested in measuring this in our experimental setup.

In our experiment, we measure accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, and receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC AUC) on the held‐out ChestMNIST test set at the end of every federated training round. To measure computational overhead, we record total training runtime, encryption and secret sharing overhead, and gradient computation time. Each metric is also measured on an average per‐iteration and per‐client basis. We present measures as mean with standard deviation sampled from all 200 training iterations for each model. All metrics are evaluated at varying client counts , comparing secure versus non‐secure to give empirical insights into the performance‐security trade‐off and scalability.

19.4 Results

Across all experiments, the secure federated learning approach achieved virtually identical model performance to the non‐secure approach. Table 19.2 provides the key metrics as measured for the final global model in each scenario.

We observed no consistent difference in the model performance across ablation for runs with to clients. Minor differences in this bracket are within the variability expected from one training run to another. For example, with clients, the model after non‐secure training attained an accuracy of 75.34% on the test set, whereas the secure federated learning attained 75.24%. This is a difference of only 0.10 percentage points. Precision and recall were also very close, with the non‐secure version achieving 0.72 precision and 0.76 recall and the secure version 0.7 precision, 0.77 recall both resulting in an score of 0.74. The ROC AUC for both non‐secure and secure models at 5 clients is both at 0.82.

At , we notice that scores become unstable, in some cases secure and in other cases non‐secure achieving higher scores. After investigation, this appears to be an artifact of the way we split the data for our experiment. Since we split the data equally among , each client sees and trains on less data. At high this causes overfitting, which can be identified by the increasing precision at and 10, while recall plummets. The ROC is a better metric in this case, as this is not as significantly affected by the decision threshold boundary of 0.5 on evaluation, which causes the unstable score. ROC AUC shows more consistent scores all across the training process, with an expected drop in performance as increases due to less data being seen by individual trained models.

The main noticeable trend in the data, which is not directly related to our ablation study, is that as the number of clients increases, the model's performance tends to slightly decrease across the board for both non‐secure and secure. For instance, with the model has been evaluated at 77.08% and 77.92% accuracy, respectively, with scores of 0.83 for both cases. At measured accuracy drops to around 69.09% and 69.69% and F1 drops to 0.77. The drop in performance with a greater is expected because each client has fewer data to train on, as we have previously discussed. In our experiments, we kept the number of iterations fixed at 200, while the size of each local data set decreased, which means there is a potential for overfitting when a small data set has been trained on for too many iterations locally. From our investigation, this explains the lower metrics at greater .

In Figure 19.2, we show the ROC curves for each model on binary ChestMNIST classification using ResNet18. Comparing the non‐secure and secure federated learning approaches more in depth, we see that most curves overlap almost completely. For example, with we see almost identical performance with for both non‐secure and secure models. Similar results can be seen across all , with slight variation seen in and due to random effects, which stabilized at . This indicates through our ablation that the encryption and key sharing process does not impact the model's performance.

The second focus of our ablation study is to determine the effect of the security measures we proposed in relation to the computational time. The runtime data that we have collected is presented in Table 19.3 for runtime totals and Table 19.4 for per‐client averages. The data demonstrates a consistent computational overhead with secure federated learning compared to the non‐secure baseline.

For a single‐client scenario, the total runtime increased from 119.19 to 133.43 s when security measures were applied, which is an overhead of 11.09%. As the number of federated clients increases, the total overhead increases reaching up to 25.29% at . We observe a linear relationship between the number of clients and the absolute overhead, with a Pearson correlation between and the absolute overhead. This shows that the total computational overhead of encryption and secret sharing scales linearly with .

To get a better picture, we have also calculated per‐client averages for runtime as shown in Table 19.4. Analysis of these per‐client runtimes shows that with an increase in , we see an overall decrease in runtime per client. This is because each client has to process less data, resulting in a much lower training time per client as indicated by the data: from 92.87 s with down to 34.08 s with . The computational overhead stays surprisingly stable, ranging from 14.80 to 14.92 s. This is explained by the fact that there is no communication overhead in our setup and the encryption method that we use depends on model size, not on data size. Since each client uses ResNet18 with approximately 12 million parameters [8], and we add each together before decrypting, we get a similar average overhead for each .

19.5 Conclusion

In this chapter, we presented benchmarks for secure federated learning using ablation on gradient encryption and secret key sharing. We used a ResNet18 model on the ChestMNIST medical imaging dataset to perform experiments on varying the number of federating clients and measuring the performance across both non‐secure and secure training instances.

Our first key finding is that model performance, which we evaluate using accuracy, precision, recall, F1, and ROC AUC, is equivalent with and without encryption and secret sharing as expected. We have confirmed that FHE using ConcreteML preserves model performance. The ResNet18 models that we have trained achieved an average score of 0.706 across our unsecure training benchmark and 0.708 across our secure benchmarks, with AUC ranging from 0.83 to 0.77 for both across our task of detecting pathologies in chest X‐rays.

Our second key finding is that total training time and latency increased by an average of 11.09–25.29% due to encryption and secret sharing overhead. This averages to an overhead of about 19.46% across all benchmarks. Surprisingly, the overhead scales almost perfectly linear with , as each client adds an average of 14.89 s of overhead for encryption. Since we controlled for communication time by running our simulations locally, we could precisely measure the overhead in the code, which scales directly with model complexity rather than data size.

To conclude, our analysis shows that encryption for federated learning is essentially a tradeoff between performance and security. While the encryption and secret sharing techniques that we implemented do not significantly impact model classification performance, they incur an overhead to the overall and per‐client runtime during model training. The increased runtime depends primarily on the size of the model, meaning that performance degradation is likely less of an issue on very small machine learning models but more of an issue on very large models. More research is required to measure the exact impact of model size to the model training performance of secure federated learning.
